passages.label: Title
passages.text:
DIRECTIVE 2009/24/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 23 April 2009
on the legal protection of computer programs
(Codified version)
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty establishing the European Community and in particular Article 95 thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 251 of the Treaty ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | The content of Council Directive 91/250/EEC of 14 May 1991 on the legal protection of computer programs ( 3 ) has been amended ( 4 ) . In the interests of clarity and rationality the said Directive should be codified.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | The development of computer programs requires the investment of considerable human, technical and financial resources while computer programs can be copied at a fraction of the cost needed to develop them independently.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Computer programs are playing an increasingly important role in a broad range of industries and computer program technology can accordingly be considered as being of fundamental importance for the Community's industrial development.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | Certain differences in the legal protection of computer programs offered by the laws of the Member States have direct and negative effects on the functioning of the internal market as regards computer programs.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | Existing differences having such effects need to be removed and new ones prevented from arising, while differences not adversely affecting the functioning of the internal market to a substantial degree need not be removed or prevented from arising.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | The Community's legal framework on the protection of computer programs can accordingly in the first instance be limited to establishing that Member States should accord protection to computer programs under copyright law as literary works and, further, to establishing who and what should be protected, the exclusive rights on which protected persons should be able to rely in order to authorise or prohibit certain acts and for how long the protection should apply.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | For the purpose of this Directive, the term ‘computer program’ shall include programs in any form, including those which are incorporated into hardware. This term also includes preparatory design work leading to the development of a computer program provided that the nature of the preparatory work is such that a computer program can result from it at a later stage.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | In respect of the criteria to be applied in determining whether or not a computer program is an original work, no tests as to the qualitative or aesthetic merits of the program should be applied.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | The Community is fully committed to the promotion of international standardisation.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | The function of a computer program is to communicate and work together with other components of a computer system and with users and, for this purpose, a logical and, where appropriate, physical interconnection and interaction is required to permit all elements of software and hardware to work with other software and hardware and with users in all the ways in which they are intended to function. The parts of the program which provide for such interconnection and interaction between elements of software and hardware are generally known as ‘interfaces’. This functional interconnection and interaction is generally known as ‘interoperability’; such interoperability can be defined as the ability to exchange information and mutually to use the information which has been exchanged.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | For the avoidance of doubt, it has to be made clear that only the expression of a computer program is protected and that ideas and principles which underlie any element of a program, including those which underlie its interfaces, are not protected by copyright under this Directive. In accordance with this principle of copyright, to the extent that logic, algorithms and programming languages comprise ideas and principles, those ideas and principles are not protected under this Directive. In accordance with the legislation and case-law of the Member States and the international copyright conventions, the expression of those ideas and principles is to be protected by copyright.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | For the purposes of this Directive, the term ‘rental’ means the making available for use, for a limited period of time and for profit-making purposes, of a computer program or a copy thereof. This term does not include public lending, which, accordingly, remains outside the scope of this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | The exclusive rights of the author to prevent the unauthorised reproduction of his work should be subject to a limited exception in the case of a computer program to allow the reproduction technically necessary for the use of that program by the lawful acquirer. This means that the acts of loading and running necessary for the use of a copy of a program which has been lawfully acquired, and the act of correction of its errors, may not be prohibited by contract. In the absence of specific contractual provisions, including when a copy of the program has been sold, any other act necessary for the use of the copy of a program may be performed in accordance with its intended purpose by a lawful acquirer of that copy.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) | A person having a right to use a computer program should not be prevented from performing acts necessary to observe, study or test the functioning of the program, provided that those acts do not infringe the copyright in the program.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) | The unauthorised reproduction, translation, adaptation or transformation of the form of the code in which a copy of a computer program has been made available constitutes an infringement of the exclusive rights of the author. Nevertheless, circumstances may exist when such a reproduction of the code and translation of its form are indispensable to obtain the necessary information to achieve the interoperability of an independently created program with other programs. It has therefore to be considered that, in these limited circumstances only, performance of the acts of reproduction and translation by or on behalf of a person having a right to use a copy of the program is legitimate and compatible with fair practice and must therefore be deemed not to require the authorisation of the rightholder. An objective of this exception is to make it possible to connect all components of a computer system, including those of different manufacturers, so that they can work together. Such an exception to the author's exclusive rights may not be used in a way which prejudices the legitimate interests of the rightholder or which conflicts with a normal exploitation of the program.

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) | Protection of computer programs under copyright laws should be without prejudice to the application, in appropriate cases, of other forms of protection. However, any contractual provisions contrary to the provisions of this Directive laid down in respect of decompilation or to the exceptions provided for by this Directive with regard to the making of a back-up copy or to observation, study or testing of the functioning of a program should be null and void.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) | The provisions of this Directive are without prejudice to the application of the competition rules under Articles 81 and 82 of the Treaty if a dominant supplier refuses to make information available which is necessary for interoperability as defined in this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) | The provisions of this Directive should be without prejudice to specific requirements of Community law already enacted in respect of the publication of interfaces in the telecommunications sector or Council Decisions relating to standardisation in the field of information technology and telecommunication.

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) | This Directive does not affect derogations provided for under national legislation in accordance with the Berne Convention on points not covered by this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 20
passages.text: (20) | This Directive should be without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time-limits for transposition into national law of the Directives set out in Annex I, Part B,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAVE ADOPTED THIS DIRECTIVE:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Object of protection
1. In accordance with the provisions of this Directive, Member States shall protect computer programs, by copyright, as literary works within the meaning of the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works. For the purposes of this Directive, the term ‘computer programs’ shall include their preparatory design material.
2. Protection in accordance with this Directive shall apply to the expression in any form of a computer program. Ideas and principles which underlie any element of a computer program, including those which underlie its interfaces, are not protected by copyright under this Directive.
3. A computer program shall be protected if it is original in the sense that it is the author's own intellectual creation. No other criteria shall be applied to determine its eligibility for protection.
4. The provisions of this Directive shall apply also to programs created before 1 January 1993, without prejudice to any acts concluded and rights acquired before that date.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
Authorship of computer programs
1. The author of a computer program shall be the natural person or group of natural persons who has created the program or, where the legislation of the Member State permits, the legal person designated as the rightholder by that legislation.
Where collective works are recognised by the legislation of a Member State, the person considered by the legislation of the Member State to have created the work shall be deemed to be its author.
2. In respect of a computer program created by a group of natural persons jointly, the exclusive rights shall be owned jointly.
3. Where a computer program is created by an employee in the execution of his duties or following the instructions given by his employer, the employer exclusively shall be entitled to exercise all economic rights in the program so created, unless otherwise provided by contract.

passages.label: Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
Beneficiaries of protection
Protection shall be granted to all natural or legal persons eligible under national copyright legislation as applied to literary works.

passages.label: Article 4
passages.text:
Article 4
Restricted acts
1. Subject to the provisions of Articles 5 and 6, the exclusive rights of the rightholder within the meaning of Article 2 shall include the right to do or to authorise:
(a) | the permanent or temporary reproduction of a computer program by any means and in any form, in part or in whole; in so far as loading, displaying, running, transmission or storage of the computer program necessitate such reproduction, such acts shall be subject to authorisation by the rightholder;
(b) | the translation, adaptation, arrangement and any other alteration of a computer program and the reproduction of the results thereof, without prejudice to the rights of the person who alters the program;
(c) | any form of distribution to the public, including the rental, of the original computer program or of copies thereof.
2. The first sale in the Community of a copy of a program by the rightholder or with his consent shall exhaust the distribution right within the Community of that copy, with the exception of the right to control further rental of the program or a copy thereof.

passages.label: Article 5
passages.text:
Article 5
Exceptions to the restricted acts
1. In the absence of specific contractual provisions, the acts referred to in points (a) and (b) of Article 4(1) shall not require authorisation by the rightholder where they are necessary for the use of the computer program by the lawful acquirer in accordance with its intended purpose, including for error correction.
2. The making of a back-up copy by a person having a right to use the computer program may not be prevented by contract in so far as it is necessary for that use.
3. The person having a right to use a copy of a computer program shall be entitled, without the authorisation of the rightholder, to observe, study or test the functioning of the program in order to determine the ideas and principles which underlie any element of the program if he does so while performing any of the acts of loading, displaying, running, transmitting or storing the program which he is entitled to do.

passages.label: Article 6
passages.text:
Article 6
Decompilation
1. The authorisation of the rightholder shall not be required where reproduction of the code and translation of its form within the meaning of points (a) and (b) of Article 4(1) are indispensable to obtain the information necessary to achieve the interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs, provided that the following conditions are met:
(a) | those acts are performed by the licensee or by another person having a right to use a copy of a program, or on their behalf by a person authorised to do so;
(b) | the information necessary to achieve interoperability has not previously been readily available to the persons referred to in point (a); and
(c) | those acts are confined to the parts of the original program which are necessary in order to achieve interoperability.
2. The provisions of paragraph 1 shall not permit the information obtained through its application:
(a) | to be used for goals other than to achieve the interoperability of the independently created computer program;
(b) | to be given to others, except when necessary for the interoperability of the independently created computer program; or
(c) | to be used for the development, production or marketing of a computer program substantially similar in its expression, or for any other act which infringes copyright.
3. In accordance with the provisions of the Berne Convention for the protection of Literary and Artistic Works, the provisions of this Article may not be interpreted in such a way as to allow its application to be used in a manner which unreasonably prejudices the rightholder's legitimate interests or conflicts with a normal exploitation of the computer program.

passages.label: Article 7
passages.text:
Article 7
Special measures of protection
1. Without prejudice to the provisions of Articles 4, 5 and 6, Member States shall provide, in accordance with their national legislation, appropriate remedies against a person committing any of the following acts:
(a) | any act of putting into circulation a copy of a computer program knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is an infringing copy;
(b) | the possession, for commercial purposes, of a copy of a computer program knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is an infringing copy;
(c) | any act of putting into circulation, or the possession for commercial purposes of, any means the sole intended purpose of which is to facilitate the unauthorised removal or circumvention of any technical device which may have been applied to protect a computer program.
2. Any infringing copy of a computer program shall be liable to seizure in accordance with the legislation of the Member State concerned.
3. Member States may provide for the seizure of any means referred to in point (c) of paragraph 1.

passages.label: Article 8
passages.text:
Article 8
Continued application of other legal provisions
The provisions of this Directive shall be without prejudice to any other legal provisions such as those concerning patent rights, trade-marks, unfair competition, trade secrets, protection of semi-conductor products or the law of contract.
Any contractual provisions contrary to Article 6 or to the exceptions provided for in Article 5(2) and (3) shall be null and void.

passages.label: Article 9
passages.text:
Article 9
Communication
Member States shall communicate to the Commission the provisions of national law adopted in the field governed by this Directive.

passages.label: Article 10
passages.text:
Article 10
Repeal
Directive 91/250/EEC, as amended by the Directive indicated in Annex I, Part A, is repealed, without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time-limits for transposition into national law of the Directives set out in Annex I, Part B.
References to the repealed Directive shall be construed as references to this Directive and shall be read in accordance with the correlation table in Annex II.

passages.label: Article 11
passages.text:
Article 11
Entry into force
This Directive shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .

passages.label: Article 12
passages.text:
Article 12
Addressees
This Directive is addressed to the Member States.

passages.text:

impact_families.title: Mandatory seizure rather than exposure to seizure
impact_families.effect: A copy established as infringing and meeting national seizure conditions could have to be seized where an authority otherwise could leave it unseized.
impact_families.rationale: The reading materially changes an important remedy from availability to compulsory interference with possession.
impact_families.uncertainty: National seizure conditions and contextual interpretation could preserve discretion.

impact_families.title: Transitional safeguard refers to adopted legal instruments rather than completed acts
impact_families.effect: Completed pre-1993 reproduction without acquired rights could lose the express safeguard against the Directive's copyright restrictions.
impact_families.rationale: The changed saving could materially alter temporal exposure to core copyright duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual temporal interpretation and acquired rights may preserve particular completed acts.

impact_families.title: Commercial use replaces commercial possession in the special-remedies provisions
impact_families.effect: Qualifying circumvention tools held as unused commercial stock could fall outside mandatory Article 7(1)(c) remedies.
impact_families.rationale: An independently protected category of conduct would lose the Directive's express remedial guarantee.
impact_families.uncertainty: Commercial use may be construed broadly; national remedies remain unspecified.

impact_families.title: Prior provision may bar decompilation despite information never being readily accessible
impact_families.effect: If interoperability information was previously provided but never readily accessible, otherwise qualifying indispensable code analysis could require permission under Bulgarian while qualifying for the English exception.
impact_families.rationale: The condition determines access to an exception permitting otherwise restricted code reproduction and translation without the rightholder’s authorization.
impact_families.uncertainty: Provision may be interpreted as ready availability; the stringent necessity requirement and remaining safeguards still apply.

impact_families.title: Development replaces running in the protection against contractual prohibition
impact_families.effect: If development receives mandatory protection through interpretation of Article 5(1), a lawful acquirer could disregard a contractual ban on development necessary to use the program.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed recital could change enforceability of restrictions on otherwise controlled development or adaptation, materially changing the acquirer’s permission and the rightholder’s control.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recital concerns technical reproduction; matching operative provisions strongly support harmonization with running.

impact_families.title: Romanian technical-protection rule may omit means that merely assist circumvention
impact_families.effect: A tool solely intended to assist a separate circumvention operation could fall outside the Romanian direct-neutralization limb, removing Article 7’s requirement for appropriate remedies against its circulation.
impact_families.rationale: The distinction changes the scope of mandatory technical-protection remedies. Article 7(3) also links optional seizure to the same class of means.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may support reading neutralization as an operation whose facilitation is covered.

impact_families.title: Decompilation safeguard lacks the unreasonable-prejudice qualification
impact_families.effect: If potential harm suffices, interoperability decompilation satisfying Article 6(1)–(2) could require permission despite reasonable prejudice and no conflict with normal exploitation.
impact_families.rationale: This could withdraw the core permission to reproduce and translate code for interoperability.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Berne reference, legitimate-interests limitation and recital 15 support harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Communication duty limited to main national provisions
impact_families.effect: A Member State could omit an ancillary provision while communicating its main implementing provisions.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns administrative communication. The Directive does not condition copyright protection, remedies or national legislation's validity on that communication.
impact_families.uncertainty: Main provisions may encompass all materially relevant implementing rules.

impact_families.title: Mandatory seizure rather than liability to seizure
impact_families.effect: An infringing copy could require actual seizure under applicable national procedures when availability of seizure alone would satisfy English.
impact_families.rationale: The reading materially changes the seizure remedy and corresponding enforcement duty.
impact_families.uncertainty: National procedural rules and harmonized interpretation may reconcile the formulations.

impact_families.title: Normal-exploitation restriction may be qualified by unjustified prejudice
impact_families.effect: Otherwise qualifying decompilation could proceed without authorisation despite conflicting with normal exploitation, if that interference were considered justified.
impact_families.rationale: This would relax an operative limit on the exception to exclusive reproduction and translation rights under Articles 4 and 6.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 15 and the Berne reference strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Remedies condition may require actual belief rather than grounds for belief
impact_families.effect: A distributor with objective grounds to believe infringement but no actual belief could escape the express personal-remedy trigger.
impact_families.rationale: This materially narrows the mandatory remedy against a defined category of infringing circulation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Grounded belief may be interpreted objectively; other copyright protections remain.

impact_families.title: Employer ownership of economic rights rather than exclusive entitlement to exercise them
impact_families.effect: Absent contrary agreement, employee economic title subject to exclusive employer exercise could satisfy English while conflicting with Spanish’s express allocation of title to the employer.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading determines default ownership of all economic rights, an important proprietary entitlement, even where exploitation control remains equivalent.
impact_families.uncertainty: Exclusive exercise may be interpreted as economic ownership; neither formulation determines moral rights.

impact_families.title: Liability to seizure is expressed as mandatory confiscation
impact_families.effect: An established infringing copy could require confiscation where seizure otherwise need only be available.
impact_families.rationale: Compulsory removal materially changes an important property remedy.
impact_families.uncertainty: National legislation may reconcile application; permanent forfeiture is not established.

impact_families.title: Observation and testing exception tied to performance of a contract
impact_families.effect: If contractual performance is required, an otherwise entitled user acting without a contract could lose permission to study or test the program during lawful operation.
impact_families.rationale: This materially narrows eligibility for an express user permission protected against contrary contractual terms by Article 8.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 14 and Article 8 support broader eligibility; no actual excluded user is established.

impact_families.title: Annex II redirects the former exclusive-rights introduction to Article 5(1)
impact_families.effect: If the Italian mapping prevailed, a legacy reference to former Article 4’s introductory words would point to Article 5(1)’s exception instead of Article 4(1)’s exclusive-rights introduction.
impact_families.rationale: Article 10 gives the mapping legal effect, but no referring provision is supplied to establish its consequence for an entitlement, permission, duty, or remedy.
impact_families.uncertainty: Consequences depend on the referring provision; neighbouring rows and operative articles support harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Polish observation exception links entitlement to the program rather than each act
impact_families.effect: An observation-only contractual restriction could be invalidated during storage outside the licence, while the storage itself remains subject to Article 4.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the observation exception’s contractual reach. Article 4 continues to govern the underlying restricted acts; permission to transmit or reproduce beyond the licence is not established.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 14 supports an act-specific reading; Article 8 operates only within the exception’s interpreted scope.

impact_families.title: Mandatory confiscation rather than liability to seizure
impact_families.effect: An identified infringing copy could have to be confiscated under national law rather than merely remain legally liable to seizure.
impact_families.rationale: The reading materially changes the enforcement obligation and requires deprivation of possession.
impact_families.uncertainty: National conditions may reconcile the formulations; permanent forfeiture is not established.

impact_families.title: Circumvention-means provision omits the sole-purpose limitation
impact_families.effect: A multifunctional means intended partly for unauthorised circumvention could attract mandatory remedies when circulated.
impact_families.rationale: The reading expands substantive remedial exposure and the class potentially covered by Article 7(3).
impact_families.uncertainty: Purpose may be construed restrictively; seizure depends on national measures.

impact_families.title: Back-up copying safeguard uses a temporal limitation instead of a necessity condition
impact_families.effect: A lawful user could defeat a contractual ban on an unnecessary back-up made during the period protected by the temporal reading.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change concerns an ancillary back-up safeguard. Lawful-use eligibility and restrictions on other reproduction, alteration and distribution remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Necessity may still qualify the back-up itself, reconciling the versions.

impact_families.title: Restriction on decompilation information omits the limitation to similarity in expression
impact_families.effect: Otherwise qualifying interoperability work could be prohibited solely because the independently expressed program is functionally similar.
impact_families.rationale: The broader condition would materially narrow the decompilation permission.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 1, recital 11 and the reference to other infringement favour an expression-limited interpretation.

impact_families.title: Romanian transitional protection expressly saves contracts rather than all completed acts
impact_families.effect: A completed pre-1993 non-contractual act generating no acquired right could lack the express saving. The resulting consequences for later restrictions or remedies are not established.
impact_families.rationale: The wording potentially narrows transitional protection, but omission from the saving does not itself establish retrospective application of copyright restrictions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The scope of concluded acts, acquired rights and temporal enforcement remains unresolved.

impact_families.title: Marketing rather than sale as the distribution-right exhaustion trigger
impact_families.effect: If commercialisation includes an authorised rental, subsequent non-rental distribution of that copy could cease to require copyright consent before any sale.
impact_families.rationale: The core exclusive distribution right would end earlier for that copy, while control of subsequent rental remains.
impact_families.uncertainty: Commercialisation may mean sale contextually; exhaustion does not itself confer ownership or override other legal obligations.

impact_families.title: Communication duty limited to main national provisions
impact_families.effect: A subsidiary national provision could be omitted while satisfying the Czech communication duty.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence is narrower administrative notification; no major effect on rights, permissions or remedies is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: Main provisions may be interpreted broadly.

impact_families.title: Output similarity replaces similarity in protected expression
impact_families.effect: A licensee satisfying the remaining conditions could be barred from developing an independently expressed interoperable program with substantially similar output.
impact_families.rationale: This would materially narrow the permission to use decompilation information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Expression-only protection supports a harmonized reading.

impact_families.title: Hungarian circumvention-tool provision lacks an express authorisation limit
impact_families.effect: Circulating a tool intended solely for authorised removal of protection could attract remedies and nationally provided seizure where Articles 4–6 do not independently protect the conduct.
impact_families.rationale: The broader reading materially extends a substantive boundary of mandatory remedies and potential seizure to tools intended exclusively for authorised activity.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may imply an authorisation limit; national law determines available remedies and whether tool seizure is provided.

impact_families.title: Possible mandatory seizure rather than exposure to seizure
impact_families.effect: An infringing copy satisfying national procedural conditions could have to be seized where authorities otherwise could leave the remedy unused.
impact_families.rationale: This materially changes an important property-directed remedy by making its execution compulsory.
impact_families.uncertainty: The national-law qualification could preserve discretion under contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Possible narrower knowledge threshold for remedies against infringing copies
impact_families.effect: A commercial possessor with reason to believe a copy infringes but without actual belief could fall outside the mandatory special remedies.
impact_families.rationale: The threshold materially changes an express remedial entitlement. Preserved exclusive rights and seizure do not fully replace remedies directed against commercial possessors.
impact_families.uncertainty: Objective inference of belief and contextual interpretation could maintain equivalent coverage.

impact_families.title: Different acts protected against contractual prohibition
impact_families.effect: If the recital's enumeration controlled Article 5(1), a contract could prohibit necessary execution of a lawfully acquired program while necessary display remained expressly protected.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed interpretation could remove contractual protection for the central act of running the program.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general necessary-use rationale supports equivalent protection; the differing enumeration appears in a recital.

impact_families.title: Circumvention-tool remedy lacks a shared unauthorised-use qualification
impact_families.effect: Circulating a tool intended solely for authorised circumvention could trigger the obligation to provide appropriate national remedies.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading extends the mandatory remedies regime to conduct outside the unauthorised-purpose restriction.
impact_families.uncertainty: The authority qualifier could govern both branches; Articles 4–6 remain preserved, and remedies are nationally determined.

impact_families.title: Rental is defined by non-profit rather than profit-making purposes
impact_families.effect: After a consented first Community sale, commercial rental could escape the continuing rental control preserved by Article 4(2).
impact_families.rationale: The reversed definition could materially alter an exclusive distribution entitlement surviving exhaustion.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation may reconcile the opposing purpose conditions.

impact_families.title: Preparatory design work may qualify through later use rather than generating a program
impact_families.effect: Original preparatory design expression usable by a later program, but incapable of yielding one, could acquire program-specific copyright protection.
impact_families.rationale: The changed subject-matter boundary could confer Article 4 exclusive rights over otherwise ineligible material.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared development requirement supports harmonization; originality and expression remain necessary.

impact_families.title: Communication duty is limited to main provisions
impact_families.effect: A Member State could omit secondary national provisions while communicating the principal provisions to the Commission.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change narrows an ancillary information duty without altering substantive copyright entitlements or remedies.
impact_families.uncertainty: The text does not define principal provisions; a broad interpretation may reduce omissions.

impact_families.title: Commercial-purpose qualifier may narrow remedies for circulation of protection-removal tools
impact_families.effect: Non-commercial distribution of a sole-purpose unauthorised protection-removal tool could fall outside mandatory special remedies.
impact_families.rationale: The interpretation removes remedial protection for tool circulation even where circulation itself does not reproduce a program.
impact_families.uncertainty: The qualifier may govern only possession.

impact_families.title: Latvian public-use exclusion could extend beyond public lending
impact_families.effect: A time-limited, profit-making supply of a program for public use could fall outside rental protection under the broader Latvian exclusion, although English excludes only public lending.
impact_families.rationale: Applied to an arrangement otherwise constituting rental, the exclusion could remove the rightholder’s core authorization right, including control of further rental after sale.
impact_families.uncertainty: The rental definition and Article 4 strongly support limiting the exclusion to public lending.

impact_families.title: Decompilation condition omits ready availability of interoperability information
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying user could require permission to decompile because interoperability information was technically obtainable but accessible only with substantial difficulty.
impact_families.rationale: The condition controls eligibility for the exception to exclusive code reproduction and translation rights.
impact_families.uncertainty: Availability could mean practical accessibility; the separate indispensability condition also remains applicable.

impact_families.title: Finnish decompilation safeguard omits the unreasonable-prejudice threshold
impact_families.effect: Otherwise qualifying interoperability decompilation could lose its authorization exemption solely because of reasonable prejudice, without normal-exploitation conflict.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed safeguard materially changes access to a core statutory permission.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Berne reference and interoperability purpose may restore the reasonableness threshold.

legislation.title: REGULATION (EU) No 1231/2010 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 24 November 2010 extending Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 to nationals of third countries who are not already covered by these Regulations solely on the ground of their nationality

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
REGULATION (EU) No 1231/2010 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 24 November 2010
extending Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 to nationals of third countries who are not already covered by these Regulations solely on the ground of their nationality

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and in particular Article 79(2)(b) thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the European Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | The European Parliament ( 3 ) , the Council and the European Economic and Social Committee ( 4 ) have called for the better integration of nationals of third countries who are legally resident in the territory of the Member States by giving them a set of uniform rights which match as closely as possible those enjoyed by citizens of the Union.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | The Justice and Home Affairs Council of 1 December 2005 stressed that the Union must ensure fair treatment of third-country nationals residing legally in the territory of the Member States and that a more vigorous integration policy should be geared to granting them rights and obligations comparable to those of citizens of the Union.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Council Regulation (EC) No 859/2003 ( 5 ) extended Regulation (EEC) No 1408/71 and Regulation (EEC) No 574/72 on the coordination of Member States’ statutory social security schemes to the nationals of third countries who were not already covered by those Regulations solely on the ground of their nationality.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | This Regulation respects the fundamental rights and observes the principles recognised, in particular, by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, notably Article 34(2) thereof.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the coordination of social security systems ( 6 ) replaces Regulation (EEC) No 1408/71. Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 September 2009 laying down the procedure for implementing Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 ( 7 ) replaces Regulation (EEC) No 574/72. Regulations (EEC) No 1408/71 and (EEC) No 574/72 are to be repealed with effect from the date of application of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 significantly update and simplify the coordination rules for insured persons as well as social security institutions. For the latter, the updated coordination rules aim to accelerate and facilitate the processing of data on insured persons’ rights to benefits and to reduce the corresponding administrative costs.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | Promoting a high level of social protection and raising the standard of living and the quality of life in the Member States are objectives of the Union.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | In order to avoid a situation where employers and national social security bodies have to manage complex legal and administrative situations concerning only a limited group of persons, it is important to enjoy the full benefits of modernisation and simplification in the field of social security by making use of a single legal coordination instrument combining Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | It is therefore necessary to replace Regulation (EC) No 859/2003 with a legal instrument, the basic aim of which is to substitute Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 for Regulation (EEC) No 1408/71 and Regulation (EEC) No 574/72 respectively.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | The application of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 to nationals of third countries who are not already covered by those Regulations solely on the ground of their nationality must not give them any entitlement to enter, to stay or to reside in a Member State or to have access to its labour market. Accordingly, the application of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 should be without prejudice to the right of the Member States to refuse to grant, to withdraw or to refuse to renew a permit to enter, to stay, to reside or to work in the Member State concerned, in accordance with the law of the Union.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 should, by virtue of this Regulation, be applicable only in so far as the person concerned is already legally resident in the territory of a Member State. Legal residence should therefore be a prerequisite for the application of those Regulations.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 should not apply in a situation which is confined in all respects within a single Member State. This concerns, inter alia, the situation of a third-country national who has links only with a third country and a single Member State.

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | The condition of residing legally in the territory of a Member State should not affect the rights deriving from the application of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 concerning invalidity, old age or survivors’ pensions, on behalf of one or more Member States, for a third-country national who has previously fulfilled the conditions of this present Regulation, or the survivors of such third-country national, insofar as they derive their rights from a worker, when residing in a third country.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) | The continued right to unemployment benefit, as laid down in Article 64 of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004, is subject to the condition of registering as a job-seeker with the employment services of each Member State entered. Those provisions should only therefore apply to a third-country national provided that that individual has the right, where appropriate pursuant to his or her residence permit or long-term resident status, to register as a job-seeker with the employment services of the Member State entered and the right to work there legally.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) | This Regulation should be without prejudice to rights and obligations arising from international agreements with third countries to which the Union is a party and which confer benefits in terms of social security.

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) | Since the objectives of this Regulation cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States on account of the cross-border situations involved and can therefore, by reason of the Union-wide scale of the proposed action, be better achieved at Union level, the Union may adopt measures in accordance with the principles of subsidiarity enshrined in Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union. In accordance with the principle of proportionality, as set out in that Article, this Regulation does not go beyond what is necessary to achieve those objectives.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) | In accordance with Article 3 of Protocol (No 21) on the position of United Kingdom and Ireland in respect of the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice, annexed to the Treaty on European Union and to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Ireland has notified, by letter of 24 October 2007, its wish to take part in the adoption and application of this Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) | In accordance with Articles 1 and 2 of Protocol (No 21) on the position of United Kingdom and Ireland in respect of the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice, annexed to the Treaty on European Union and to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and without prejudice to Article 4 of that Protocol, the United Kingdom is not taking part in the adoption of this Regulation and is not bound by it or subject to its application.

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) | In accordance with Articles 1 and 2 of Protocol (No 22) on the position of Denmark, annexed to the Treaty on European Union and to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Denmark is not taking part in the adoption of this Regulation and is not bound by it or subject to its application,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAVE ADOPTED THIS REGULATION:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 987/2009 shall apply to nationals of third countries who are not already covered by those Regulations solely on the ground of their nationality, as well as to members of their families and to their survivors, provided that they are legally resident in the territory of a Member State and are in a situation which is not confined in all respects within a single Member State.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
Regulation (EC) No 859/2003 shall be repealed between the Member States that are bound by this Regulation.

passages.label: Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
This Regulation shall enter into force on the third day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in Member States in accordance with the Treaties.
Done at Strasbourg, 24 November 2010.
For the European Parliament
The President
J. BUZEK
For the Council
The President
O. CHASTEL
( 1 ) OJ C 151, 17.6.2008, p. 50 .
( 2 ) Position of the European Parliament of 9 July 2008 ( OJ C 294 E, 3.12.2009, p. 259 ), position of the Council at first reading of 26 July 2010 ( OJ C 253 E, 21.9.2010, p. 1 ), and position of the European Parliament of 7 October 2010 (not yet published in the Official Journal).
( 3 ) European Parliament resolution of 27 October 1999 on the European Council meeting in Tampere ( OJ C 154, 5.6.2000, p. 63 ).
( 4 ) EESC opinion of 26 September 1991 on the status of migrant workers from third countries ( OJ C 339, 31.12.1991, p. 82 ).
( 5 ) OJ L 124, 20.5.2003, p. 1 .
( 6 ) OJ L 166, 30.4.2004, p. 1 .
( 7 ) OJ L 284, 30.10.2009, p. 1 .

impact_families.title: Potentially broader repeal of the previous social-security coordination framework
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, a participating State could stop applying Regulation (EC) No 859/2003 to an otherwise covered third-country national’s case involving a non-participating State, removing that coordination route.
impact_families.rationale: Recital 3 identifies the previous Regulation as extending social-security coordination to third-country nationals. Removing that framework from otherwise covered cross-border cases would materially alter its applicability and the corresponding coordination duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Harmonization may preserve the route; the supplied text establishes neither an individual benefit loss nor particular cases affected.

impact_families.title: Pension residence safeguard identifies dependants rather than survivors
impact_families.effect: A survivor with pension rights could fall outside the residence safeguard if the Latvian reference imposed a separate dependency condition that the survivor did not satisfy.
impact_families.rationale: The underlying survivor and dependency definitions are absent. It cannot be established whether these categories differ for the relevant pensions or which entitlement would change.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 1 and the pension context may identify the same beneficiaries despite the different terms.

impact_families.title: Possible additional condition for retaining unemployment benefit
impact_families.effect: If the restrictive reading governed eligibility, an otherwise eligible third-country national with lawful job-seeking and work rights on another basis could be denied continued unemployment benefit, absent an independently protected entitlement.
impact_families.rationale: Recital 14 expressly connects these conditions to continued unemployment benefit. Exclusion would change access to an important financial entitlement, rather than merely the procedure for registering as a job-seeker.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recital may be harmonized with Article 1; no actual claimant or alternative legal basis is established.

impact_families.title: Slovenian repeal wording could extend beyond relations between participating States
impact_families.effect: If Regulation 859/2003 otherwise governs a participating State's relations with a non-participating State, the broader repeal could remove that legal basis in the participating State.
impact_families.rationale: The repeal mechanism is identifiable, but the previous Regulation's operative territorial coverage and transitional protections are absent. The supplied text does not establish a specific resulting loss of coordination rights.
impact_families.uncertainty: Prior coverage requires missing operative provisions; contextual interpretation could also preserve the relational limitation.

impact_families.title: Cross-border eligibility may require every aspect to involve multiple States
impact_families.effect: If every aspect had to involve multiple Member States, an otherwise eligible person with mixed domestic and cross-border circumstances could lose access to both extended coordination Regulations.
impact_families.rationale: The condition controls entry into the coordination regime itself, so the stricter reading could materially restrict core coverage.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 12 and the cross-border coordination purpose strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Repeal may extend beyond relations between participating States
impact_families.effect: A participating State could treat the earlier coordination extension as repealed in a relationship with a non-participating State.
impact_families.rationale: The supplied act establishes the earlier extension’s purpose, but not its participation rules or continuing application in mixed relationships. A resulting loss of coverage cannot be established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The earlier Regulation’s territorial and transitional provisions are absent; contextual harmonization remains plausible.

impact_families.title: Pension safeguard may depend on where rights were acquired
impact_families.effect: If the acquisition-location condition governed, a survivor who acquired pension rights before moving to a third country could lose protection against the Member-State residence prerequisite.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition could materially restrict the protection of an existing pension entitlement after relocation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recital’s protective purpose supports harmonization; separate pension rules may also preserve entitlement.

impact_families.title: Territorial repeal may reach relations with non-participating States
impact_families.effect: A participating State could apply the territorial repeal to a relationship involving a non-participating State.
impact_families.rationale: The earlier Regulation’s participation and transitional rules are absent. The sources therefore do not establish that a particular mixed relationship retains coverage which this reading would remove.
impact_families.uncertainty: Non-participation in the new Regulation does not itself establish coverage under the earlier Regulation.

impact_families.title: Slovenian wording could require permanent residence for coordination coverage
impact_families.effect: An otherwise eligible third-country national with lawful temporary residence and qualifying cross-border circumstances could be denied access to both social-security coordination Regulations.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition governs eligibility for the coordination framework itself. Excluding an otherwise qualifying resident would materially restrict core coverage.
impact_families.uncertainty: A harmonized interpretation could treat permanence as settled residence without requiring permanent immigration status.

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
COMMISSION REGULATION (EU) No 655/2013
of 10 July 2013
laying down common criteria for the justification of claims used in relation to cosmetic products
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on cosmetic products ( 1 ) , and in particular the second subparagraph of Article 20(2) thereof,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | End users as defined in Article 2(1)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 are faced with a wide diversity of claims relating to the function, content and effects of a cosmetic product. As cosmetic products play such a big part in end users’ lives, it is important to ensure that the information conveyed to them through such claims is useful, understandable and reliable, and that it enables them to take informed decisions and to choose the products that best suit their needs and expectations.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | Product claims of cosmetic products serve mainly to inform end users about the characteristics and qualities of the products. Those claims are essential ways of differentiating between products. They also contribute to stimulating innovation and fostering competition.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Common criteria should be laid down at Union level in order to justify the use of a claim made in relation to cosmetic products. The main objective of laying down common criteria is to guarantee a high level of protection for end users, in particular from misleading claims in relation to cosmetic products. A common approach at Union level should also ensure better convergence of actions taken by the Member States’ competent authorities, and prevent distortions in the internal market. Such an approach should also enhance cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection as laid down in Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 October 2004 on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws (the Regulation on consumer protection cooperation) ( 2 ) .

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | Article 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 applies to products that fall under the definition of a cosmetic product in Article 2 of this Regulation. The common criteria only apply when it has been assessed that the product in question is indeed a cosmetic product. It is for the national competent authorities and national courts to decide on a case-by-case basis which regulatory framework applies.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | The common criteria should apply without prejudice to Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2005 concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal market and amending Council Directive 84/450/EEC, Directives 97/7/EC, 98/27/EC and 2002/65/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council (‘Unfair Commercial Practices Directive’) ( 3 ) , to Directive 2006/114/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006 concerning misleading and comparative advertising ( 4 ) , and to other applicable Union legislation.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | A flexible approach should be taken towards communicating the messages to end users so as to take into account the social, linguistic and cultural diversity of the Union and to preserve the innovation and the competitiveness of European industry. Such an approach is consistent with the principles enunciated by the Court of Justice, which has pointed out on several occasions that, in order to determine whether a claim is capable of misleading the consumer, it is necessary to consider the latter’s expectations, taking account of the specific context and circumstances in which the claim is made, including social, cultural and linguistic factors ( 5 ) .

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | Whilst ensuring that the same principles are respected throughout the Union, the common criteria should not aim at defining and specifying the wording that can be used for cosmetic product claims.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | In order to ensure that the common criteria for cosmetic claims apply from the same date as Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, this Regulation should apply from 11 July 2013.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | The measures provided for in this Regulation are in accordance with the opinion of the Standing Committee on Cosmetic Products,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAS ADOPTED THIS REGULATION:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
This Regulation shall apply to claims in the form of texts, names, trademarks, pictures and figurative or other signs that convey explicitly or implicitly product characteristics or functions in the labelling, the making available on the market and advertising of cosmetic products. It shall apply to any claim, irrespective of the medium or type of marketing tool used, the product functions claimed, and the target audience.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
The responsible person referred to in Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 shall ensure that the wording of the claim in relation to cosmetic products is in compliance with the common criteria set out in the Annex and is consistent with the documentation proving the effect claimed for the cosmetic product in the product information file referred to in Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009.

passages.label: Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
This Regulation shall enter into force on the day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .
It shall apply from 11 July 2013.

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.
Done at Brussels, 10 July 2013.
For the Commission
The President

passages.label: Annex 1
passages.text:
ANNEX
COMMON CRITERIA
1. Legal compliance
 | (1) | Claims that indicate that the product has been authorised or approved by a competent authority within the Union shall not be allowed.
 | (2) | The acceptability of a claim shall be based on the perception of the average end user of a cosmetic product, who is reasonably well-informed and reasonably observant and circumspect, taking into account social, cultural and linguistic factors in the market in question.
 | (3) | Claims which convey the idea that a product has a specific benefit when this benefit is mere compliance with minimum legal requirements shall not be allowed.
2. Truthfulness
 | (1) | If it is claimed on the product that it contains a specific ingredient, the ingredient shall be deliberately present.
 | (2) | Ingredient claims referring to the properties of a specific ingredient shall not imply that the finished product has the same properties when it does not.
 | (3) | Marketing communications shall not imply that expressions of opinions are verified claims unless the opinion reflects verifiable evidence.
3. Evidential support
 | (1) | Claims for cosmetic products, whether explicit or implicit, shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence regardless of the types of evidential support used to substantiate them, including where appropriate expert assessments.
 | (2) | Evidence for claim substantiation shall take into account state of the art practices.
 | (3) | Where studies are being used as evidence, they shall be relevant to the product and to the benefit claimed, shall follow well-designed, well-conducted methodologies (valid, reliable and reproducible) and shall respect ethical considerations.
 | (4) | The level of evidence or substantiation shall be consistent with the type of claim being made, in particular for claims where lack of efficacy may cause a safety problem.
 | (5) | Statements of clear exaggeration which are not to be taken literally by the average end user (hyperbole) or statements of an abstract nature shall not require substantiation.
 | (6) | A claim extrapolating (explicitly or implicitly) ingredient properties to the finished product shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, such as by demonstrating the presence of the ingredient at an effective concentration.
 | (7) | Assessment of the acceptability of a claim shall be based on the weight of evidence of all studies, data and information available depending on the nature of the claim and the prevailing general knowledge the end users.
4. Honesty
 | (1) | Presentations of a product’s performance shall not go beyond the available supporting evidence.
 | (2) | Claims shall not attribute to the product concerned specific (i.e. unique) characteristics if similar products possess the same characteristics.
 | (3) | If the action of a product is linked to specific conditions, such as use in association with other products, this shall be clearly stated.
5. Fairness
 | (1) | Claims for cosmetic products shall be objective and shall not denigrate the competitors, nor shall they denigrate ingredients legally used.
 | (2) | Claims for cosmetic products shall not create confusion with the product of a competitor.
6. Informed decision-making
 | (1) | Claims shall be clear and understandable to the average end user.
 | (2) | Claims are an integral part of products and shall contain information allowing the average end user to make an informed choice.
 | (3) | Marketing communications shall take into account the capacity of the target audience (population of relevant Member States or segments of the population, e.g. end users of different age and gender) to comprehend the communication. Marketing communications shall be clear, precise, relevant and understandable by the target audience.

impact_families.title: Romanian provides for entry into force on publication day
impact_families.effect: The Regulation formally enters into force on publication day rather than the following day, while retaining the same express application date.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is a one-day difference in formal commencement. The shared application clause limits the supported effect and establishes no additional substantive compliance period.
impact_families.uncertainty: No further consequence of the commencement difference is established by the supplied material.

impact_families.title: Hungarian ingredient claims require actual presence rather than expressly deliberate inclusion
impact_families.effect: An accurately qualified on-product composition statement identifies an incidentally present ingredient. Hungarian could accept it under Annex 2(1), while English would exclude it.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns a truthful composition statement. Independent evidence, honesty and ingredient-benefit restrictions limit the change.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation of ingredient could restore intentional inclusion.

impact_families.title: Hungarian study-relevance requirement refers to therapeutic effects
impact_families.effect: Studies adequately supporting a nontherapeutic cosmetic benefit are rejected because they do not relate to a therapeutic effect, preventing reliance on them to substantiate the claim.
impact_families.rationale: A literal therapeutic-effect condition could materially change the core substantiation duty and exclude otherwise relevant studies supporting cosmetic benefits.
impact_families.uncertainty: The cosmetic context may support interpreting therapeutic effect as the claimed cosmetic benefit.

impact_families.title: Polish ingredient claims omit the express deliberate-presence condition
impact_families.effect: A substantiated on-product statement identifies an ingredient present only incidentally. Polish could accept it under Annex 2(1), while English would exclude it.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns a truthful composition statement. It does not relax efficacy substantiation or the restrictions on attributing ingredient properties to the finished product.
impact_families.uncertainty: Ingredient may be interpreted as necessarily involving intentional inclusion.

impact_families.title: Slovak requires actual rather than deliberate ingredient presence
impact_families.effect: An otherwise compliant claim identifying an incidentally present ingredient could satisfy the Slovak criterion while failing the English deliberate-presence condition.
impact_families.rationale: Article 2 makes the Annex criteria mandatory. Removing deliberate presence could change substantive eligibility to make an ingredient-content claim, rather than merely changing how presence is proved.
impact_families.uncertainty: The meaning of “ingredient” and multilingual interpretation could restore intentional presence; other claim criteria remain applicable.

impact_families.title: Italian ingredient claims require actual presence without expressly requiring deliberate inclusion
impact_families.effect: An ingredient is verifiably present through incidental carry-over. An accurately qualified content statement could satisfy Italian Annex 2(1) but fail the English condition.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns intentional inclusion behind a truthful composition statement. Evidence, honesty and benefit-related restrictions remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Ingredient may be interpreted contextually as requiring intentional incorporation.

impact_families.title: Finnish denigration prohibition names competing products instead of competitors
impact_families.effect: An otherwise compliant cosmetic-product claim disparages a rival undertaking rather than its products. The Finnish reading could exclude it from the express denigration prohibition.
impact_families.rationale: This could remove entity-directed denigration from a core fairness prohibition. The impartiality requirement does not necessarily prohibit all factually supported disparagement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may reconcile the protected targets; separate advertising rules may independently prohibit the communication.

impact_families.title: Estonian requires using best practices to substantiate claims
impact_families.effect: A responsible person using an adequate alternative method could have to supplement the evidence after considering, but not using, best practices.
impact_families.rationale: The identified additional burden concerns substantiation methodology. Adequate, verifiable evidence remains mandatory in both versions; no separate major consequence is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: Best practices may encompass justified alternative methods.

impact_families.title: Slovak strengthens the requirement concerning evidentiary methods
impact_families.effect: An otherwise adequately substantiated claim could require revised or additional evidence because its existing support considers current practices without being based on them.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the methodological basis of substantiation. The text identifies no compulsory replacement test, substantial expenditure, or categorical exclusion of a particular claim.
impact_families.uncertainty: Both formulations may accept established methods; any additional work depends on the interpretation of the methodological requirement.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian denigration prohibition names competitors’ products instead of competitors
impact_families.effect: An otherwise compliant cosmetic-product claim disparages a competing undertaking rather than its products. Lithuanian could exclude the claim from the express denigration prohibition.
impact_families.rationale: The reading could remove entity-directed denigration from a core fairness prohibition. Objectivity does not necessarily prohibit all factually supported disparagement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may reconcile the targets; separate advertising rules may independently prohibit the communication.

impact_families.uncertainty: A contextual meaning of ingredient may imply intentional inclusion.
