1. The Commission shall establish and maintain a reliable and secure information sharing system supporting communications between Digital Services Coordinators, the Commission and the Board. Other competent authorities may be granted access to this system where necessary for them to carry out the tasks conferred to them in accordance with this Regulation.
2. The Digital Services Coordinators, the Commission and the Board shall use the information sharing system for all communications pursuant to this Regulation.
3. The Commission shall adopt implementing acts laying down the practical and operational arrangements for the functioning of the information sharing system and its interoperability with other relevant systems. Those implementing acts shall be adopted in accordance with the advisory procedure referred to in Article 88.

passages.label: Article 86
passages.text:
Article 86
Representation
1. Without prejudice to Directive (EU) 2020/1828 or to any other type of representation under national law, recipients of intermediary services shall at least have the right to mandate a body, organisation or association to exercise the rights conferred by this Regulation on their behalf, provided the body, organisation or association meets all of the following conditions:
(a) | it operates on a not-for-profit basis;
(b) | it has been properly constituted in accordance with the law of a Member State;
(c) | its statutory objectives include a legitimate interest in ensuring that this Regulation is complied with.
2. Providers of online platforms shall take the necessary technical and organisational measures to ensure that complaints submitted by bodies, organisations or associations referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article on behalf of recipients of the service through the mechanisms referred to in Article 20(1) are processed and decided upon with priority and without undue delay.

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
SECTION 6
Delegated and implementing acts

passages.label: Article 87
passages.text:
Article 87
Exercise of the delegation
1. The power to adopt delegated acts is conferred on the Commission subject to the conditions laid down in this Article.
2. The delegation of power referred to in Articles 24, 33, 37, 40 and 43 shall be conferred on the Commission for five years starting from 16 November 2022. The Commission shall draw up a report in respect of the delegation of power not later than nine months before the end of the five-year period. The delegation of power shall be tacitly extended for periods of an identical duration, unless the European Parliament or the Council opposes such extension not later than three months before the end of each period.
3. The delegation of power referred to in Articles 24, 33, 37, 40 and 43 may be revoked at any time by the European Parliament or by the Council. A decision of revocation shall put an end to the delegation of power specified in that decision. It shall take effect the day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union or at a later date specified therein. It shall not affect the validity of any delegated acts already in force.
4. Before adopting a delegated act, the Commission shall consult experts designated by each Member State in accordance with the principles laid down in the Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making.
5. As soon as it adopts a delegated act, the Commission shall notify it simultaneously to the European Parliament and to the Council.
6. A delegated act adopted pursuant to Articles 24, 33, 37, 40 and 43 shall enter into force only if no objection has been expressed by either the European Parliament or the Council within a period of three months of notification of that act to the European Parliament and the Council or if, before the expiry of that period, the European Parliament and the Council have both informed the Commission that they will not object. That period shall be extended by three months at the initiative of the European Parliament or of the Council.

passages.label: Article 88
passages.text:
Article 88
Committee procedure
1. The Commission shall be assisted by a committee (‘the Digital Services Committee’). That Committee shall be a Committee within the meaning of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011.
2. Where reference is made to this paragraph, Article 4 of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 shall apply.

CHAPTER V
FINAL PROVISIONS

passages.label: Article 89
passages.text:
Article 89
Amendments to Directive 2000/31/EC
1. Articles 12 to 15 of Directive 2000/31/EC are deleted.
2. References to Articles 12 to 15 of Directive 2000/31/EC shall be construed as references to Articles 4, 5, 6 and 8 of this Regulation, respectively.

passages.label: Article 90
passages.text:
Article 90
Amendment to Directive (EU) 2020/1828
In Annex I to Directive (EU) 2020/1828, the following point is added:
‘(68) | Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market for Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) ( OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1 ).’.

passages.label: Article 91
Article 92
passages.text:
Article 92
Anticipated application to providers of very large online platforms and of very large online search engines
This Regulation shall apply to providers of very large online platforms and of very large online search engines designated pursuant to Article 33(4) from four months after the notification to the provider concerned referred to in Article 33(6) where that date is earlier than 17 February 2024.

passages.label: Article 93
passages.text:
Article 93
Entry into force and application
1. This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .
2. This Regulation shall apply from 17 February 2024.
However, Article 24(2), (3) and (6), Article 33(3) to (6), Article 37(7), Article 40(13), Article 43 and Sections 4, 5 and 6 of Chapter IV shall apply from 16 November 2022.

variants.quote: Leverantörer av onlineplattformar ska vidta de tekniska och organisatoriska åtgärder som är nödvändiga för att säkerställa att anmälningar som lämnas in på tjänstemottagares vägnar av de organ, organisationer eller sammanslutningar som avses i punkt 1 i denna artikel, via de mekanismer som avses i artikel 20.1, behandlas och blir föremål för beslut utan onödigt dröjsmål.
variants.translation: Providers of online platforms shall take the technical and organisational measures necessary to ensure that notices submitted on behalf of service recipients by the bodies, organisations or associations referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article, through the mechanisms referred to in Article 20(1), are processed and decided upon without undue delay.
variants.explanation: Swedish Article 86(2) could allow representative complaints to remain in the ordinary processing queue, provided they are decided without undue delay. English additionally requires priority. The reference to Article 20(1) identifies the submissions as internal complaints.

review.method: Source-matched reuse of independent full-text Sol discovery/review and Astra audit; explicitly authorized completion supplements; diagnosed provision gaps closed by separate Sol discovery/review and Astra source audit with full-act context.

notes: Source currency checked on 16 October 2026. The latest consolidated work is 02022R2065-20221027; its language expressions incorporate later corrigenda despite retaining the nominal date 27 October 2022.

Danish, German, Estonian, French, Hungarian, Italian, Polish and Slovenian use their current consolidated operative expressions. The sixteen other languages, including English, use original expressions after verification that no linked corrigendum affects them.

Consolidations omit recitals. Original publications and language-specific corrigenda accompany them as separately identified context documents. Consolidated texts are documentation tools; authentic acts and corrigenda are those published in the Official Journal.

English is a comparison reference with equal authority to the other authentic languages. Review concerns possible differences in legal meaning and their conditional consequences, not adjudicated legal errors.
This review used signed-in Codex: one blind Sol discovery, separate Sol review with bounded follow-up, and independent Astra source audit. No direct model API calls were made.

All 23 English-anchored target-language comparisons completed. The 192 previously withheld supported claims are included. Explicit provision supplements close every concrete reported gap, with full authentic-act context and independent source audits. Completion does not prove exhaustive detection or adjudicate legal correctness.
English provides navigation; all official language versions are equally authoritative. Findings are potential discrepancies reviewed by agents, not adjudicated legal errors.

ai_processing.estimate_basis: Based on saved usage for the original current-source review and its completion supplements, including independent audits and failed attempts. 5 timed-out or interrupted attempt(s) with unavailable usage are approximated by successful retries of the same legal prompt and schema. Uses Standard API rates without cache discounts, rounded to whole dollars; excludes the superseded initial source assembly.

impact_families.title: Dutch text leaves the form of trusted-flagger assistance unspecified
impact_families.effect: The Commission could provide individual assistance on trusted-flagger status instead of issuing guidelines when assistance is necessary.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the prescribed form of administrative support. Eligibility, suspension, revocation and the opportunity to respond remain governed by the same substantive rules.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Commission could still choose guidelines as the means of assistance.

impact_families.title: Management action-plan power may arise before serious harm occurs
impact_families.effect: After other powers are exhausted, management could be required to adopt, implement and report an action plan before the continuing infringement causes its anticipated serious harm.
impact_families.rationale: The additional consequence is management-level compliance supervision. Cessation and preventive interim powers already exist, and access restrictions retain an independent present-harm condition.
impact_families.uncertainty: Irish legislative future tense and the exceptional-enforcement context may support the same temporal condition as English.

impact_families.title: Slovenian makes necessary trusted-flagger guidance discretionary
impact_families.effect: If guidance is necessary for applying the trusted-flagger rules, the Commission could nevertheless decline to issue it under the Slovenian reading.
impact_families.rationale: This changes an ancillary guidance duty. The operative conditions for awarding, suspending and revoking trusted-flagger status remain binding and do not depend on issuance of guidelines.
impact_families.uncertainty: The necessity condition and consistent-application objective favour harmonization, but do not expressly eliminate the additional discretion.

impact_families.title: Future-offence reporting uses possibility rather than likelihood
impact_families.effect: Concrete information suggesting a possible but unlikely life-threatening offence could trigger reporting and disclosure of relevant available information, potentially including identifying user information.
impact_families.rationale: The difference expands a compulsory disclosure duty to authorities and can materially affect users’ privacy.
impact_families.uncertainty: Reasonably justified suspicion, recital 56 and preserved data-protection rules constrain the broader reading.

impact_families.title: Article 24(5) omits machine readability for the moderation database
impact_families.effect: A publicly searchable database without machine-readable output could satisfy the Maltese wording.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence concerns a technical access characteristic; submission, public accessibility and personal-data exclusion remain required.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 66’s structured-database and querying objectives favour machine readability.

impact_families.title: Responsibility for describing proposed access restrictions shifts to consultees
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, the Commission could invite observations without identifying its proposed restrictions or addressees, leaving interested parties to formulate their own requested measures.
impact_families.rationale: This changes preliminary consultation disclosure. Article 51(3) retains judicial authorization, participation rights, substantive restriction conditions and proportionality safeguards; the difference does not itself authorize restricting access.
impact_families.uncertainty: The parallel consultation wording in Article 51(3) strongly supports harmonization.

impact_families.title: Interface-design provision omits the general category of compliance information
impact_families.effect: A marketplace might omit facilities and completeness checks for compliance information outside the retained categories, if applicable Union law requires such information.
impact_families.rationale: The supplied act does not identify a concrete residual information requirement. Without the governing external obligations, the extent and importance of the changed outcome cannot be established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The retained information categories may overlap substantially; the relevant external requirements are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Recommender-system definition may require both suggestion and prioritization
impact_families.effect: A platform’s suggestion-only system could escape Article 27 transparency requirements and, for a designated very large platform, Article 38’s requirement for a non-profiling option.
impact_families.rationale: The definition controls substantive information and choice entitlements. General systemic-risk duties do not independently reproduce those specific recommender-system requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Suggestion may itself confer prominence; the concluding definition and recital 70 support a broader functional reading.

impact_families.title: Public-data access conditions may apply only to nonprofit-affiliated researchers
impact_families.effect: A researcher lacking commercial independence or the specified systemic-risk research purpose could claim compulsory access to public interface data, including technically available real-time data.
impact_families.rationale: This changes eligibility for a statutory data-access entitlement and the corresponding provider duty by removing substantive safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 98 supports universal eligibility safeguards; independent personal-data requirements remain applicable.

impact_families.title: Reopening commitment proceedings could become mandatory
impact_families.effect: If the mandatory reading prevailed, a material change in facts underlying a commitment decision could require the Commission to reopen proceedings despite preferring to leave them closed.
impact_families.rationale: This materially changes enforcement discretion and the conditional finality of a decision declaring no further grounds for action.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 139 supports discretion generally. Reopening alone neither establishes an infringement nor requires a sanction.

impact_families.title: Order reporting may measure notification instead of implementation
impact_families.effect: If the notification reading prevailed, a provider could report median time until notifying the authority about implementation instead of median time until implementing the order.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns an aggregate reporting metric. Articles 9 and 10 retain information about whether and when orders were implemented; the disputed phrase changes neither the orders nor their enforceability.
impact_families.uncertainty: The final Bulgarian phrase can alternatively attach to the timing requirement, preserving implementation as a separately timed activity.

impact_families.title: Article 51 escalation gateway may exclude completed but unremedied infringements
impact_families.effect: After other enforcement powers are exhausted, a completed but unremedied infringement causing serious harm could escape the compulsory management-action stage and consequently the subsequent access-restriction procedure.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed gateway controls exceptional enforcement remedies for serious harm that cannot be avoided through other available powers.
impact_families.uncertainty: Point (b) expressly includes unremedied infringements and strongly supports harmonization.

impact_families.title: Research-publication condition omits recipients’ express rights
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading prevailed, a coordinator could assess a researcher’s publication commitment against recipients’ interests and GDPR compliance without separately applying the omitted rights qualification.
impact_families.rationale: The changed criterion concerns a subsidiary publication safeguard. Interests, confidentiality, personal-data protection and independently applicable rights remain protected; the supplied text does not establish a major substantive loss.
impact_families.uncertainty: A rights-inclusive interpretation of interests, supported by recitals 97 and 153, could eliminate the practical difference.

impact_families.title: Technical feasibility may condition ordinary research access to public data
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, a provider could invoke technical infeasibility to deny an otherwise qualifying researcher ordinary access to publicly accessible data, rather than merely declining real-time access.
impact_families.rationale: The broader condition could remove the paragraph 12 research-access entitlement altogether. The separate vetted-researcher procedure does not preserve that entitlement for every researcher eligible under paragraph 12.
impact_families.uncertainty: Bulgarian recital 98 expressly links technical possibility to real-time access and strongly supports harmonization.

impact_families.title: Transient-storage exemption uses customary necessity
impact_families.effect: A neutral provider otherwise satisfying Article 4 needs an unusually long but reasonable transient-storage interval solely for transmission. A customary-duration ceiling could deny it the English provision’s liability exemption.
impact_families.rationale: Eligibility for a core liability exemption materially changes. Recital 17 requires an independent basis for liability, and Article 4(3) preserves injunctions in both versions; neither removes the significance of losing exemption protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Customary necessity may accommodate exceptional technical circumstances. Neither actual liability nor any financial loss is established.

impact_families.title: Notification trigger omits completed criminal offences
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, a hosting provider learning of a completed offence threatening life or safety could withhold notification where neither continuation nor a future offence is suspected.
impact_families.rationale: This would remove a mandatory notification duty for a class of safety-related criminal suspicions expressly covered in English, materially narrowing the rule’s core obligation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 56 and Article 18(2) expressly include past offences, strongly supporting harmonization.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian reporting provision ties transmission to audit completion
impact_families.effect: A provider could delay routine transmission of a completed risk-assessment report until completion of the audit.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns routine reporting timing. Assessment and mitigation duties persist, and Articles 34(3), 40 and 67 preserve mechanisms for authorities to obtain information.
impact_families.uncertainty: English may also support coordinated transmission of the audit-related documents as a package.

impact_families.title: Compliance reporting may be due by implementation rather than upon implementation
impact_families.effect: A provider could supply its description before implementation and argue that no further description becomes due when implementation occurs.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns a reporting milestone. Compliance duties, Commission monitoring powers and, where applicable, Article 75’s implementation updates remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Measures already taken and the separate reporting of intentions support requiring a description reflecting actual implementation.

impact_families.title: Dutch recipient-notification rule omits a description of territorial scope
impact_families.effect: A provider could notify a recipient of an order, its effects, reasons and remedies without separately describing the territory covered.
impact_families.rationale: The supported difference removes a specific notification component. It does not change territorial limits, available remedies or the duty to notify the order and its effects.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general notification duty or supplying the order itself may communicate territorial scope.

impact_families.title: Inspection authorization safeguard has a different records trigger
impact_families.effect: If the Hungarian trigger prevailed, incomplete delivery of otherwise complete records could fail to activate the express requirement to present written inspection authorization under Article 69(4).
impact_families.rationale: The change affects a specific documentary safeguard. Compulsory inspections still require the paragraph 6 decision, and coercive assistance remains subject to the applicable judicial controls.
impact_families.uncertainty: The inspection context strongly favours understanding the provision as concerning production of requested records.

impact_families.title: Caching exemption may impose a sole-purpose test on the entire service
impact_families.effect: A multifunctional transmission service could be denied the caching exemption even where its temporary storage exclusively facilitates efficient or secure onward transmission and satisfies the remaining conditions.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns eligibility for a core liability exemption, although losing that exemption does not itself establish liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 3(g)(ii) and functional separation under recitals 15 and 29 strongly support assessing the storage function separately.

impact_families.title: Researcher eligibility may turn on motivation rather than independence
impact_families.effect: A researcher whose commercial dependence compromises independence, but whose research lacks commercial motivation, could obtain compulsory data access under Article 40(4) or (12), assuming all remaining applicable conditions are satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition controls eligibility for statutory research access and the provider’s corresponding disclosure duty. Purpose, proportionality and confidentiality safeguards constrain access but do not independently restore the missing independence requirement.
impact_families.uncertainty: A contextual reading could interpret freedom from commercial motivation as requiring practical independence.

impact_families.title: Future-offence reporting expresses possibility rather than likelihood
impact_families.effect: If possibility sufficed, information grounding suspicion of a possible but unlikely future life-threatening offence could require a hosting provider to notify authorities and disclose all available relevant information.
impact_families.rationale: The changed threshold could materially expand compulsory disclosure to law-enforcement or judicial authorities, including information identifying the recipient described in recital 56.
impact_families.uncertainty: Information-based suspicion, recital 56 and continuing data-protection safeguards constrain the broader reading.

impact_families.title: Irish fact-finding clause changes the protection against imposed duties
impact_families.effect: A provider facing a compulsory general fact-finding requirement could lose the explicit protection supplied by Article 8’s English second limb.
impact_families.rationale: The affected provision establishes a core limit on investigative burdens that may be imposed on intermediary services.
impact_families.uncertainty: The heading, Article 7 and recitals 30 and 34 strongly support preserving the prohibition on compulsion.

impact_families.title: Portuguese narrows the express immediate-action benchmark to imminent threats
impact_families.effect: If the narrower benchmark governed, a provider could have more time to act on notified illegal content threatening a person’s life before the threat became imminent.
impact_families.rationale: The changed interpretation could materially weaken the timing of a protective duty concerning threats to life or personal safety.
impact_families.uncertainty: The example is non-exhaustive; urgency-sensitive handling and Article 16(6) may support the same timing in both versions.

impact_families.title: Romanian limits the notice-processing count to exclusive automation
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could omit notices handled through automation followed by human review from its reported number of automatically processed notices.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows one numerical transparency metric. Broader automation disclosures and the substantive requirements for processing notices remain binding.
impact_families.uncertainty: Reporting templates are outside the supplied evidence; contextual interpretation could require a broader count.

impact_families.title: Croatian gives routine supervisory report transmission a three-month deadline
impact_families.effect: A provider could retain completed reports until the three-month deadline after receipt of its audit report, instead of transmitting them to supervisors without undue delay upon completion.
impact_families.rationale: The established consequence is delayed automatic reporting. Supervisors retain independent access and information-request powers; assessment, mitigation, audit and enhanced-supervision duties continue.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 93 supports prompt transmission, and a supervisory request may require earlier disclosure.

impact_families.title: Romanian strengthens the duty to ensure advertising-code content
impact_families.effect: A code omitting meaningful information on data monetisation could leave the Commission in breach despite its efforts to obtain that content.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns minimum content in supplementary voluntary codes. It neither compels participation nor changes the binding advertising obligations in Articles 26 and 39.
impact_families.uncertainty: The voluntary framework could lead to interpreting the result obligation as constrained by the Commission’s available powers.

impact_families.title: The initial risk assessment may start after the completion deadline
impact_families.effect: A designated provider could enter the systemic-risk regime without completing its first assessment, postponing identification of risks requiring Article 35 mitigation.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed deadline concerns the initial performance of a core preventive duty, with consequences for the linked mitigation obligation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Immediate application of the duties and their preventive purpose support requiring a completed assessment at commencement.

impact_families.title: Compulsory crisis measures may extend beyond the service’s contribution
impact_families.effect: A crisis decision could require a provider to identify and apply measures addressing the wider threat even where those measures go beyond preventing or limiting its service’s contribution.
impact_families.rationale: The omission potentially expands the scope of compulsory crisis intervention. Provider choice and proportionality constrain the measures but do not necessarily restore the narrower objective.
impact_families.uncertainty: Paragraph 1(a), strict necessity and the service-focused examples strongly support a narrower contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Irish recommender-disclosure duty refers only to very large platforms
impact_families.effect: A platform outside Article 19’s enterprise exclusions, but not designated very large, could withhold the recommender disclosures required by Article 27(1).
impact_families.rationale: The narrower scope removes an entire substantive transparency duty and the corresponding information entitlement for users of qualifying platforms.
impact_families.uncertainty: The section structure, Article 27(3) and recitals 70 and 94 strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Search engines may fall outside specific advertising-repository safeguards
impact_families.effect: A very large search engine includes advertisement recipients’ personal data in its public repository while claiming that Article 39’s categorical exclusion applies only to platforms.
impact_families.rationale: The omission could remove a specific privacy prohibition governing a mandatory public repository. Other data-protection requirements remain applicable but do not expressly reproduce that categorical prohibition here.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared repository framework strongly supports applying the safeguards to search engines; other privacy law still constrains disclosure.

impact_families.title: Description of proposed access restrictions may shift to interested parties
impact_families.effect: If the Dutch reading prevailed, the Commission could invite observations without describing its proposed restriction or identifying its addressees before referring the matter to the coordinator.
impact_families.rationale: The changed requirement concerns preliminary consultation information. Article 51(3) retains judicial participation, substantive conditions for access restrictions and proportionality safeguards; the discrepancy does not itself authorize a restriction.
impact_families.uncertainty: The consultation’s purpose and Article 51(3)’s express allocation of disclosure strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Article 33(6) changes the four-month transition wording
impact_families.effect: Following termination of designation, a provider could claim that its Section 5 duties cease before four full months have elapsed.
impact_families.rationale: The timing difference can affect the application of the entire set of systemic-risk duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 92 and consistent interpretation support a fixed four-month transition.

impact_families.title: Voluntary standards address interface selection rather than interfaces for user choice
impact_families.effect: The Commission could support standards for selecting interfaces without specifically supporting standards for user choice controls.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns the scope of voluntary standardization. Articles 27 and 38 continue to govern recommender information and user options directly.
impact_families.uncertainty: The express references to Articles 27 and 38 support interpreting the standards as addressing user choice.

impact_families.title: Latvian Board consultation provision states a duty
impact_families.effect: The Board could be required to arrange stakeholder consultation in its work instead of choosing whether to consult.
impact_families.rationale: The difference adds an institutional procedural duty without establishing a decision-specific consultation entitlement or altering the Board’s substantive powers.
impact_families.uncertainty: The text does not specify consultation frequency or the decisions requiring consultation.

impact_families.title: Future-offence reporting may be triggered by possibility rather than likelihood
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could have to notify authorities and disclose relevant available information about a supported possibility of a future offence even without suspecting that its occurrence is likely.
impact_families.rationale: The difference expands the trigger for a mandatory criminal-suspicion report and accompanying information disclosure, materially changing a core provider duty.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared suspicion requirement and recital 56’s reasonable-justification standard may support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian text also authorizes Commission decisions on data-access amendments
impact_families.effect: The Commission could decide a provider’s request to amend researcher data access even though the establishment Coordinator issued the original access request.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes the competent decision-maker for this procedural step. It does not change the stated amendment grounds, required alternatives or researcher eligibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: The relationship between the alternative Commission authority and the Coordinator’s continuing administrative responsibilities is unspecified.

impact_families.title: Romanian narrows the express inspection category subject to the 1% fine ceiling
impact_families.effect: A provider’s sanctionable failure to comply with an inspection order, without refusal, could fall under the general 6% ceiling instead of the special 1% ceiling.
impact_families.rationale: Changing the applicable maximum from 1% to 6% of worldwide turnover can materially increase potential financial liability; Article 51 expressly covers investigative-order noncompliance.
impact_families.uncertainty: Refusal may encompass negligent omissions; national rules, proportionality and the parallel Commission regime may preserve the special ceiling.

impact_families.title: Portuguese omits the significant-contribution threshold for crisis response
impact_families.effect: If the unqualified reading governed, a designated platform with only a minor crisis contribution could be required to change its moderation processes or service systems to address that contribution.
impact_families.rationale: The omission could broaden compulsory crisis-response duties involving substantive service changes under Article 36(1)(b), beyond contributions meeting the English significance threshold.
impact_families.uncertainty: Strict necessity, proportionality, time limits and provider choice constrain the measures; their application may narrow the practical difference.

impact_families.title: Board-structure review omits heightened consideration of the Board’s opinion
impact_families.effect: The Commission could give the Board’s opinion ordinary consideration when deciding whether to accompany its review report with a proposal concerning the Board’s structure.
impact_families.rationale: This changes the weight of advisory input into a review and possible proposal. Consultation remains mandatory, and any structural amendment requires a further legislative act.
impact_families.uncertainty: The provision’s institutional context could support heightened consideration despite the omitted qualifier.

impact_families.title: Romanian makes necessary trusted-flagger guidance discretionary
impact_families.effect: The Commission could decline to issue guidance despite an identified need for clarification of trusted-flagger designation, suspension or revocation.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns supplementary guidance; the operative status criteria, investigation requirements and procedural protections remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Commission retains judgment about necessity, and contextual interpretation could reconcile the formulations.

impact_families.title: Transparency reports additionally require a standardized format
impact_families.effect: Without an applicable reporting template, a provider could be required to reformat an accessible, machine-readable annual report to meet an additional standardization requirement.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence concerns report presentation. The underlying content, frequency and publication duties remain the same; no concrete major consequence is established by the supplied text.
impact_families.uncertainty: No standard is specified; applicable implementing templates could remove practical divergence.

impact_families.title: Crisis duties could begin before a serious threat exists
impact_families.effect: If the broader trigger prevailed, the Commission could require a designated provider to assess risks and implement crisis measures before extraordinary circumstances have produced a serious threat.
impact_families.rationale: The difference could advance the availability of compulsory service-related mitigation duties. Board involvement, proportionality and time limits constrain their exercise but do not remove the changed trigger.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 91 supports prevention in both languages; circumstances capable of producing harm may already constitute a serious threat.

impact_families.title: Organisations may obtain complaint standing without a recipient’s mandate
impact_families.effect: An organisation without a recipient’s mandate could claim Article 53 standing, requiring assessment of its complaint and access to the associated hearing and information rights.
impact_families.rationale: The added wording materially expands eligibility for a statutory complaint mechanism and its procedural entitlements, beyond merely allowing authorities to receive informal information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 86 and the representative-standing recitals favor harmonization, but do not explain away the express independent-standing language.

impact_families.title: Conduct-based reversal ground omits monetisation and visibility restrictions
impact_families.effect: A user whose conduct does not justify a monetisation restriction could lose the express entitlement to prompt reversal, even where some underlying content breached the platform’s terms.
impact_families.rationale: The difference can materially narrow a remedy protecting users against unwarranted restrictions; the separate lawful-content reversal ground would not necessarily apply.
impact_families.uncertainty: General proportionality duties and other remedies may still provide relief.

impact_families.title: Irish moderation-reasons exception refers to high-demand content
impact_families.effect: A recipient could receive no statement of reasons for an account or service restriction involving deceptive, high-demand commercial content that was not disseminated in high volume.
impact_families.rationale: The changed exception can remove an important procedural entitlement supporting challenges to content, payment, service and account restrictions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 55’s manipulation examples support harmonization; independent complaint and judicial remedies remain available.

impact_families.title: Reasoned rejection of commitments may follow closure of proceedings
impact_families.effect: The Commission could conclude proceedings before issuing its formal reasoned rejection of the provider’s proposed commitments.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns procedural sequence and the timing of formal reasons. The duty to issue a reasoned rejection remains, and loss of judicial review is not established.
impact_families.uncertainty: No interval is specified; conclusion might be understood as completion of the investigative stage.

impact_families.title: Trader traceability potentially requires combined advertising and offering
impact_families.effect: A trader using a covered marketplace solely to advertise could avoid the identification prerequisite and associated verification requirements under a cumulative reading.
impact_families.rationale: The difference potentially removes a core traceability safeguard for a category of commercial use expressly contemplated by the Regulation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 72 and Article 31(2)(a) strongly support alternative triggers.

impact_families.title: Crisis protocols may specify an adoption deadline instead of a duration
impact_families.effect: A voluntary crisis protocol could satisfy this particular specification by setting an adoption deadline without separately determining how long its measures operate.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns protocol preparation, not an independent power to impose restrictions. Temporary activation, fundamental-rights safeguards, duration reporting and Commission revision remain relevant.
impact_families.uncertainty: English also uses action-taking language; recital 108 strongly supports reading both versions as requiring temporal limitation.

impact_families.title: A mitigation example may concern processing notifications instead of notice handling
impact_families.effect: A provider evaluates the speed and quality of processing-status notifications under this example instead of evaluating how quickly and well it handles illegal-content notices.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects one mitigation benchmark. Article 16 and Article 35’s broader duties still require diligent notice handling and effective responses to identified systemic risks.
impact_families.uncertainty: Czech recital 87 expressly supports interpreting the example as notice processing.

impact_families.title: Representative complaints lack express processing priority
impact_families.effect: A platform handles a representative complaint in its ordinary queue without preferential treatment, while still reaching a decision without undue delay.
impact_families.rationale: The difference removes preferential sequencing. Access to the complaint procedure, timely handling, reasoned decisions and further redress remain protected.
impact_families.uncertainty: The provision's purpose could support an implied priority requirement.

impact_families.title: Croatian purchaser-notification period may run forward from awareness
impact_families.effect: A consumer who purchased an illegal product shortly before awareness could lose individual notification under Article 32(1), even where the platform holds that consumer’s contact details.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading removes an important notification entitlement concerning illegal purchases and available redress. Paragraph 2 does not guarantee replacement individual notice.
impact_families.uncertainty: The focus on completed purchases and consumer protection strongly supports a retrospective harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Enhanced-supervision information goes directly to one coordinator
impact_families.effect: The provider could communicate its action plan directly to one coordinator, and the Commission could likewise update only that coordinator, while continuing to inform the Board.
impact_families.rationale: The change narrows direct information distribution. Commission monitoring, Board participation and coordinators’ representation on the Board remain, supporting an ancillary rather than major consequence.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 145 and the information-sharing framework support wider circulation; the singular coordinator is not expressly identified.

impact_families.title: Articles 3 and 5 present caching characteristics as alternatives
impact_families.effect: A provider using automatic but non-temporary transmission-related storage could claim the caching exemption if the remaining conditions were satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading changes eligibility for a liability exemption and could determine whether liability under applicable law remains available.
impact_families.uncertainty: The technical meaning of caching, neutrality and the sole transmission purpose favour cumulative characteristics.

impact_families.title: Supervision trigger may address an inadequate plan rather than inadequate implementation
impact_families.effect: A provider challenges reliance on Article 75(4)(c) because its plan is sufficient on paper, although implementation has failed.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns a particular procedural ground. Articles 73, 76(1)(e) and 82 independently preserve compliance orders, coercive payments and access-restriction procedures; no exemption from those powers follows.
impact_families.uncertainty: The implementation audit, monitoring provisions and Recital 145 strongly support a harmonizing reading.

impact_families.title: Stakeholder involvement is described without an appropriateness qualification
impact_families.effect: A provider is expected to include stakeholder representatives in its assessment methodology despite considering their involvement inappropriate in the particular circumstances.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns how assessment and mitigation are prepared. Articles 34, 35 and 42 retain contextual limits; the omission establishes no separate participation entitlement or sanction.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recital’s effect on operative diligence requirements remains interpretative, particularly alongside Article 42(4)(e).

impact_families.title: Public-security redaction ground adds a seriousness threshold
impact_families.effect: A provider could have to retain report information presenting a non-serious public-security risk where confidentiality, service-security and recipient-harm grounds do not independently justify redaction.
impact_families.rationale: The residual difference concerns lesser public-security risks. Serious risks and the independent protective grounds remain covered, supporting a narrower consequence rather than a major loss of protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: English ‘undermine’ may itself imply meaningful impairment, reducing the difference between the thresholds.

impact_families.title: Procedural fine ceiling omits annual income
impact_families.effect: A professionally involved person with income but no turnover could avoid a positive procedural fine for refusing a qualifying investigative order.
impact_families.rationale: The omission can remove financial sanction exposure for an expressly covered category of persons and materially weaken enforcement of investigative duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: The outcome depends on the person’s finances and national implementation of penalties.

impact_families.title: Exclusive national competence lacks the main-establishment qualification
impact_families.effect: For a provider with establishments in several Member States, a State hosting a secondary establishment could assert exclusive national supervisory and enforcement competence under Article 56(1).
impact_families.rationale: The connecting factor determines which State may exercise core investigation, cessation, remedial and sanctioning powers under Articles 51 and 52.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 123, Article 3(n) and Article 56(4) strongly favor the main-establishment interpretation.

impact_families.title: Dutch wording weakens the express advance-information condition for sanctions
impact_families.effect: If prior delivery alone sufficed, a third party facing a fine could lose the specific objection that information about the compliance deadline and possible penalties arrived too late.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns an express condition on financial enforcement against third parties, including potentially substantial fines under Article 52(3).
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 51(6) and recital 116 may independently require timely disclosure sufficient to protect defence rights.

impact_families.title: Latvian national investigation powers use a provider-business connection
impact_families.effect: A professional evidence holder without the required provider-business connection could resist a Coordinator’s compulsory information request and linked inspection.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes the persons subject to core investigative duties, including orders backed by fines and periodic penalty payments under Article 51(2).
impact_families.uncertainty: A broad reading of the business connection could substantially reduce the exclusion.

impact_families.title: Trader traceability may exclude consumers temporarily in the Union
impact_families.effect: A trader serving only visitors temporarily in the Union could use a covered marketplace without supplying the identification and compliance information required by Article 30.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower territorial condition could remove a core marketplace admission requirement and its associated suspension safeguard for those transactions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 2 and recital 72 strongly favour a harmonized, location-based interpretation.

impact_families.title: Irish electronic-notice requirement is expressed as a recommendation
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could require a non-electronic step for illegal-content notices while maintaining an otherwise accessible and user-friendly notification mechanism.
impact_families.rationale: The reading removes the guaranteed electronic route for exercising a central notification entitlement available to any individual or entity.
impact_families.uncertainty: The online-service context, Article 12 and Article 44 support treating electronic submission as mandatory.

impact_families.title: Information-order reasons specify appropriateness instead of proportionality
impact_families.effect: An authority supplies reasons explaining necessity and suitability without expressly explaining the proportionality of the requested disclosure.
impact_families.rationale: The changed requirement concerns the content of reasons. Union-law safeguards, necessity, limits on obtainable information and redress remain; the provision supplies no broader disclosure power.
impact_families.uncertainty: Appropriateness may encompass proportionality when interpreted with the Charter and recital 153.

impact_families.title: Irish criminal-suspicion reporting duty lacks express timing
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could delay reporting a suspected impending offence threatening life or safety while maintaining that Article 18 imposes no express promptness requirement.
impact_families.rationale: Prompt reporting is a central component of a protective duty expressly covering offences likely to occur and threats to persons.
impact_families.uncertainty: Irish recital 56 expressly requires reporting without delay and confines disclosure to available information.

impact_families.title: Dutch definition could broaden the exception from online-platform status
impact_families.effect: A non-minor but purely ancillary, technically inseparable feature could escape online-platform status, provided integration does not circumvent the Regulation, removing otherwise applicable platform-specific complaint and advertising duties.
impact_families.rationale: The exception determines whether a service falls within a category subject to substantial additional obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: The social-network example in recital 13 supports a narrower reading despite the repeated Dutch disjunction.

impact_families.title: Croatian general secrecy duty may cover a narrower class of information
impact_families.effect: An enforcement participant could disclose professionally confidential, non-business information obtained during an investigation without breaching Article 84, where no separate confidentiality provision covers that disclosure.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading removes a category of information from a general nondisclosure duty binding authorities, their personnel and other participants, materially narrowing that duty.
impact_families.uncertainty: A broader contextual meaning may preserve professional confidentiality; independent confidentiality and data-protection duties remain applicable.

impact_families.title: Standalone well-being risks may lose express assessment coverage
impact_families.effect: A provider could dispute an express duty to assess and mitigate serious well-being risks unconnected to gender-based violence, public health or protection of minors.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed relationship can narrow a substantive category within the core systemic-risk assessment and mitigation duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general systemic-risk duty and overlapping fundamental rights may independently cover particular well-being risks.

impact_families.title: Later procedural steps may fail to restart the penalty limitation period
impact_families.effect: If no other interrupting act occurred, communication of later preliminary findings could preserve the power to impose a fine under English but fail to do so under Finnish.
impact_families.rationale: The difference could determine whether the Commission remains entitled to impose substantial financial penalties, within the retained outer limitation period and suspension rules.
impact_families.uncertainty: The non-exhaustive list supports broader interruption; information requests and inspections remain expressly covered.

impact_families.title: Limitation interruption may exclude later procedural steps
impact_families.effect: A later non-investigative procedural act could restart limitation only under English, leaving a subsequent Commission fine timely there but time-barred under the narrower Estonian reading.
impact_families.rationale: The changed interruption gateway can remove the power to impose substantial sanctions, even within the shared outer limitation period.
impact_families.uncertainty: A broad understanding of investigation could cover many later procedural acts; judicial suspension may also affect particular cases.

impact_families.title: Content-restriction reasons duty identifies information supplied by the provider
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could deny reasons for removing a user’s post because Article 17(1)(a) identifies information supplied by the provider.
impact_families.rationale: Where Article 17 otherwise applies, this reading could remove an important procedural entitlement enabling recipients to understand and challenge content restrictions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The introductory sentence, paragraph 3 and recital 54 strongly support interpreting the duty as covering user content.

impact_families.title: Board findings could become a required basis for the review report
impact_families.effect: The Commission could need to obtain and use Board findings as a basis for its review report instead of relying solely on its own assessment.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects report preparation and institutional input. The Commission retains its assessment duty, and the Board gains no power to amend the Regulation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Consultation may generate shared findings that satisfy both formulations.

impact_families.title: Romanian strengthens the duty to ensure complete crisis protocols
impact_families.effect: A crisis protocol lacking a clear public-reporting process could breach the Commission’s obligation despite its efforts to obtain that process.
impact_families.rationale: The difference strengthens responsibility for protocol completeness within a voluntary framework. Existing crisis limits and the mandatory revision mechanism constrain the additional consequence.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Commission’s limited control over voluntary participants may influence interpretation of the result obligation.

impact_families.title: Ground for refusing mutual assistance turns on competence to request information
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, a coordinator could refuse an otherwise valid assistance request where no relevant authority has competence to demand the information, despite another lawful means of obtaining it.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence changes an inter-authority information-assistance exception. It does not directly change providers’ substantive obligations, available penalties or recipients’ remedies.
impact_families.uncertainty: The investigative context supports interpreting competence to request as lawful ability to obtain information.

impact_families.title: Dutch active-recipient definition could require a request to view information
impact_families.effect: If unrequested exposure were excluded, a platform otherwise reaching 45 million average monthly active recipients could fall below the designation threshold and avoid the additional systemic-risk obligations.
impact_families.rationale: Article 33 makes audience size a condition for designation and the application of substantial additional assessment, mitigation and audit duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 77 and a broad understanding of requesting access strongly support counting passive exposure.

impact_families.title: Judicial-review suspension names enforcement rather than imposition
impact_families.effect: After judicial review necessitating a replacement penalty decision, the ordinary imposition period could have expired under the German reading while remaining suspended under English.
impact_families.rationale: The difference can determine whether the Commission retains power to impose fines or periodic penalties under Articles 74 and 76.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 77(4) and the separate enforcement regime in Article 78 strongly favour the imposition reading.

impact_families.title: Initial risk assessment could be completed after the application date
impact_families.effect: If the Hungarian timing prevailed, a newly designated service could reach its compliance date without completing the initial assessment of systemic risks.
impact_families.rationale: This changes the initial deadline for a core duty underpinning systemic-risk mitigation, potentially postponing the assessment on which protective measures depend.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general diligence obligation and linked mitigation duties may constrain delay; no specific additional grace period is stated.

impact_families.title: Automation reporting may exclude partly automated notices
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider excludes notices automatically classified and subsequently reviewed by staff from its reported automation count.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows one reporting metric. Disclosure of automation under Article 15(1)(e), individual notifications and substantive processing duties remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation or reporting templates could resolve the counting difference.

impact_families.title: Apparent platform permission may remove the consumer-law hosting exemption
impact_families.effect: A marketplace loses its hosting exemption in a consumer-law claim because its presentation suggests permission to trade, although consumers perceive no relationship of authority or control.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading materially expands an exception to an important liability protection. Any resulting liability still requires a basis in applicable consumer-protection law.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recitals 23–24 strongly favour an authority-based interpretation; actual liability remains a separate question.

impact_families.title: Irish national-fine rule permits a ceiling below six percent
impact_families.effect: A Member State could establish a lower statutory maximum, preventing its authority from imposing a fine reaching six percent for a serious breach.
impact_families.rationale: The difference directly changes the available maximum financial sanction for substantive breaches within national enforcement competence.
impact_families.uncertainty: Penalties must remain effective, proportionate and dissuasive; Commission fines are governed separately.

impact_families.title: Article 3(h) omits the Union-law compatibility condition
impact_families.effect: Information prohibited only by incompatible national legislation could be treated as illegal content for hosting-liability or moderation mechanisms.
impact_families.rationale: The definition governs important conditions for liability exemptions and treatment of content, although official orders retain separate compatibility requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Maltese recital 12 and Union-law primacy strongly favour retaining the compatibility condition.

impact_families.title: Legal representatives’ cooperation loses an express timeliness requirement
impact_families.effect: A provider could defend staffing sufficient for effective but slower cooperation where no decision or separate provision specifies the required timing.
impact_families.rationale: The changed criterion concerns supporting resources. Decision compliance, information-production duties and applicable deadlines remain enforceable; the text does not support a broader exemption from supervision or substantive obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: Effective and appropriate cooperation may be interpreted to require timeliness in the circumstances.

impact_families.title: Irish trusted-flagger notification omits the Board
impact_families.effect: A Coordinator could notify the Commission alone of a trusted-flagger suspension, without sending the Board the required identifying information directly.
impact_families.rationale: The change removes a specific administrative communication. Commission publication, trusted-flagger status conditions and platform obligations remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: General cooperation duties and the shared information system may supply another route for informing the Board.

impact_families.title: Interim measures may require manifest unlawfulness
impact_families.effect: The Commission cannot order urgent interim protection against serious harm because a provisionally substantiated infringement is not manifestly unlawful.
impact_families.rationale: A stricter threshold could prevent an important protective intervention during an investigation, despite the expressly required risk of serious damage to service recipients.
impact_families.uncertainty: The interim context may support reading the Czech expression as a preliminary assessment rather than a higher threshold.

impact_families.title: Necessary trusted-flagger guidance becomes discretionary
impact_families.effect: The Commission could decline to issue guidance after determining that guidance on trusted-flagger status, suspension or revocation is necessary.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns interpretive assistance. Eligibility, priority treatment, investigation and revocation requirements remain directly applicable without that guidance.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may align the permission with the English conditional duty; necessity itself remains evaluative.

impact_families.title: Irish periodic-penalty formula omits the reference year and daily accrual
impact_families.effect: A person subject to a Commission coercive payment could obtain a different payment calculation by contesting daily accrual or use of the preceding financial year.
impact_families.rationale: The omitted specifications directly determine the calculation and accumulation of potentially substantial financial liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: Periodicity and Article 52(4) support harmonization, but Article 76 supplies no express equivalent specifications.

impact_families.title: Crisis-response weighting duty expressly concerns opinions
impact_families.effect: If the distinct-opinions reading prevailed, the Commission could owe heightened consideration to subsequent Board opinions without owing that same express weighting duty to the recommendation supporting its crisis decision.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change concerns advisory weighting. Recommendations remain prerequisites; necessity, proportionality, temporal limits and provider choice remain operative. The wording does not independently establish a major change in permissible compulsory measures.
impact_families.uncertainty: Opinions may encompass recommendations contextually. No actual crisis decision or resulting measure is established.

impact_families.title: Risk assessments may exclude risks arising from use outside the Union
impact_families.effect: If the territorial restriction prevailed, a provider could omit Union electoral risks attributed solely to foreign use, where those risks were not independently captured through the design or functioning limb.
impact_families.rationale: Excluding such systemic risks materially narrows the core assessment obligation and the corresponding Article 35 mitigation duty, which follows the risks identified under Article 34.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 34(2), the enumerated risks and recitals strongly support assessment regardless of the manipulation’s origin.

impact_families.title: Romanian requires researchers to have no commercial interests
impact_families.effect: An otherwise eligible researcher whose unrelated commercial interests do not compromise independence could be denied statutory research access or have existing vetted access terminated.
impact_families.rationale: The stricter condition can remove eligibility for the substantive data-access framework, including public-data access under paragraph 12 and continuing access under paragraph 10.
impact_families.uncertainty: Interests may be interpreted as interests affecting the particular research, substantially narrowing the discrepancy.

impact_families.title: Risk mitigation may concern a decision about dispute-settlement bodies
impact_families.effect: A provider treats action concerning a dispute-settlement body's institutional status as the listed mitigation measure instead of implementing that body's dispute outcomes.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects an illustrative mitigation measure. The general duty to implement effective mitigation and Article 21's good-faith participation obligation remain; dispute outcomes are not independently binding.
impact_families.uncertainty: Articles 21 and 24 strongly support reading the provision as referring to dispute outcomes.

impact_families.title: Portuguese describes safeguards for content concerning law rather than all lawful content
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading governed, a provider could retain Article 7 protection for voluntary moderation despite lacking this specific safeguard against unjustified removal of lawful content unrelated to law.
impact_families.rationale: The difference could materially alter conditions protecting lawful expression and preserving eligibility for intermediary liability exemptions.
impact_families.uncertainty: General rights protections strongly favour harmonization; Articles 4–6 conditions and separate moderation duties remain applicable.

impact_families.title: Romanian narrows the express audience-publication duty to platform providers
impact_families.effect: A search-engine-only provider not yet designated as very large could omit routine public audience figures while remaining obliged to supply updated figures on an authority’s request.
impact_families.rationale: The changed outcome concerns periodic public reporting. Article 24(3) preserves information requests, and Article 33 permits designation using other available evidence.
impact_families.uncertainty: References to search engines within Article 24(2), recital 65 and Article 33 strongly favor harmonization.

impact_families.title: Management body may face an additional independence requirement
impact_families.effect: A provider whose management body includes senior management could need to alter that body's composition or governance arrangements to meet the additional independence condition.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading imposes a structural requirement on the body responsible for compliance oversight and systemic-risk governance under Article 41.
impact_families.uncertainty: The clause could instead be understood as describing the compliance head, consistently with the surrounding independence requirements.

impact_families.title: Initial systemic-risk assessment may start at the application date
impact_families.effect: A designated provider could reach the application date without a completed initial systemic-risk assessment and claim that undertaking it from that date satisfies the timing requirement.
impact_families.rationale: This alters the initial deadline for a core preventive obligation underpinning the tailored mitigation required by Article 35.
impact_families.uncertainty: Immediate identification and mitigation duties support readiness at application; the wording does not establish any specific permitted delay.

impact_families.title: Member State recipient reporting could exclude very large search engines
impact_families.effect: A very large online search engine could omit the Member State breakdown while publishing its Union-wide recipient figures and general transparency reports.
impact_families.rationale: The omission removes a specific reporting detail. Articles 24 and 33 preserve recipient counting and designation, and Article 42(1) preserves general transparency reporting.
impact_families.uncertainty: The surrounding provisions support including search engines; the report cross-reference can be harmonized contextually.

impact_families.title: Crisis definition potentially permits earlier activation
impact_families.effect: The Commission could activate binding crisis assessment, mitigation and reporting duties before extraordinary circumstances have produced a serious threat.
impact_families.rationale: The difference potentially expands the threshold for exceptional compulsory intervention affecting providers’ services, even though necessity, proportionality and duration safeguards remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 91 and the prospective nature of a threat strongly support harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Latvian procedural-fine ceiling omits the annual-income alternative
impact_families.effect: A person with annual income but no relevant turnover could challenge an income-based fine for refusing an investigative request or inspection.
impact_families.rationale: Removing an alternative calculation base can materially restrict the financial sanction available for non-cooperation under Articles 51 and 52.
impact_families.uncertainty: Classification of particular receipts depends on the incorporated turnover definition and applicable financial rules.

impact_families.title: Union seat replaces establishment as an automatic connecting factor
impact_families.effect: An overseas-seated provider with a Union establishment could lose automatic qualification and fall outside the Regulation if no alternative factual connection were established.
impact_families.rationale: Through Article 3(d), the changed connecting factor could determine whether the Regulation’s substantive duties and recipient protections apply.
impact_families.uncertainty: A Union branch could itself satisfy the factual criteria; contextual interpretation could equate seat with establishment.

impact_families.title: Representative duty may extend to providers already established in the Union
impact_families.effect: An overseas-seated provider with a Union establishment fails to appoint a representative. Under the expanded duty, Article 56(7) could permit enforcement by any Member State.
impact_families.rationale: The appointment trigger can activate a material exception to exclusive establishment-based supervision. This supports a major jurisdictional consequence beyond the administrative arrangement, while safeguards against duplicate proceedings remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Harmonization may prevent the expansion; wider enforcement competence requires failure to appoint, not merely an overseas seat.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian initial risk-assessment wording starts from the application date
impact_families.effect: A designated provider could start its initial systemic-risk assessment when the obligations become applicable and finish afterward, instead of having completed it by that date.
impact_families.rationale: This alters the initial deadline for the core assessment duty underpinning mitigation of illegal-content, fundamental-rights, public-security and public-health risks.
impact_families.uncertainty: The continuing diligence and mitigation duties may require immediate compliance and restrict any permissible delay.

impact_families.title: Advertisement repository statistic omits actual reach
impact_families.effect: If the population-count reading prevailed, a provider could supply its service-recipient total in an advertisement entry without disclosing the advertisement’s actual reach.
impact_families.rationale: This changes a specific public transparency metric. Other advertisement disclosures, advertising restrictions, risk-management obligations and Article 40 data-access powers remain; the established consequence is narrower than removal of the transparency regime.
impact_families.uncertainty: The advertisement-specific context and recital 95 strongly favour actual reach.

impact_families.title: Alternative conditions may widen exclusion from online-platform status
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, a hosting service with substantial but purely ancillary public dissemination, satisfying the remaining exclusion conditions, could avoid otherwise applicable platform complaint-handling and dispute-settlement duties.
impact_families.rationale: The definition controls application of substantive platform obligations and corresponding user protections. Widening the exclusion could remove those duties even for providers otherwise outside the small-enterprise exemption.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 13’s examples support a narrower interpretation, although its general exclusion wording repeats the alternative conditions.

impact_families.title: Additional moderation reporting names search engines instead of platforms
impact_families.effect: A very large online platform could omit the additional moderation particulars, while a search-engine provider could be required to report them.
impact_families.rationale: The difference reallocates supplementary reporting particulars. General transparency, moderation and systemic-risk duties remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: The platform-specific wording within Article 42(2) strongly supports harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian recital treats platform price-setting as establishing control
impact_families.effect: A platform setting a trader’s prices could lose the hosting liability exemption without a further assessment establishing authority or control.
impact_families.rationale: The categorical illustration could remove a core liability protection through Article 6(2). It does not itself establish liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: The illustrative recital and the operative control requirement support a contextual, non-automatic assessment.

impact_families.title: Search-engine reports may trigger an additional opportunity to comment
impact_families.effect: Designation based solely on a search engine’s published Article 24(2) report requires an additional ten-working-day opportunity to comment because the report counts as other available information.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence is a limited procedural opportunity before designation. Evidence remains admissible, the threshold is unchanged, and failure to comment cannot prevent designation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The express coverage of search engines elsewhere supports treating both service types’ reports identically.

impact_families.title: Greek expressly requires free access to standards-update information
impact_families.effect: A charge for otherwise publicly available and easily accessible standards-update information could satisfy the English wording but breach the express Greek requirement.
impact_families.rationale: The changed requirement concerns the cost of ancillary update information. It does not alter substantive compliance duties or require free access to the standards themselves.
impact_families.uncertainty: Public availability and easy accessibility might already require free access in this context.

impact_families.title: Croatian changes the recipient count used when extending access restrictions
impact_families.effect: If the infringement-based count changes the proportionality assessment, a Coordinator could extend a service-access restriction that would fail an assessment counting the recipients affected by the restriction.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed factor governs renewal of restrictions on access to a service or online interface, potentially materially changing recipients’ access to lawful information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Both versions require consideration of all affected interests and prohibit undue restrictions; these safeguards strongly support harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Slovenian auditor eligibility reverses the ten-year comparison
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualified audit organisation with several consecutive years of service could be excluded under the Slovenian wording although it remains within the English ten-year tenure limit.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes an express eligibility condition for mandatory independent audits. It can prevent an organisation from performing the required role despite satisfying the maximum-tenure rule expressed in English.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 92 and the independence objective strongly favour harmonization as a maximum-tenure restriction.

impact_families.title: Latvian secrecy provision could also protect non-confidential information
impact_families.effect: An authority could decline discretionary disclosure of non-confidential information received under the Regulation where no applicable publication or access requirement governs disclosure.
impact_families.rationale: The supported residual consequence concerns discretionary transparency. Article 84’s saving clause and specific disclosure provisions constrain any broader interference with statutory information rights.
impact_families.uncertainty: The heading and surrounding confidentiality provisions strongly favour a cumulative, harmonised reading.

impact_families.title: Irish liability-exemption example omits the main-purpose qualification
impact_families.effect: Where deliberate collaboration is inferred from the example, a secondary illegal-facilitation purpose could suffice under Irish wording to deny a provider a liability exemption.
impact_families.rationale: Broadening the example used to establish non-neutrality could materially affect eligibility for the Regulation’s core liability protections.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared deliberate-collaboration principle limits the difference; losing an exemption does not itself establish liability.

impact_families.title: Slovenian standardisation provision refers to selected interfaces
