impact_families.effect: The Commission could support standards for selected recommender-system interfaces without specifically covering the controls through which recipients choose their recommendation options.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns support for voluntary standards. Articles 27 and 38 independently preserve binding transparency, selection-functionality and non-profiling-option requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: The express references to Articles 27 and 38 strongly favour interpreting the provision as covering choice interfaces.

impact_families.title: Portuguese omits the Union-law compatibility condition from Article 7
impact_families.effect: If the unqualified reading governed, a provider’s compliance with an incompatible national requirement could receive Article 7 protection against disqualification from liability exemptions solely because of those compliance measures.
impact_families.rationale: The omission could materially broaden the statutory protection preserving eligibility for the core liability exemptions in Articles 4–6.
impact_families.uncertainty: Union-law primacy supports harmonization; underlying exemption conditions and liability for separate unlawful conduct remain unaffected.

impact_families.title: Article 48(2) strengthens responsibility for crisis-protocol content
impact_families.effect: A protocol containing none of the listed measures could breach the Commission’s duty even after reasonable efforts to obtain their inclusion.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns an ancillary protocol-content responsibility within a voluntary framework, without expanding compulsory provider measures.
impact_families.uncertainty: The voluntary framework supports interpreting the obligation as one of effort.

impact_families.title: Portuguese prior-sanction guidance identifies natural rather than legal persons
impact_families.effect: If the natural-person restriction governed, a corporate provider could face a DSA fine without the express requirement to consider final sanctions already imposed for the same facts under another regime.
impact_families.rationale: Removing this specific consideration could materially affect cumulative financial liability within Article 74’s turnover-based fine framework.
impact_families.uncertainty: Proportionality and protection against double punishment remain; neither a particular reduction nor an actual increased fine is established.

impact_families.title: Advertising disclosures require prominence without expressly requiring concision
impact_families.effect: An unnecessarily lengthy advertising disclosure could comply if recipients can still identify the required information clearly, prominently, unambiguously and in real time.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects presentation length without removing disclosure subjects, accessibility or real-time identification. No major additional consequence follows from length alone under those retained conditions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Clarity and real-time identification may require sufficient brevity in practice.

impact_families.title: Recipient-count reporting refers to a different delegated power
impact_families.effect: A provider could contest the express methodological requirement for its published recipient count because the Polish reporting provision points to threshold-adjustment acts.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects the reporting instruction. Article 33(3) expressly connects counting methodology to Article 24(2), and Article 33(4) preserves designation using other information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 33(3) strongly supports harmonization; no delegated methodology act is supplied.

impact_families.title: Advertising-code stakeholder category omits service recipients
impact_families.effect: The Commission could encourage development of an advertising code without specifically encouraging organisations representing service recipients to participate.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns participation in voluntary code development. Binding advertising duties, civil-society participation and the codes’ protective objectives remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The open stakeholder list and recital 107 support including recipient representatives through contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Illegal-purchase notices may omit nonjudicial remedies
impact_families.effect: A marketplace informs purchasers of an illegal product about court proceedings but omits an applicable nonjudicial dispute-resolution route.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns the scope of remedial guidance. It does not remove remedies, alter entitlement to compensation or displace preserved consumer-protection rules.
impact_families.uncertainty: A broader contextual interpretation of judicial review could encompass additional remedies.

impact_families.title: Irish researcher-eligibility condition refers to compliance-monitoring purposes
impact_families.effect: A systemic-risk research project could be refused vetted status because its planned activities do not also pursue paragraph 2’s compliance-monitoring purposes.
impact_families.rationale: All paragraph 8 conditions govern vetted status and compelled data access; the changed reference can defeat an important access entitlement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Paragraphs 4 and 8(e), together with recital 97, strongly support reading the reference as paragraph 4.

impact_families.title: Other authorities’ system access lacks an express necessity condition
impact_families.effect: Another competent authority could receive system access useful for its assigned regulatory tasks without establishing that access is necessary.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated change concerns institutional access arrangements. Assigned-task limits, system security, professional secrecy and applicable data-protection rules remain; unrestricted disclosure or a major change to substantive investigative powers is not supported.
impact_families.uncertainty: Purpose protection and proportionality may lead interpreters to require necessity despite the wording.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian caching condition refers to removal of the source itself
impact_families.effect: A caching provider could retain an item after learning of its removal at origin and retain the exemption because the originating source remains available, assuming the other exemption conditions are satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading narrows a condition for retaining a core liability exemption. Article 5(2) separately preserves orders to terminate or prevent infringements.
impact_families.uncertainty: The source may contextually mean the original information or its specific location.

impact_families.title: Slovenian purchase-notification period runs from awareness of illegality
impact_families.effect: A consumer purchasing an illegal product one month before the platform discovers its illegality could lose individual notification despite the platform having the consumer’s contact details.
impact_families.rationale: The temporal reversal can remove the information entitlement for the retrospective purchaser group. Public information under paragraph 2 and preserved consumer-law remedies do not replace that individual notification entitlement.
impact_families.uncertainty: The reference to completed purchases and the consumer-protection purpose strongly favour a retrospective interpretation.

impact_families.title: Withdrawal provision expressly names only platform status
impact_families.effect: If the restrictive reading prevailed, a search engine below the threshold for an uninterrupted year could lose its mandatory withdrawal entitlement and remain subject to designation-dependent obligations.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 33(6), 34, 35 and 37 link withdrawal to cessation of substantial systemic-risk assessment, mitigation and independent-audit duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Search-engine references in paragraphs 5 and 6 strongly support applying withdrawal to both service categories.

impact_families.title: Access-restriction recital may impose a narrower last-resort condition
impact_families.effect: A court could refuse temporary access restriction because another statutory power exists, although it cannot avert the serious harm and all other Article 51(3) conditions are met.
impact_families.rationale: If that restrictive interpretation prevailed, an important enforcement measure addressing persistent infringement involving a criminal threat to life or safety could become unavailable.
impact_families.uncertainty: The operative harm-prevention tests in Articles 51(3) and 82(1) strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Article 8 omits the limitation to general monitoring obligations
impact_families.effect: A provider could resist an otherwise permissible monitoring obligation directed at a specific case by invoking the unqualified prohibition.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading expands a core prohibition and restricts the availability of targeted supervisory obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Maltese heading and recital 30 expressly support allowing monitoring obligations in specific cases.

impact_families.title: The illustrative dismissal safeguard extends beyond reform-related dismissal
impact_families.effect: During institutional restructuring, a Member State could treat premature dismissals unrelated to the reform as falling within the recital’s illustrative safeguard.
impact_families.rationale: The difference broadens an example of possible independence safeguards. Its permissive wording and Article 50 do not establish an additional mandatory right to complete a term.
impact_families.uncertainty: The merger context supports a narrower harmonized interpretation of the Czech alternative.

impact_families.title: Penalty-enforcement limitation refers to making the final decision
impact_families.effect: Without intervening interruption or suspension, enforcement could become time-barred five years after adoption while remaining timely under a later finality trigger.
impact_families.rationale: The difference can determine whether a Commission fine or coercive payment remains recoverable, materially changing financial liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: The reference to a final decision may incorporate legal finality; enforcement actions and specified suspensions can prevent expiry.

impact_families.title: Terms summary requirement substitutes accuracy for concision
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, a designated provider could supply an accurate but unnecessarily lengthy summary without violating an express operative concision requirement.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns presentation length. Summary provision, accessibility, machine readability, clear language and information about remedies remain mandatory; no independent loss of a remedy or core entitlement is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The ordinary meaning of summary and recital 48 strongly support preserving concision through contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: The two-month reporting deadline may qualify the measures instead
impact_families.effect: The coordinator could notify the institutions after two months while reporting measures taken during that period, without breaching an express two-month notification deadline.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns the timing of inter-authority reporting. It does not remove investigative duties, enforcement powers or the obligation to inform the institutions.
impact_families.uncertainty: English attachment is itself somewhat ambiguous; the cooperation framework supports timely notification.

impact_families.title: Researcher access may require absence of commercial interests
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualified researcher with an unrelated commercial interest is denied vetted status or access under Article 40(12), despite conducting research independently.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading changes eligibility for a statutory data-access entitlement, potentially excluding the researcher entirely rather than requiring additional disclosure or safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: Research-specific vetting may confine the condition to commercial interests that compromise research independence.

impact_families.title: Article 33(6) omits search engines from the published designation list
impact_families.effect: The Commission could publish and update a list containing designated platforms but omitting designated search engines.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change affects public notice, without removing search-engine designation or making substantive obligations depend on publication.
impact_families.uncertainty: The surrounding provisions consistently include search engines and favour their inclusion in the list.

impact_families.title: Different turnover bases for the Commission’s daily penalty ceiling
impact_families.effect: If the annual-turnover reading prevailed, a provider failing to comply with a Commission decision could face daily penalties capped at 5 % of annual worldwide turnover instead of its daily average.
impact_families.rationale: The competing calculation bases materially change the maximum recurring financial liability used to compel compliance under Article 76.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 52(4), proportionality and contextual interpretation strongly support harmonising the ceiling around daily averages.

impact_families.title: Advertising disclosure could cover additional targeting parameters
impact_families.effect: A platform could need to explain a secondary targeting parameter omitted from a disclosure describing only the main parameters.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the detail of advertising disclosures. The advertising permissions and profiling prohibitions remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 68 and the meaningful, concise-information requirements strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Search-engine definition may include searches confined to selected websites
impact_families.effect: A selected-site search service answering queries on any subject could enter the search-engine category and, if Article 33’s audience threshold and designation requirements are met, acquire systemic-risk and independent-audit duties.
impact_families.rationale: The definition controls eligibility for a regulatory category carrying core assessment, mitigation and audit duties. The major consequence depends on satisfying the additional statutory designation conditions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Universal coverage may be implicit in Spanish; no particular service’s classification or designation is established.

impact_families.title: Latvian trader-traceability rule substitutes an electronic document
impact_families.effect: A platform could accept an electronic document instead of electronic identification when determining whether a trader may use its marketplace.
impact_families.rationale: Article 30 links documentation to trader admission and suspension. The absent incorporated definitions prevent determining whether the change is ancillary or materially weakens the identification condition.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 3 of Regulation 910/2014 is not supplied; its definitions are material to the impact assessment.

impact_families.title: Irish online-platform exclusion separates the minor and ancillary conditions
impact_families.effect: A technically dependent, substantial ancillary dissemination feature could escape online-platform classification where its integration does not circumvent the Regulation.
impact_families.rationale: Losing online-platform classification can remove the additional platform duties, including internal complaint handling and interface protections, while hosting duties remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 13 expressly supports cumulative conditions and gives an example excluding substantial ancillary social-network comments from the exception.

impact_families.title: Accessibility-code encouragement specifies commencement instead of a deadline
impact_families.effect: The Commission could promote a common commencement on 18 August 2025 instead of promoting application no later than that date, including earlier implementation.
impact_families.rationale: The changed outcome concerns an ancillary encouragement timetable. It neither delays binding accessibility requirements nor independently creates provider obligations or sanctions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Both versions permit application on the named date; practical implementation may coincide.

impact_families.title: Advertising codes may face a mandatory commencement deadline
impact_families.effect: An advertising code schedules application after 18 August 2025; the Swedish reading would require an earlier commencement.
impact_families.rationale: The changed requirement concerns the timetable for voluntary codes. Articles 46(1) and (4) do not make participation compulsory, and statutory advertising obligations remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The voluntary-code context supports interpreting the date as a target.

impact_families.title: The special fine ceiling may omit ordinary non-response
impact_families.effect: If the restrictive reading prevailed, a provider ignoring an investigative information order could face a 6% turnover ceiling instead of the special 1% ceiling.
impact_families.rationale: The difference could materially increase maximum financial liability for the same procedural infringement under Articles 51 and 52.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 74’s parallel rule and proportionate interpretation of penalties strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Non-confidential versions accompany different audit documents
impact_families.effect: A provider attaches a non-confidential audit report without preparing a separate accompanying non-confidential implementation-report version under Article 37(2), while complying with Article 42.
impact_families.rationale: Article 42 still requires publication of both reports, permits confidentiality redactions and requires complete reports for authorities. The supported difference concerns document preparation and accompaniment.
impact_families.uncertainty: The references to paragraphs 4 and 6 and Article 42 support restoring the intended two-report requirement.

impact_families.title: Dutch wording could postpone completion of the initial risk assessment
impact_families.effect: A newly designated provider could reach the application date without completing its initial systemic-risk assessment, beginning the assessment only then.
impact_families.rationale: This removes the express completion deadline for a core systemic-risk duty that supplies the basis for tailored mitigation under Article 35.
impact_families.uncertainty: Immediate application of the general duty constrains delay; assessments before critical new functionalities remain required.

impact_families.title: Audit recital addresses inconclusive findings outside the audit scope
impact_families.effect: An audit opinion could be expected to explain an inability to conclude on excluded elements, in addition to the explanations required in the audit report.
impact_families.rationale: The remaining possible consequence concerns explanatory documentation. Article 37 preserves the substantive audit scope and explanations for elements that could not be audited.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 37 and the surrounding recital strongly constrain any independent effect of the reversed scope.

impact_families.title: Voluntary access blocking lacks express liability-exemption protection
impact_families.effect: A provider voluntarily blocking access, without deleting content or acting under a legal requirement, could lose protection against disqualification from a liability exemption solely because of that intervention.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed scope affects eligibility for the central liability exemptions in Articles 4–6. Actual liability would still require an independent legal basis.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 26 and a functional understanding of removal strongly favor protecting voluntary blocking too.

impact_families.title: Search engines are omitted from mandatory termination of designation
impact_families.effect: If the omission governed, a designated search engine below the threshold for a full year could lack mandatory termination and remain subject to additional systemic-risk, audit and supervisory-fee duties.
impact_families.rationale: The difference could remove an important entitlement to exit a designation carrying substantial continuing obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 33(6) expressly anticipates termination for search engines and strongly supports a harmonized reading.

impact_families.title: Article 56(4) omits the main-establishment limitation on national enforcement competence
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, a secondary-establishment Member State could order cessation and impose fines for a designated provider’s Article 20 infringement before Commission proceedings began.
impact_families.rationale: This would materially expand coercive enforcement jurisdiction under Articles 51–52, including access to fines capped at 6% of annual worldwide turnover. Substantive duties and penalty ceilings would remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: The main-establishment rule, Coordinator definition and recitals strongly favor harmonization; no actual enforcement outcome is established.

impact_families.title: Article 13(1) makes representative designation appear optional
impact_families.effect: A provider offering Union services without a Union establishment could contest liability for failing to appoint a legal representative.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading removes a core organizational duty supporting receipt and enforcement of regulatory decisions, even though alternative enforcement jurisdiction survives.
impact_families.uncertainty: The remaining article, recital 44 and Article 56(7) strongly support mandatory designation.

impact_families.title: The marketplace exemption may depend on traders’ size
impact_families.effect: A provider exceeding the small-enterprise thresholds, but not designated very large, could claim exemption from Articles 30–32 because its marketplace serves only small traders.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading changes eligibility for exemption from trader traceability, compliance-by-design and purchaser-information obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 57 strongly supports provider-size eligibility; the very-large-platform exception remains applicable.

impact_families.title: Irish illegal-content definition omits the national-law compatibility condition
impact_families.effect: Content prohibited solely by an incompatible national rule could be treated as illegal content when applying moderation duties and liability-exemption conditions.
impact_families.rationale: The definition determines the reach of important duties and liability protections across the Regulation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Irish recital 12, Union-law primacy and repeated compatibility requirements strongly oppose the broader reading.

impact_families.title: Automation reporting may omit notices also reviewed by people
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider excludes notices processed through both automated tools and human review from its reported automation count.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows one transparency metric. General disclosures about automation and substantive duties governing notice processing remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Reporting templates are outside the supplied evidence and could clarify the required count.

impact_families.title: Recital 133 misidentifies the compliance benchmark
impact_families.effect: The Commission could describe its consideration of a departure from Board advice by reference to compliance with a decision instead of the Regulation.
impact_families.rationale: The changed benchmark occurs in explanatory guidance. Article 63(2) preserves the operative explanation duty, and the express non-binding qualification prevents deriving an independent compliance obligation from Board advice.
impact_families.uncertainty: The decision’s referent is unclear, and the operative framework strongly supports correction through interpretation.

impact_families.title: Territorial limits on content orders omit express strict necessity
impact_families.effect: An otherwise legally authorized content order with wider territorial reach could satisfy the Regulation’s minimum conditions where ordinary necessity is accepted but strict necessity would exclude that reach.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition protects expression and access to information against geographically excessive restrictions. Weakening that safeguard can materially affect those entitlements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 36 and the retained Charter requirements strongly support strict necessity; Article 9 supplies no independent ordering power.

impact_families.title: Romanian adds Commission requests as a trigger for researcher data access
impact_families.effect: A Commission request alone could require a provider to disclose non-public data to eligible vetted researchers, although the English provision requires a Coordinator request.
impact_families.rationale: Adding an independent trigger materially expands a substantive disclosure duty, including access to confidential information where the applicable safeguards permit it.
impact_families.uncertainty: Coordinator vetting and amendment powers may constrain or reconcile the additional Commission role.

impact_families.title: Misuse recital contemplates measures breaching the platform’s own terms
impact_families.effect: If the recital’s disputed permission were given legal effect, a platform could justify an additional misuse-related suspension despite a contractual restriction on that measure, while remaining subject to mandatory statutory safeguards.
impact_families.rationale: Permitting departure from contractual moderation safeguards could materially weaken a recipient’s entitlement to continued service under the agreed terms.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recital cannot independently override Articles 14 and 23 or applicable contractual law; the permissive interpretation is strongly contestable.

impact_families.title: The recipient fee ceiling is expressed as a recommendation
impact_families.effect: A recipient could be charged a non-nominal initial fee without an enforceable nominal-fee ceiling, potentially preventing use of certified out-of-court dispute settlement.
impact_families.rationale: The difference could materially weaken access to an important redress mechanism. Reimbursement after success does not eliminate an initial financial barrier.
impact_families.uncertainty: The binding regulatory setting and certification requirements may support treating the Danish formulation as mandatory.

impact_families.title: Order-processing reports could require an average instead of a median
impact_families.effect: A provider could publish an arithmetic average for order-processing times while omitting the median, satisfying the Italian reading but not the English wording.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence is a different mandatory reporting statistic. The underlying duties to acknowledge, process and report the effect given to orders remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Reporting templates adopted under Article 15(3) are outside the supplied evidence.

impact_families.title: Latvian auditor qualification combines codes and standards
impact_families.effect: An otherwise suitable organisation demonstrating objectivity and ethics through appropriate standards alone could be excluded from conducting the mandatory independent audit.
impact_families.rationale: The cumulative condition materially changes eligibility to perform a legally required audit and restricts providers’ choice of qualifying auditor.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 92 and the voluntary-standards provisions support a more flexible, harmonised interpretation.

impact_families.title: Commission penalty-payment ceiling lacks express daily accrual
impact_families.effect: A provider continuing to disregard a Commission compliance decision could argue that the percentage ceiling applies once to the whole payment rather than anew each day.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading materially changes cumulative financial liability under the Commission’s coercive enforcement mechanism.
impact_families.uncertainty: The starting date, coercive purpose and definitive calculation support recurring accrual without expressly stating its daily unit.

impact_families.title: Referral condition attributes disagreement to the Committee
impact_families.effect: The Board could be unable to refer an assessment solely because it disagrees, unless the Committee also supplies the disagreement required by the German wording.
impact_families.rationale: This changes one procedural referral ground. Other referral grounds and the underlying investigative and enforcement powers remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 129 and Articles 58 to 60 strongly support interpreting the reference as the Board.

impact_families.title: Nondisclosure duty may extend to nonconfidential information
impact_families.effect: An auditor or official covered by Article 84 is prohibited from voluntarily disclosing nonconfidential information acquired under the Regulation outside the exchanges and uses preserved by Chapter IV.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading materially expands a direct nondisclosure duty across the provision’s covered participants and information. The professional-secrecy limitation no longer governs its first category.
impact_families.uncertainty: The heading, statutory publication duties and express saving support limits; no actual disclosure or sanction is established.

impact_families.title: Crisis measures may address the threat beyond the service’s contribution
impact_families.effect: A binding crisis decision could require a provider to address aspects of a serious threat beyond the contribution made by its service.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading broadens the substantive objective of compulsory crisis action. Provider choice and proportionality constrain implementation without necessarily restoring the contribution limit.
impact_families.uncertainty: The assessment required by Article 36(1)(a) strongly supports limiting action to the service’s contribution.

impact_families.title: The content-moderation definition may narrow disclosures about lawful content
impact_families.effect: A provider could omit detailed accuracy and error-rate disclosures for automated tools used exclusively to moderate lawful contractual violations, treating those tools as outside Article 15(1)(e).
impact_families.rationale: The residual consequence concerns transparency detail. Express contractual-violation provisions preserve reporting coverage, reasons, complaint rights and systemic-risk obligations independently of the disputed definition.
impact_families.uncertainty: The definition’s non-exhaustive wording and express contractual-violation provisions strongly support broader coverage.

impact_families.title: Slovenian general secrecy duty refers specifically to business secrets
impact_families.effect: An external expert involved in enforcement could disclose confidential investigation information that is not a business secret without breaching Article 84 under the narrower Slovenian reading.
impact_families.rationale: The reading removes a core non-disclosure duty for non-business information protected by professional secrecy. The surrounding provisions impose specific safeguards without expressly restoring this general prohibition for all enforcement participants.
impact_families.uncertainty: An autonomous professional-secrecy interpretation may resolve the wording; separate rules may independently prohibit a particular disclosure.

impact_families.title: Latvian illegal-content definition omits the national-law compatibility condition
impact_families.effect: If the unqualified definition prevailed, content prohibited only by incompatible national legislation could be treated as illegal for hosting-liability and content-moderation mechanisms.
impact_families.rationale: The definition feeds central liability and moderation rules, potentially altering providers’ legal position and recipients’ ability to impart information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 12, related operative safeguards and Union-law primacy strongly oppose the expanded reading.

impact_families.title: Commission referral may require systematic conduct as well as systemic infringement
impact_families.effect: A Coordinator could be prevented from using Article 65(2) for an isolated structural infringement outside Section 5 because systematic conduct has not been demonstrated.
impact_families.rationale: The changed condition concerns one referral channel. Commission investigation and enforcement on its own initiative, and referrals concerning Section 5, remain available.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 65(3)(b) and recitals 125 and 138 strongly support a systemic interpretation.

impact_families.title: Notice particulars may be alternative rather than cumulative
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could design its notice mechanism around alternative identifying particulars rather than expressly facilitating both a location and necessary supplementary details.
impact_families.rationale: The possible change concerns notice-mechanism requirements. Sufficient precision and the independent Article 16(3) actual-knowledge condition continue to constrain legal consequences.
impact_families.uncertainty: The alternative can also describe different means of supplying the required exact location.

impact_families.title: Reporting recommendations lose an express appropriateness qualification
impact_families.effect: A coordinator finding no appropriate improvements could nevertheless have to formulate recommendations in its biennial report.
impact_families.rationale: The additional requirement is an ancillary reporting element. It does not itself change certification, dispute outcomes, fees, deadlines or binding obligations of settlement bodies.
impact_families.uncertainty: A statement that no improvement is needed might satisfy the Polish requirement.

impact_families.title: Dispute statistics count handled cases rather than received cases
impact_families.effect: A certified dispute body could omit received but unprocessed cases from its annual count, with the same narrower count appearing in the coordinator’s biennial report.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects oversight statistics. Access to dispute settlement, the receipt-based decision deadline and the coordinator’s power to request additional information remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Handling might be interpreted to include registering every received dispute.

impact_families.title: Latvian initial risk-assessment timing starts at the application date
impact_families.effect: A designated provider could reach its application date without a completed initial systemic-risk assessment and begin that assessment on the date itself.
impact_families.rationale: This changes the initial deadline for a core systemic-risk duty and could postpone the assessment informing tailored mitigation under Article 35.
impact_families.uncertainty: Immediate diligence and mitigation duties constrain delay; the text establishes no fixed grace period.

impact_families.title: National penalty-payment ceiling lacks an express daily accrual unit
impact_families.effect: For noncompliance lasting several days, a provider could invoke a single overall ceiling of 5% of the daily financial base instead of a ceiling applying each day.
impact_families.rationale: An overall ceiling would materially reduce cumulative coercive liability and the continuing financial pressure to comply with enforcement or investigative orders.
impact_families.uncertainty: The starting date and coercive purpose support recurring payments, but do not expressly supply the daily accrual unit.

impact_families.title: The complaint forum may depend on residence rather than presence
impact_families.effect: A recipient residing outside the Union receives a service during a visit to a Member State but is denied the Article 53 complaint route there.
impact_families.rationale: The residence condition could remove access to an important statutory complaint mechanism where the recipient has no residence or establishment elsewhere in the Union.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 2 and Czech recital 118 strongly support a location-based interpretation.

impact_families.title: Inspection access may exclude an inspected third party’s own systems
impact_families.effect: An inspected audit organisation could resist compulsory direct access to its own audit-processing systems relevant to suspected provider non-compliance, because Article 69(2)(d) expressly identifies only platform or search-engine systems.
impact_families.rationale: This would materially narrow a compulsory investigative power over expressly covered third parties. Records examination, information requests and questioning remain available, but need not provide equivalent direct access to functioning systems.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 69(1), the remaining inspection powers and recital 141 strongly favour a broader contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Latvian researcher-access provision additionally names the Commission
impact_families.effect: For already vetted research, the Commission could directly require qualifying data access without a further access request from the establishment Coordinator.
impact_families.rationale: The additional authority could independently trigger a substantial duty to disclose potentially non-public data to researchers, while existing qualification and purpose restrictions remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Coordinator-controlled vetting, amendment and termination procedures may constrain or harmonise the added Commission role.

impact_families.title: Potentially broader trigger for pre-launch risk assessment
impact_families.effect: A designated very large service introducing a functionality with a credibly possible but unlikely critical impact would have to assess systemic risks before deployment under the broader Polish reading.
impact_families.rationale: This materially expands the deployments subject to a core preventive duty. Annual assessment does not replace the separate pre-launch requirement, although assessment remains proportionate.
impact_families.uncertainty: The risk context may harmonize the modal expressions; neither version supplies a numerical probability threshold.

impact_families.title: Caching immunity may turn on the purpose of interference
impact_families.effect: A caching provider otherwise meeting Article 5’s conditions could retain immunity despite interfering with lawful usage measurement for a purpose other than obtaining usage information.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition determines access to a liability exemption. Recital 17 confirms that these exemptions cover any type of liability concerning illegal content.
impact_families.uncertainty: The neutrality requirements and the clause’s technical context support harmonization; loss of exemption does not itself establish liability.

impact_families.title: Commission's crisis-protocol duty could require a result
impact_families.effect: A protocol containing none of the listed measures could fail the Italian requirement despite the Commission having made reasonable efforts to secure inclusion.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns the Commission's responsibility for negotiated protocol content. It neither makes participation compulsory nor directly imposes a particular operational measure on providers.
impact_families.uncertainty: The voluntary framework may qualify how an obligation to ensure inclusion is interpreted.

impact_families.title: Transparency reports measure execution notification rather than execution itself
impact_families.effect: A provider could report the median interval ending with notification of execution without separately disclosing the median interval ending with execution itself.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes an aggregate transparency metric. It does not alter the underlying order or the separate notification requirements in Articles 9 and 10.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation or reporting templates could align the metrics; no implementing templates are supplied.

impact_families.title: Researcher access may lack the requested-interface requirement
impact_families.effect: A provider could dispute paragraph 7’s requirement to use a researcher’s requested interface while providing effective access through another suitable method.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence concerns the delivery interface. Paragraph 4 retains the substantive access duty, and paragraphs 5–6 regulate alternative access arrangements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Technical rules under paragraph 13 are outside the packet and may independently require particular interfaces.

impact_families.title: Illegal-content definition omits the national-law compatibility qualification
impact_families.effect: Content prohibited solely by Union-incompatible national law could be treated as illegal for notice handling, hosting-liability conditions or suspension for repeated manifestly illegal content.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed qualification controls a central definition affecting content restrictions and liability exemptions, beyond orders separately conditioned on Union-law compatibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 12 and the Regulation’s Union-law safeguards strongly oppose applying incompatible national law.

impact_families.title: Dutch caching exemption could require action before knowledge of an order
impact_families.effect: A caching provider unaware of a removal order could lose its liability exemption for failing to act after issuance, although English retains the knowledge condition.
impact_families.rationale: Loss of a statutory liability exemption is a major change to legal protection. It does not itself establish liability, which still requires an applicable legal basis.
impact_families.uncertainty: Knowledge may be implied contextually; Article 8 prohibits general monitoring, and liability requires a separate legal basis.

impact_families.title: Article 58(2) ambiguously attaches the three-Coordinator request
impact_families.effect: The Board could initiate an Article 58 assessment without three Coordinators’ support, including during a Commission investigation initiated on another basis.
impact_families.rationale: The changed gateway triggers national assessment and response duties and possible referral under Article 59. It does not itself authorize sanctions or override Articles 56 and 66.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 58(1), the cooperation structure and Article 60 support treating the request as a separate prerequisite.

impact_families.title: Accessibility-code objective specifies visibility rather than perceivability
impact_families.effect: When preparing accessibility codes, the Commission treats visual presentation and general functionality as the express objectives, giving less specific attention to nonvisual perception and operation through assistive methods.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects the specification of code objectives. Article 47 preserves full and equal participation, disability accessibility and compliance with applicable law; it creates no exemption from those requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Swedish recital 105 directly supports perceivability and operability, substantially strengthening a harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Stakeholder-involvement guidance is narrowed to platforms
impact_families.effect: A search-engine provider could treat the specific recommendation to involve representatives, independent experts and civil society organisations as inapplicable when designing assessments and mitigation.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns supplementary recital guidance. Both versions retain consultation with affected groups in the opening sentence and the operative assessment and mitigation obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: The opening sentence and shared methodology support applying the guidance to both service categories.

impact_families.title: Recommender controls may lack a direct-and-easy-access requirement
impact_families.effect: A platform could provide a usable recommender control through extra interactions within the relevant section while disputing any separate requirement for direct and easy access.
impact_families.rationale: Selection and modification at any time remain required, and Article 25 constrains material impairment of choice. The supported residual difference concerns accessibility convenience.
impact_families.uncertainty: The retained functionality requirement and recital 70 may support an equivalent usability standard.

impact_families.title: National enforcement competence may extend beyond the main establishment
impact_families.effect: Before Commission proceedings begin, a Member State hosting only a secondary establishment exercises supervisory and enforcement powers over a designated provider's obligations outside Chapter III, Section 5.
impact_families.rationale: If that reading prevailed, it would change the State entitled to exercise coercive powers under Articles 51 and 52, including cessation orders and substantial fines.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 56(1), Article 3(n) and Recitals 123 and 125 strongly support main-establishment competence.

impact_families.title: Very-large-service duties may cease before four months have elapsed
impact_families.effect: Following notification that designation has ended, a provider could cease Section 5 duties before the full four-month continuation period has elapsed.
impact_families.rationale: The timing controls continued applicability of core risk assessment, mitigation, independent audit and other obligations for designated very large services.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 92 and references to a fixed application date support harmonization but do not expressly settle termination timing.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian conduit provision makes storage characteristics alternatives
impact_families.effect: Non-automatic intermediate storage, used solely for transmission and retained only as reasonably necessary, could qualify for conduit protection if all other exemption conditions are satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: Treating the characteristics as alternatives could extend a core liability exemption to storage outside the cumulative English formulation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The technical-service context and neutrality requirements support a cumulative harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Individual notifications may extend to purchases outside the platform
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, an identifiable consumer offered an illegal product through the platform but purchasing elsewhere within six months could acquire a right to individual illegality and redress information.
impact_families.rationale: This changes eligibility for an important consumer-protection entitlement and the corresponding mandatory notification duty. The contact-details and six-month conditions remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The offer-based trigger and surrounding marketplace provisions strongly support limiting notifications to purchases through the platform.

impact_families.title: Fallback crime notification could exclude the provider's home authorities
impact_families.effect: An EU-established host without a legal representative could not satisfy the Italian fallback rule solely by notifying its home authorities; it could still notify Europol.
impact_families.rationale: The changed outcome concerns the permitted reporting destination. The duty to report suspected threats and an available recipient remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Home authorities remain appropriate if their State independently meets the definition of the Member State concerned.

impact_families.title: Dutch text omits publication of coordinator identity and contact details
impact_families.effect: A Member State could fulfil Article 49(3) by communicating coordinator details to the Commission and Board without separately making those details publicly available.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns administrative accessibility information. The coordinator’s powers, duties and recipients’ complaint rights remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 50’s transparency requirement or applicable national rules may independently require public access.

impact_families.title: Latvian Commission information powers use a provider-business connection
impact_families.effect: A professional evidence holder whose activities lack the required provider-business connection could resist a compulsory information decision and an inspection under Article 69.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed connection changes who is subject to compulsory investigative duties and the associated fines and periodic penalty payments under Articles 74 and 76.
impact_families.uncertainty: A broad provider-business connection could cover independent evidence holders; no contractual relationship is expressly required.

impact_families.title: Search-only providers could avoid routine audience publication
impact_families.effect: If the narrower subject prevailed, a search-only provider could omit six-monthly public audience figures while remaining obliged to provide updated figures to authorities on request.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence is a specific public-transparency gap. Article 24(3) preserves authority access, and Article 33(4) permits designation using other available information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 65 and Article 33(4) strongly support including search-only providers in the publication duty.

impact_families.title: Article 15 narrows the automated-processing count
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could exclude notices receiving both automated and human processing from its reported automated-processing count.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence affects one transparency statistic; broader automation disclosures and underlying notice-processing duties remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context supports comprehensive transparency, but the express exclusivity qualifier resists that reading.

impact_families.title: National investigative powers may exclude unaware evidence holders
impact_families.effect: A professional evidence holder challenges a compulsory production or inspection order because the coordinator lacked grounds to presume awareness of the suspected infringement when issuing it.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower class could remove an important compulsory investigative duty and associated inspection power in that proceeding, affecting the authority’s ability to obtain evidence.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recitals support harmonization; informing the evidence holder may establish awareness for subsequent orders.

impact_families.title: Access restriction could require a separate finding of offence seriousness
impact_families.effect: Even when every other safeguard is satisfied, temporary service-access restriction could be unavailable if the threatening offence is not separately considered serious.
impact_families.rationale: The added condition could determine the availability of an exceptional judicial remedy restricting access to a service, including following a Commission request under Article 82.
impact_families.uncertainty: The required serious harm and threat to life or safety may already establish offence seriousness.

impact_families.title: Implementing powers additionally cover interim measures and commitments
impact_families.effect: The Commission could prescribe practical procedural arrangements for interim measures and commitments using Article 83(a).
impact_families.rationale: The additional competence concerns procedural implementation; it does not independently expand the substantive powers or remove their safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: The supplied sources contain no implementing measure exercising this additional competence.

impact_families.title: Emergency action-plan wording reallocates oversight and reporting
impact_families.effect: Management submits the action plan without itself ensuring implementation or reporting; the Coordinator ensures that the provider performs and reports those measures.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns responsibility within an existing remedial process. Corrective action, provider reporting and the conditions for judicial access restrictions remain required.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation could restore management’s responsibility for all listed tasks.

impact_families.title: Latvian information-order notices additionally require territorial scope
impact_families.effect: A provider notifying a recipient about an information order would additionally have to identify the order’s territorial scope.
impact_families.rationale: The change adds an ancillary notification item without changing the order’s reach, the information obtainable or substantive redress rights.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 10(6) preserves national procedural law; paragraph 2 contains no corresponding territorial-scope requirement.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian synthetic-content example focuses on a person’s authenticity
impact_families.effect: Fabricated footage of an event involving no person could fall outside the expressly described marking measure because it creates no false impression about a person’s authenticity.
impact_families.rationale: The change narrows an illustrative mitigation measure. Article 35(1) still requires reasonable, proportionate and effective measures addressing the identified systemic risk.
impact_families.uncertainty: The express inclusion of objects, places and events supports interpreting the qualifier as concerning content authenticity.

impact_families.title: Notification may prevent proceedings for distinct breaches involving the same conduct
impact_families.effect: For a provider lacking the required legal representative, notification concerning one breach could prevent another Member State from initiating proceedings for a distinct breach arising from the same conduct.
impact_families.rationale: The changed outcome concerns allocation of enforcement proceedings. The notifying authority retains competence over the other breach; substantive obligations, sanction powers and private compensation rights are not removed.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared Charter safeguard and recital 123 may produce the same procedural boundary in both versions.

impact_families.title: Initial action-plan transmission names one coordinator
impact_families.effect: The provider initially sends its action plan to one coordinator, the Commission and the Board; other coordinators receive information through institutional cooperation and subsequent updates.
impact_families.rationale: The changed duty concerns initial distribution. Board scrutiny, Commission approval and monitoring, and collective implementation updates remain, supporting an ancillary information consequence.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 145 expressly supports collective transmission; the singular may be read generically.

impact_families.title: Appointment of an EU legal representative could appear optional
impact_families.effect: A provider offering services in the Union without an EU establishment could decline to appoint a legal representative without breaching Article 13(1).
impact_families.rationale: This removes a core organizational duty supporting receipt, compliance and enforcement of regulatory decisions. Article 56(7) preserves jurisdiction but does not itself impose appointment.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 44 and the surrounding operative duties strongly support mandatory designation.

impact_families.title: Commission information requests omit an express reasonableness threshold
impact_families.effect: If mere possible awareness sufficed, an additional professional third party could receive a binding information decision and face a fine for intentionally or negligently failing to respond.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 67(3) and 74(2)(b) connect the disputed eligibility threshold to compulsory disclosure and fines reaching 1% of annual income or worldwide turnover.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 141 expressly retains reasonableness; proportionality and judicial review strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Stronger expectation to consider unexplained refusal of a code of conduct
impact_families.effect: An authority could be expected to address a relevant unexplained refusal in its compliance assessment, where English leaves that consideration optional.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns consideration of evidence or context. Participation remains voluntary, and infringement still requires breach of an applicable obligation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recommendation may be harmonized with the permissive English wording as guidance preserving enforcement discretion.

impact_families.title: National periodic-penalty ceiling lacks express daily accrual
impact_families.effect: For prolonged non-compliance, a provider could claim a single ceiling of 5% of its average daily financial base instead of a ceiling accumulating each day.
impact_families.rationale: Removing daily accumulation can materially reduce financial liability for continuing non-compliance and weaken the coercive remedy available under Article 51(2)(d).
impact_families.uncertainty: The periodic character, starting date and express daily wording in Article 76 favor harmonized daily accrual.

impact_families.title: Translated content orders may use another delivery channel
impact_families.effect: An authority could send a properly translated order through another channel and still invoke Article 9’s duty to report the effect given to it.
impact_families.rationale: The changed condition concerns transmission and an ancillary reporting duty. The legal basis and enforceability of the underlying order remain governed by applicable law.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 11 and the parallel Article 10 wording favour retaining the designated channel.

impact_families.title: Dutch wording could make applicable mitigation measures mandatory
impact_families.effect: A provider could be required to change an applicable recommender or advertising system despite having implemented another effective, proportionate response to the identified risk.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading could materially expand the provider’s core mitigation duties by making particular operational interventions obligatory.
impact_families.uncertainty: Tailoring, proportionality and the illustrative recitals support interpreting applicability as preserving meaningful choice.

impact_families.title: Certification notices could omit expertise and language particulars
impact_families.effect: If the Hungarian reference governed, a certification notification and the Commission's public directory could omit the body's certified expertise and dispute-settlement languages.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns administrative notification and directory content. Certification conditions, certificate particulars and the entitlement to select a certified body remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Paragraph 3 supplies the only relevant certification particulars and strongly supports correcting the reference through interpretation.

impact_families.title: Foreign use causing Union systemic risks may fall outside assessment
impact_families.effect: A provider could exclude manipulation conducted outside the Union that creates systemic risks inside it, narrowing assessment and corresponding mitigation.
impact_families.rationale: The territorial limitation could remove a source of serious Union risks from the core obligations in Articles 34 and 35.
impact_families.uncertainty: Union exposure, the design-and-functioning limb, and paragraph 2’s manipulation requirement may independently bring particular risks within scope.

impact_families.title: Standards may address interface selection instead of choice controls
impact_families.effect: The Commission promotes standards for selecting recommender-system interfaces without specifically promoting standards for controls through which recipients choose recommendation options.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns the subject of voluntary standards. It does not remove providers' operative duties to offer recommendation choices and accessible selection functionality.
impact_families.uncertainty: The express references to Articles 27 and 38 strongly favour harmonization.

impact_families.title: Reopening commitment proceedings lacks an express materiality threshold
impact_families.effect: The Commission reopens a concluded commitment proceeding because a fact underlying the decision has changed only slightly.
impact_families.rationale: The immediate difference is reduced procedural finality and renewed proceedings. Findings of non-compliance, sanctions and changed substantive obligations still require their own grounds and safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: Proportionality and the purpose of reopening may imply a materiality requirement.

impact_families.title: Recital 90 omits a qualifier for stakeholder involvement
impact_families.effect: An assessment prepared without stakeholder involvement could attract stronger methodological criticism even where involvement was considered inappropriate.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns interpretation of preparation methods; the operative provisions retain proportionate assessments and do not independently require universal consultation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recital’s interpretive role limits its ability to impose additional duties.

impact_families.title: Romanian omits public accessibility from the moderation-decisions database requirement
impact_families.effect: If the omission prevailed, the Commission could withhold public access to the database of submitted moderation decisions and statements of reasons.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence would remove public access to the entire mandated scrutiny resource, materially weakening the database’s central transparency function identified in recital 66.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 66 expressly requires publication as an objective and strongly supports preserving public access.

impact_families.title: Complaint handling substitutes objectivity for express diligence
impact_families.effect: A platform could resist a separate obligation to examine new complaint evidence diligently when reconsidering a refusal to act, materially weakening the complainant’s internal remedy despite objective handling.
impact_families.rationale: Loss of a distinct diligence standard could materially impair the guaranteed remedy. Effectiveness, reasons, reversal and qualified supervision remain, but do not expressly prescribe the same standard of care.
impact_families.uncertainty: The effective-system requirement and surrounding diligence duties strongly support careful review under both versions.

impact_families.title: Mandatory reversal ground replaces conduct-based justification with necessity
impact_families.effect: If necessity supplies an additional reversal ground, a complainant could obtain restoration of an account despite their conduct otherwise warranting the challenged suspension.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading changes entitlement to a mandatory remedy affecting account or service access, beyond the mechanics of complaint handling.
impact_families.uncertainty: Conduct-based justification and necessity may converge under Article 14’s proportionality duty and Article 23’s individualized assessment.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian consumer-notification period runs from awareness of illegality
impact_families.effect: A consumer whose contact details are known and who purchased an illegal product shortly before awareness could lose the right to individual notification about illegality, trader identity and redress.
impact_families.rationale: Reversing the period materially changes beneficiaries of an express consumer-protection entitlement. Public information under paragraph 2 does not replace the excluded individual notification right.
impact_families.uncertainty: The completed-purchase wording and notification purpose strongly support a retrospective harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Illegal-content definition omits the Union-law compatibility qualification
impact_families.effect: If the broader definition prevailed, content prohibited only by a national rule incompatible with Union law could be treated as illegal when determining removal conditions for hosting liability protection.
impact_families.rationale: The definition governs core content-treatment and liability-exemption rules. Expanding it could materially affect expression and providers’ eligibility for liability protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 12, Union-law primacy and express safeguards elsewhere strongly oppose the broader reading.

impact_families.title: Automation count may exclude notices also handled by humans
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider excludes notices screened automatically and then reviewed by staff from its reported automated-processing count.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows one reporting metric. General automation disclosure under Article 15(1)(e), individual notification requirements and substantive notice-processing duties remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: The precise boundary of automated processing remains interpretative, but Spanish explicitly requires exclusivity.

impact_families.title: Automation count may exclude notices also reviewed by people
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could exclude notices processed through combined automated and human workflows from its reported automation count.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows one numerical transparency metric. General automation disclosures under Article 15(1)(e) and notice-handling duties under Article 16 remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Implementing reporting templates were not supplied and could independently require the omitted count.

impact_families.title: Compulsory crisis measures may extend beyond the service’s contribution
impact_families.effect: A crisis decision requires a provider to deploy its service against aspects of a public-health or security threat beyond the contribution attributable to its service.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed wording could materially expand the objective of compulsory crisis-response duties, even within the remaining proportionality and temporal safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: The assessment required by point (a) strongly supports limiting intervention to the service’s contribution.

impact_families.title: The express compliance-advice duty omits search-engine staff
impact_families.effect: Compliance officers at a very large online search engine could dispute a separate duty to inform and advise its management and employees under paragraph 3(d).
impact_families.rationale: The omission concerns a supporting compliance task; independent oversight, risk management, audit coordination and compliance monitoring remain required.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 41’s common framework and recital 99 strongly favour extending the advisory task to both provider types.

impact_families.title: The reasons standard may protect only effective judicial redress
impact_families.effect: A provider could contest a demand for additional explanation needed specifically for an internal complaint while supplying clear reasons adequate for judicial proceedings.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows a supplementary information-quality standard; detailed reasons, information about all remedies, and access to the remedies remain required.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared clarity requirements and paragraph 3(f) may largely prevent practical divergence.

impact_families.title: Referral for a judicial access restriction becomes mandatory
impact_families.effect: Once all statutory preconditions are met, a coordinator could be obliged to seek a judicial restriction of service access despite otherwise deciding against referral.
impact_families.rationale: Compulsory invocation of this exceptional access-restriction remedy materially changes an important enforcement duty. Judicial determination and safeguards remain, so restriction itself is not automatic.
impact_families.uncertainty: The powers-conferral chapeau and proportionality requirements support interpreting the provision as conferring discretion.

impact_families.title: Public-report redactions lack an express significance threshold
impact_families.effect: A provider removes a security-sensitive passage from its public audit report because publication could create a minor vulnerability.
impact_families.rationale: The exception broadens permissible public redaction of vulnerability-related information. Complete reports and reasons still reach regulators; audit, risk-assessment and mitigation duties remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Transparency requirements and proportionality may constrain redaction for minor vulnerabilities.

impact_families.title: Crisis assessment can encompass possible rather than likely significant contributions
impact_families.effect: During a qualifying crisis, a provider could face compulsory recommender-system or moderation adaptations for a possible but insufficiently likely significant contribution, provided strict necessity and proportionality are otherwise established.
impact_families.rationale: Article 36(1)(b) connects the broadened assessment to compulsory preventive measures. This can materially expand core crisis-response duties; provider choice, monitoring and temporal limits constrain implementation without eliminating that expansion.
impact_families.uncertainty: Neither version fixes a probability threshold; preventive purpose and strict necessity support a harmonising interpretation.

impact_families.title: Notice declaration could require an unqualified accuracy assurance
impact_families.effect: If the Hungarian declaration prevailed, a notice form could request confirmation of factual accuracy from someone able to attest only to an honest belief in accuracy.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the assurance requested in a procedural declaration. The act does not prescribe automatic rejection or strict liability for an honestly mistaken notice.
impact_families.uncertainty: Good faith and the mechanism's facilitative purpose support interpreting the assurance as a statement of honest belief.

impact_families.title: Certification may assess the body’s remuneration instead of its members’ pay
impact_families.effect: If institutional remuneration sufficed, a body paying members outcome-linked bonuses could pass the Danish remuneration condition while failing the English condition, provided the separate impartiality requirement was otherwise met.
impact_families.rationale: The difference can change certification eligibility and remove an explicit financial safeguard for individuals deciding disputes within the statutory redress mechanism.
impact_families.uncertainty: The separate impartiality requirement and recital 59 may prevent certification despite fixed institutional remuneration.

impact_families.title: Data-sharing delegation omits expressly required procedures
impact_families.effect: The Commission could specify data-sharing conditions and indicators without separately laying down procedures as a required component of its delegated acts.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns supplementary procedural specification; the underlying access duties, safeguards, eligibility conditions and amendment deadlines remain operative.
impact_families.uncertainty: Technical and specific conditions may be interpreted as encompassing the necessary procedures.

impact_families.title: Crisis assessment may encompass possible rather than likely significant contributions
impact_families.effect: During an existing public-health crisis, identifying a possible but unlikely significant service contribution could support compulsory additional moderation or algorithm changes under Article 36(1)(b), where the English contribution criterion would not be satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: Point (b) connects prevention to the assessment under point (a). Broadening qualifying contributions can expand a core crisis-response duty. Necessity, proportionality, provider choice and time limits constrain measures without expressly restoring likelihood.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation may restore likelihood. The separate indexed omission in point (b) is unnecessary to this conditional mechanism.

impact_families.title: Research-data access eligibility may require organizational membership
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualified researcher affiliated with, but not a member of, a qualifying research organization could be denied vetted status and access to non-public data.
impact_families.rationale: The condition directly determines eligibility for compulsory research-data access under Article 40(4) and (8). Public-data access under paragraph 12 does not replace it.
impact_families.uncertainty: Membership may receive a functional reading; the incorporated organization definition and delegated access rules are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Auditor eligibility may require more than ten years without audit services
impact_families.effect: If an immediately preceding audit-free period were required, an otherwise independent auditor that audited the provider last year could be excluded despite having served for fewer than ten consecutive years.
impact_families.rationale: Replacing a tenure ceiling with a decade-long exclusion materially changes eligibility to perform mandatory annual audits under Article 37(1).
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 92 strongly favors rotation; the Dutch provision does not specify the audit-free period’s endpoint.

impact_families.title: Irish transient-storage condition reverses the duration limit
impact_families.effect: A conduit provider retaining information only for the reasonably necessary transmission period could fail Article 4(2)’s literal Irish condition.
impact_families.rationale: The reversed comparison affects eligibility for the core liability exemption covering transmission-related storage.
impact_families.uncertainty: The transient-storage and sole-transmission-purpose requirements strongly support harmonization; losing the exemption does not itself establish liability.

impact_families.title: Temporary presence may not identify the authorities receiving a criminal report
impact_families.effect: If a victim’s temporary presence provides the only identifiable territorial connection, the Danish reading could require reporting to fallback authorities instead of authorities in that Member State.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence changes reporting destination. Article 18 preserves prompt reporting and provision of relevant information through its express fallback.
impact_families.uncertainty: The offence-location limb or another residence connection may identify the same authorities.

impact_families.title: Illegal-content definition omits the Union-law compatibility condition
impact_families.effect: If incompatible national prohibitions nevertheless counted under the definition, repeated provision of content prohibited solely by those rules could contribute to mandatory service suspension under Article 23.
impact_families.rationale: Expanding the central illegal-content definition can materially expand restrictions and provider obligations. Article 9’s separate compatibility safeguard does not expressly govern every use of that definition.
impact_families.uncertainty: Union-law primacy and recital 12 strongly oppose giving incompatible national prohibitions this effect.

impact_families.title: Romanian omits the provider’s establishment as a fallback reporting destination
impact_families.effect: A Union-established hosting provider without a legal representative would need to notify Europol instead of relying solely on notification to its own national authorities.
impact_families.rationale: The omission changes a permissible reporting destination. It preserves an available reporting route and does not remove the duty to report suspicions or supply relevant information.
impact_families.uncertainty: The reporting purpose and establishment framework support restoring the omitted route through contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Croatian permits security-based report redaction without an express significance threshold
impact_families.effect: A provider could remove information from a public report because publication creates a minor security vulnerability, even though the English significance threshold would not be met.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change concerns particular public-report information. Supervisors still receive complete reports and reasons for removal, and the underlying assessment, mitigation and audit duties remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation and proportionality may constrain redaction for minor vulnerabilities.

impact_families.title: Dutch wording could limit the alternative-option duty to non-profiling systems
impact_families.effect: A very large platform or search engine using a profiling-based recommender system could avoid providing a non-profiling option for that system.
impact_families.rationale: The restrictive reading removes an important recipient choice and the corresponding substantive provider obligation under Article 38.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 94 explicitly supports non-profiling alternatives and strongly favors harmonization.

impact_families.title: Researcher eligibility may require membership rather than affiliation
impact_families.effect: An otherwise eligible researcher affiliated with a research organisation but lacking member status could be refused vetted status and the associated statutory access to non-public platform data.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed relationship is an express eligibility condition for an important compulsory data-access mechanism. Public-data access under paragraph 12 does not replace access under paragraph 4.
