impact_families.uncertainty: Membership may receive a broad institutional meaning consistent with the affiliation wording in recital 97.

impact_families.title: Caching exemption lacks an express initial-source removal condition
impact_families.effect: An otherwise eligible caching provider learns of intermediate-copy removal, without a removal order or source deletion. Keeping its cache then loses Article 5 protection under the disputed reading.
impact_families.rationale: Loss of the caching liability exemption materially changes an important legal protection. Recital 17 requires a separate basis for liability, but that does not negate the significance of losing the exemption.
impact_families.uncertainty: The distinction between cached information and originally transmitted information may imply removal at origin when read contextually.

impact_families.title: Irish consumer-notification trigger describes an ongoing illegal offer
impact_families.effect: A platform discovering illegality after a listing ends could withhold Article 32 information from consumers who purchased within the preceding six months.
impact_families.rationale: The narrowed trigger removes purchasers’ entitlement to information about illegality, trader identity and available redress, including the public-information fallback.
impact_families.uncertainty: The retrospective purchase period and consumer-protection context support including completed offers.

impact_families.title: Notice-based knowledge may require identification without any legal examination
impact_families.effect: A notice requiring only a brief legal check could fail to establish knowledge under the Danish reading, preserving Article 6 protection absent other knowledge or awareness.
impact_families.rationale: The threshold can determine continued eligibility for the hosting liability exemption when the provider does not remove or disable access to the content.
impact_families.uncertainty: Danish recital 53 expressly supports the detailed-examination threshold; other evidence may independently establish knowledge.

impact_families.title: The Commission may independently trigger researcher data access
impact_families.effect: For research already vetted by the Coordinator, the Commission directly requires additional data access without a new Coordinator request.
impact_families.rationale: The additional requesting authority could independently activate compulsory disclosure to researchers, materially changing the provider’s data-access duty.
impact_families.uncertainty: Coordinator-controlled amendment and termination procedures leave the operation of an independent Commission request uncertain.

impact_families.title: Slovenian court-coordination wording permits a discontinuance reading
impact_families.effect: A national court could discontinue a pending case to avoid conflict with a contemplated Commission decision, instead of preserving the proceeding through a temporary stay.
impact_families.rationale: Discontinuance materially affects access to the pending judicial remedy. A stay preserves the proceeding for continuation; discontinuance ends that proceeding, even if another procedural route might remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Effective-remedy safeguards and the coordination purpose strongly favour a stay; consequences for refiling depend on applicable procedural law.

impact_families.title: Search-engine advertising repositories could lose express safeguards
impact_families.effect: A very large search engine could face no categorical Article 39 prohibition on including advertising recipients' personal data in its public repository, subject to applicable data-protection law.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading removes an express privacy safeguard governing public disclosure, as well as the specific duty to make reasonable efforts toward accurate and complete information.
impact_families.uncertainty: The preceding sentence supports harmonization; general data-protection law continues to constrain any disclosure.

impact_families.title: Article 54 adds a direct-loss qualification to compensation
impact_families.effect: A recipient could lose compensation for consequential loss otherwise recoverable under applicable law because the loss is not direct.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading narrows a substantive compensation entitlement and the provider’s corresponding liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: The modifier’s attachment and the applicable-law reservation may support a harmonized interpretation.

impact_families.title: Caching exemption omits the exclusive-purpose condition
impact_families.effect: Otherwise qualifying multipurpose storage could receive the caching liability exemption even though improving onward transmission is not its sole purpose.
impact_families.rationale: This potentially expands a core exemption from liability. Technical conditions and preserved injunction powers limit the exemption but do not eliminate the changed eligibility boundary.
impact_families.uncertainty: Any additional purpose must remain compatible with the service’s technical characteristics, neutrality and the other exemption conditions.

impact_families.title: One-percent fine rule qualifies the failure-to-reply ground
impact_families.effect: A provider ignoring an initial information order could lose the express one-percent ceiling if that omission is instead sanctioned under the general penalty rule.
impact_families.rationale: Removing the special ceiling could materially increase financial exposure: Article 51 preserves sanctioning powers, while Article 52’s general rule permits a substantially higher turnover-based maximum.
impact_families.uncertainty: The replacement ceiling is not automatic; Article 74’s parallel rule strongly supports retaining the one-percent treatment.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian audit-report provision focuses alternatives on unfulfilled recommendations
impact_families.effect: A provider could report alternatives addressing its failure to implement recommendations without expressly connecting those alternatives to the underlying breaches identified by the audit.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects the report’s required justification. The underlying obligations, audit assessment of compliance and enforcement mechanisms remain independently applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recommendations must aim at compliance, which supports treating alternatives as addressing the same underlying breaches.

impact_families.title: Croatian advertisement definition may exclude remuneration in kind
impact_families.effect: A platform subject to Article 28(2) could treat a promotion remunerated solely in kind as outside the prohibition on profiling-based advertisements to known minors.
impact_families.rationale: The definition determines the scope of express advertising prohibitions. General protection and commercial-communication disclosure duties do not reproduce those prohibitions for an excluded promotion.
impact_families.uncertainty: A contextual interpretation could include equivalent economic consideration within monetary remuneration; other applicable protections remain.

impact_families.title: Supervisory-fee ceiling uses turnover instead of net income
impact_families.effect: If turnover substantially exceeded net income and the other fee constraints permitted it, the Hungarian base could allow an annual supervisory fee materially above the English income-based ceiling.
impact_families.rationale: Changing the financial base alters an express cap protecting providers against substantial annual financial liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: No provider finances or actual fees are supplied; delegated methodology and implementing fee decisions are outside this packet.

impact_families.title: Additional contact language carries an EU-language qualification
impact_families.effect: If EU-language status independently restricts the additional language, a provider using an otherwise qualifying language would need to offer a qualifying EU language for its regulatory contact point.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is an ancillary communication requirement. Agreed-language and translation arrangements remain available; the wording does not itself remove reporting duties, remedies or service eligibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: EU language is undefined, and the shared comprehension criterion may produce the same practical result.

impact_families.title: Periodic penalty wording could produce different turnover ceilings
impact_families.effect: If annual turnover were used for each day's English ceiling, the maximum periodic payment could substantially exceed a ceiling based on turnover generated daily under Italian.
impact_families.rationale: The competing calculations directly affect the maximum financial liability for continuing failure to comply with Commission decisions under Article 76.
impact_families.uncertainty: A shared daily-average reading, Article 52(4) and proportionality strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Crisis-protocol revision requests have a broader rights-protection trigger
impact_families.effect: The Commission could be required to request revision and additional measures to protect rights without first finding that the existing protocol fails to safeguard them.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes a Commission request concerning voluntary protocols. Article 48 does not itself compel participants to implement the requested revisions or additional measures.
impact_families.uncertainty: Paragraph 4(e) supports interpreting the rights-protection purpose as addressing an existing deficiency.

impact_families.title: Greek crisis definition includes circumstances capable of producing a serious threat
impact_families.effect: The Commission could impose compulsory crisis assessments, mitigation and reporting before extraordinary circumstances have produced a serious threat, provided the remaining Article 36 safeguards are satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition controls access to compulsory crisis intervention and significant provider duties. Necessity, proportionality and duration safeguards constrain those duties but do not erase the changed activation threshold.
impact_families.uncertainty: Shared recital 91 strongly supports an anticipatory interpretation of both operative versions.

impact_families.title: Slovenian may require prompt publication of completed audit-related reports
impact_families.effect: A provider completing the relevant reports before the three-month deadline could have to publish them without undue delay instead of waiting until that deadline.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change accelerates disclosure of reports already subject to publication. Corrected Article 42(5) preserves exclusions for confidential information, security vulnerabilities and harm to recipients.
impact_families.uncertainty: The timing expressions could be interpreted distributively, preserving the distinction between transmission and publication.

impact_families.title: Illegal-content definition omits the national-law compatibility qualification
impact_families.effect: Information prohibited solely by national legislation incompatible with Union law could be treated as illegal content for hosting-liability and notice-handling purposes.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed definition reaches core content rules and could materially affect access to information and expression.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 12, Union-law primacy and related operative provisions strongly oppose the unqualified reading.

impact_families.title: Moderation reports may use average rather than median processing times
impact_families.effect: A provider publishes arithmetic means for order, notice and complaint processing durations instead of medians, producing different figures for unevenly distributed processing times.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects the calculation and comparability of mandatory transparency metrics. It does not change processing deadlines, moderation decisions or access to remedies.
impact_families.uncertainty: Interpretation or reporting templates could resolve the terminology consistently; those templates are outside the supplied evidence.

impact_families.title: Research applicants may only need to identify requested time limits
impact_families.effect: An applicant could meet the express condition by justifying the data examination and identifying the requested time frame without separately substantiating that time frame.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns application evidence. Research-purpose restrictions, security requirements and the contextual requirement of proportionate requests remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Necessary and proportionate access may be interpreted as inherently including its temporal scope.

impact_families.title: Article 51(3) shifts description of proposed restrictions to consultation participants
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, interested parties could lose informed participation before the coordinator seeks service-access restrictions, because the invitation need not identify its proposed measures or intended addressees.
impact_families.rationale: This materially weakens an important advance-participation entitlement before potential service blocking. Subsequent judicial participation remains, but does not replace the opportunity to influence the coordinator before it initiates restriction proceedings.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 51(6) and recitals 116 and 119 strongly favour preserving informed advance consultation through harmonization.

impact_families.title: Irish removed-advertisement disclosure points to the wrong paragraph
impact_families.effect: A provider could contest which reasons must replace a removed advertisement’s information in the public repository because the referenced lettered points do not exist.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects a specific public disclosure. Direct reasons duties, the Article 9 alternative and the repository’s remaining information requirements continue.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 17(3) contains the uniquely matching list, strongly supporting contextual correction.

impact_families.title: Greek additionally limits the service-use limb of risk assessment to the Union
impact_families.effect: If the restriction excluded external service use, a provider could omit that use’s contribution to Union electoral or public-security risks from assessment and the resulting mitigation measures.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed wording could materially narrow the core systemic-risk assessment duty and the mitigation duty linked to identified risks under Article 35.
impact_families.uncertainty: The design/functioning limb, Article 34(2) and recital 84 strongly support covering externally originating risks.

impact_families.title: Transitional exemption may exclude audience-information requests
impact_families.effect: A provider within the twelve-month transition could decline an Article 24(3) request for updated audience information and supporting calculations.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns a transitional information-production duty. Article 33(4) expressly preserves designation using other information, so exemption from the very-large-platform regime does not follow.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 57 expressly preserves the information duty and strongly supports correcting the cross-reference through interpretation.

impact_families.title: Platform price setting supports a stronger inference of control
impact_families.effect: A platform setting a trader’s prices could be denied the hosting exemption through an assumed control relationship where the English formulation would leave that relationship open to further assessment.
impact_families.rationale: The inference can determine eligibility for a core liability exemption. Any resulting liability still requires an independent basis in applicable law.
impact_families.uncertainty: Both formulations may be interpreted as illustrative guidance within Article 6(2), without an automatic presumption.

impact_families.title: Article 27(1) limits recommender transparency to very large platforms
impact_families.effect: A platform covered by Section 3 but not designated very large could withhold its recommender parameters and available modification options.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading removes the principal recommender-disclosure duty for an entire otherwise covered category of platforms.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 19, paragraph 3 and recitals 70 and 94 strongly support broader application.

impact_families.title: Standards concern selecting interfaces rather than interfaces for user choice
impact_families.effect: The Commission supports standards for selecting interfaces without expressly covering the design of interfaces through which recipients exercise recommender-system choices.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns ancillary support for voluntary standards. Articles 27 and 38 retain the applicable choice and transparency duties independently of those standards.
impact_families.uncertainty: The express references to Articles 27 and 38 favour interpreting the standards as supporting recipients’ choices.

impact_families.title: Consumer notification window may also run from service performance
impact_families.effect: A platform could have to notify a consumer about a service purchased earlier than six months before awareness because performance occurred within those six months.
impact_families.rationale: The difference extends an informational duty and its temporal reach; it does not itself change illegality or establish an additional substantive remedy.
impact_families.uncertainty: The preceding purchase-based description supports harmonization, but does not expressly fix the timing of purchase.

impact_families.title: Dutch wording could require earlier publication of risk and audit materials
impact_families.effect: A provider could have to publish completed risk and audit materials without undue delay instead of selecting a later publication date within the three-month period.
impact_families.rationale: The difference accelerates an existing transparency duty. Article 42(5) retains protections for confidential information, service security, public security and recipients.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may support assigning the deadlines separately to transmission and publication.

impact_families.title: Advertising repository total may measure service reach
impact_families.effect: If the disputed reading prevailed, a provider could report the service’s total audience in an advertisement repository entry instead of that advertisement’s total audience.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns one required transparency metric. Advertisement content, sponsors, presentation period, targeting parameters and applicable Member State breakdowns remain covered.
impact_families.uncertainty: The repository structure and advertisement-specific targeting breakdown strongly support interpreting the total as advertisement reach.

impact_families.title: Residence-based complaint venue may exclude nonresident visitors
impact_families.effect: A recipient residing outside the EU, briefly using an intermediary service while visiting a Member State without residing there, could lack any express Article 53 complaint venue.
impact_families.rationale: Article 2 covers recipients merely located in the Union. A residence-only venue could therefore remove an eligible recipient’s statutory complaint route, materially affecting an important procedural entitlement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Residence wording may encompass temporary stays; recital 118 favors the place where the service was received.

impact_families.title: Initial action plan may need direct delivery to only one coordinator
impact_families.effect: A provider sends its initial action plan to one coordinator, the Commission and the Board without directly sending it to the other coordinators.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns initial distribution. Coordinators participate through the Board, and Article 75(3) separately requires the Commission to keep them informed about implementation and monitoring.
impact_families.uncertainty: Spanish Recital 145 expressly uses the plural and supports collective distribution.

impact_families.title: Minor-protection guidelines name the Committee as consultee
impact_families.effect: The Commission could consult the Committee rather than the Board before issuing guidelines on protecting minors.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns institutional participation in an advisory step, without changing Article 28(1)'s substantive protection duty.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Board’s guideline-related functions under Article 63 support harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Croatian changes the initial risk-assessment deadline into a starting date
impact_families.effect: A newly designated service could reach its application date with its initial systemic-risk assessment still underway and argue that the initial-completion deadline has not been breached.
impact_families.rationale: The difference materially changes when a core risk-assessment duty must be completed. That assessment identifies the systemic risks to which Article 35 mitigation must be tailored.
impact_families.uncertainty: Immediate diligence and mitigation duties constrain delay; Croatian supplies no explicit substitute completion deadline.

impact_families.title: Online-platform exclusion could apply to a non-minor ancillary feature
impact_families.effect: If the alternative conditions prevailed, a non-minor but purely ancillary dissemination feature satisfying technical inseparability and anti-circumvention conditions could escape online-platform classification and its additional duties.
impact_families.rationale: The definition controls eligibility for an exclusion from an entire category of substantive obligations, including platform-specific complaint and transparency requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 13 expressly requires both characteristics and directly supports harmonizing the operative definition.

impact_families.title: Fundamental-rights risk assessment may require effects to be both actual and foreseeable
impact_families.effect: A provider could omit a foreseeable fundamental-rights harm that has not materialised from its assessment and the corresponding tailored mitigation measures.
impact_families.rationale: The cumulative reading narrows a core preventive duty concerning the fundamental rights expressly protected by Articles 34 and 35.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 81, the general risk duty and a collective reading of the conjunction strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: The 1% fine category may omit complete failure to answer an information demand
impact_families.effect: A third party that entirely ignores an investigative information demand could contest its inclusion in the express 1% fine category.
impact_families.rationale: The category changes, but Article 51 retains sanction powers. The supplied text does not establish whether the resulting outcome is a different ceiling or an unavailable fine.
impact_families.uncertainty: The residual sanction and applicable national penalty rules are unresolved.

impact_families.title: Latvian platform transition omits former small enterprises
impact_families.effect: A platform losing small-enterprise status, without being designated very large, could immediately become subject to Section 3 duties instead of receiving a twelve-month transition.
impact_families.rationale: The omission changes eligibility for an exemption covering substantial complaint-handling, advertising, interface-design and minors-protection duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 57 and Article 29 strongly support extending the transition to former small enterprises.

impact_families.title: Auditor eligibility restriction extends to unrelated non-audit services
impact_families.effect: An otherwise independent organisation could become ineligible for the mandatory audit because it supplied unrelated non-audit services within the preceding twelve months, or intends to supply them within the following twelve months.
impact_families.rationale: The omission changes eligibility to perform the mandatory independent audit and broadens the required post-audit restriction on services.
impact_families.uncertainty: Different outcomes require unrelated services that do not independently compromise independence or create a conflict of interest.

impact_families.title: Irish interface prohibition omits the materiality threshold
impact_families.effect: An interface practice outside Article 25(2)’s exclusions could be prohibited solely for minor impairment of informed choices, without deception, manipulation or material impairment.
impact_families.rationale: Removing the threshold materially expands the core prohibition governing how covered platforms design, organise and operate their interfaces.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 67 expressly preserves materiality and supports a harmonized threshold.

impact_families.title: Automation reporting counts only exclusively automated notices
impact_families.effect: A hosting provider could omit notices screened automatically and then reviewed by humans from its reported automation count.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows one transparency statistic. General automation disclosures and duties governing notice processing remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Reporting templates outside the supplied sources could clarify the counting method.

impact_families.title: Commission investigative powers may exclude unaware evidence holders
impact_families.effect: An inspection decision against a professional third party holding relevant records is challenged because that person was not reasonably presumed aware of the suspected infringement when the decision was adopted.
impact_families.rationale: Exclusion from the incorporated class could remove compulsory inspection and production duties in that proceeding, materially restricting an important investigative power.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 141 supports harmonization; prior notification could establish awareness and permit subsequent compulsory measures.

impact_families.title: Article 82(1) shifts description of proposed restrictions to participants
impact_families.effect: Interested parties could have to comment before a service-access restriction is requested without receiving the Commission’s description of the proposed measures or addressees.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading materially weakens an express advance-participation safeguard preceding potentially serious restrictions on service access.
impact_families.uncertainty: General defence rights and judicial safeguards strongly support requiring equivalent notice.

impact_families.title: Statutory review names an information entitlement
impact_families.effect: The Commission evaluates information-access entitlements without fully evaluating the broader freedom to receive and impart information under Article 91(2)(f).
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the scope of a periodic evaluation. Substantive fundamental rights, risk-assessment obligations and remedies remain independently protected.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 150 expressly identifies information freedom; Article 34 and recital 153 reinforce that reading.

impact_families.title: Article 40(4) adds Commission requests for researcher access
impact_families.effect: A Commission request could compel disclosure of non-public data to vetted researchers without a coordinator-issued request for that access.
impact_families.rationale: The addition changes who can activate a substantive compulsory data-access duty, extending beyond the Commission’s own supervisory access.
impact_families.uncertainty: Coordinator-only request, amendment and termination provisions make the added route’s operation uncertain.

impact_families.title: Irish alternative-data proposal requirement uses a nonexistent reference
impact_families.effect: A provider could submit an Article 40(5) amendment request without alternative-access proposals and contest that particular submission requirement.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns supporting proposals. The access duty, limited amendment grounds, decision deadline and Coordinator’s decision-making power remain operative.
impact_families.uncertainty: The provision’s placement and the sole amendment procedure strongly support correcting the reference contextually.

impact_families.title: Risk-mitigation codes contemplate committees instead of commitments
impact_families.effect: Participants draft a code establishing a mitigation committee instead of specifying participants' commitments to take particular mitigation measures.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes a mechanism envisaged for voluntary codes. Statutory risk mitigation, reporting and evaluation remain; commitments actually undertaken remain subject to applicable auditing requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: The surrounding commitment-based provisions favour contextual harmonization.

impact_families.title: A non-compliance decision may become discretionary after an infringement finding
impact_families.effect: After finding a breach of systemic-risk obligations, the Commission declines to adopt a non-compliance decision, leaving the corrective order and enhanced supervision dependent on that decision untriggered.
impact_families.rationale: The change could remove a core enforcement duty and prevent mandatory remedial consequences under Articles 73(3) and 75.
impact_families.uncertainty: The enforcement framework and recital 145 favour mandatory action after the relevant finding.

impact_families.title: Portuguese notice declarations affirm accuracy directly
impact_families.effect: If the stricter reading governed, the notice mechanism would facilitate a direct accuracy-and-completeness declaration instead of a declaration limited to the notifier’s honest belief.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns an ancillary attestation requirement. The surrounding provisions do not establish automatic inadmissibility, loss of redress or sanctions for an honest mistake.
impact_families.uncertainty: Both formulations may be interpreted as good-faith attestations; no additional consequences under external law are established.

impact_families.title: Latvian escalation condition omits unremedied infringements
impact_families.effect: A provider whose conduct has ceased could resist the management action-plan procedure despite an unremedied infringement causing serious harm, after other enforcement powers have been exhausted.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed gateway could remove an important remedial enforcement mechanism precisely where other available powers cannot prevent serious harm.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 51(3)(b) strongly supports interpreting continuation to include an unremedied infringement.

impact_families.title: Notice declaration affirms accuracy rather than belief in accuracy
impact_families.effect: A notifier could be asked to affirm that its allegations are accurate and complete instead of affirming its sincere belief in their accuracy and completeness.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns declaration wording. Article 16 preserves notice processing and does not establish automatic exclusion, strict notifier liability or loss of redress for honest mistakes.
impact_families.uncertainty: Good faith may qualify the entire declaration; an exclusionary implementation is not established by the supplied text.

impact_families.title: Early application list omits the supervisory-fee provisions
impact_families.effect: A provider designated before general application could contest a supervisory charge for the interval before provider-specific application, although English expressly applies the fee provisions earlier.
impact_families.rationale: If that reading prevailed, it could determine whether an annual compulsory supervisory charge has an applicable legal basis during the transitional interval.
impact_families.uncertainty: Articles 33(6), 43(1), 87 and 92 require reconciliation; no actual charge or amount is established.

impact_families.title: Online-platform exclusion may cover substantial ancillary features
impact_families.effect: A hosting service with substantial but purely ancillary public dissemination could avoid online-platform classification if technical inseparability and anti-circumvention conditions are also satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: The definition controls applicability of platform-specific obligations, including complaint handling and advertising safeguards, subject to the applicable enterprise exclusions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Polish recital 13 expressly supports requiring both minor and purely ancillary character.

impact_families.title: Coordinator investigative powers omit an express reasonableness threshold
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, a professional third party could face compulsory disclosure or inspection despite insufficient grounds reasonably to presume awareness, with financial sanctions for non-compliance.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 51(1)–(2) and 52(3) connect third-party eligibility to coercive investigative duties and fines reaching 1% of annual income or worldwide turnover.
impact_families.uncertainty: Necessity, proportionality, national safeguards and judicial review may require the same reasonable connection as English.

impact_families.title: National periodic-penalty ceiling omits express daily recurrence
impact_families.effect: For continuing non-compliance, the German ceiling is applied as one total maximum instead of a maximum accruing for each day from the specified date.
impact_families.rationale: A total ceiling replacing daily accumulation can materially reduce financial liability and the coercive force of an enforcement order.
impact_families.uncertainty: The starting date, enforcement purpose and explicit daily rule in Article 76 favor harmonized daily accrual.

impact_families.title: Non-platform intermediaries may report only complaint counts
impact_families.effect: A non-platform intermediary with an internal complaint system could publish complaint counts while omitting grounds, decisions, median decision times and reversals.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change narrows annual transparency reporting. It does not itself alter complaint decisions or remove an applicable right to redress.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general reporting obligation and contextual reading of the coordinated list support broader disclosure.

impact_families.title: Standards provision expressly names only older minors
impact_families.effect: If the narrower terminology prevailed, the Commission could satisfy the expressly listed standards-promotion requirement with standards addressing older minors without specifically addressing younger children.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns promotion of voluntary standards. Article 28 retains protection for both categories, Article 44 permits additional standards, and adopting standards does not itself establish compliance.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 102 and the regulation’s consistent protection of all minors support a broader interpretation.

impact_families.title: Audience reporting refers to threshold-adjustment acts instead of methodology acts
impact_families.effect: If a methodology act were adopted, a provider could argue that its published audience figures need not follow it because Article 24(2) instead refers to threshold-adjustment acts.
impact_families.rationale: The identifiable change concerns the reporting calculation requirement. Article 33(3) separately covers designation methodology, and Article 33(4) permits designation using additional evidence despite reporting failures.
impact_families.uncertainty: The reciprocal reference strongly supports harmonization. No adopted methodology act is supplied.

impact_families.title: Post-audit commitment may omit connected legal persons
impact_families.effect: An otherwise independent audit organisation could qualify without committing to avoid relevant consultancy for a connected legal person during the twelve months after the audit.
impact_families.rationale: This materially changes a categorical eligibility safeguard for mandatory independent compliance audits. Continuing independence requirements constrain the consequence but do not necessarily restore the omitted commitment.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may extend the commitment to connected persons; arrangements compromising independence remain prohibited under either reading.

impact_families.title: Population-change trigger omits the express five-percent minimum
impact_families.effect: If a population decrease exceeding five percent failed to trigger adjustment, a service between the recalculated and unchanged thresholds could avoid designation and the associated additional duties.
impact_families.rationale: The trigger controls adjustment of the threshold governing designation and application of Section 5’s important systemic-risk obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: The ten-percent formula and recital 76 strongly favour treating five percent as a threshold, including larger changes.

impact_families.title: Automatic report transmission may be confined to the audit report
impact_families.effect: A provider could automatically transmit only its audit report, requiring regulators to obtain other listed materials through publication or a separate request, unless the redaction rule requires complete transmission.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the routine delivery channel. Publication, the redaction safeguard and Articles 34(3) and 40 preserve access to the underlying materials.
impact_families.uncertainty: The five-item list, paragraph 5 and recital 93 strongly favour transmission of all listed materials.

impact_families.title: Dispute-settlement reporting may use an average instead of the median
impact_families.effect: A platform reports the arithmetic mean of settlement durations when unusually lengthy disputes make that figure differ from the median.
impact_families.rationale: The changed requirement concerns a published transparency statistic. Article 21’s settlement access, deadlines, nonbinding outcomes and expense-allocation rules remain intact.
impact_families.uncertainty: Interpretation or reporting templates could resolve the terminology consistently; those templates are outside the supplied evidence.

impact_families.title: Crisis assessment omits express examination of how services contribute
impact_families.effect: Under an assessment-only crisis decision, a provider could assess contribution and its extent or likelihood without separately explaining the mechanism of contribution.
impact_families.rationale: One analytical component is narrowed. Article 34 retains causal systemic-risk analysis, while crisis mitigation, reporting, monitoring and proportionality requirements remain available.
impact_families.uncertainty: A meaningful assessment of contribution may itself require analysis of its mechanism.

impact_families.title: Lithuanian crisis provision makes requested dialogue mandatory
impact_families.effect: A provider requesting dialogue about its crisis measures could require the Commission to engage rather than leave engagement to the Commission’s discretion.
impact_families.rationale: The difference adds a procedural obligation. The provider’s choice of measures, proportionality safeguards and Commission decision powers remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may qualify the mandatory effect or the requests sufficient to trigger it.

impact_families.title: Latvian information-order condition places control over the service
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying order concerning previously collected information outside the provider’s current control could trigger Article 10 acknowledgment and reporting duties.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change concerns complementary order-processing duties. Recitals 31–32 leave the legal basis for issuing orders and enforcing substantive production to other applicable law.
impact_families.uncertainty: Applicable procedural law and contextual interpretation may preserve the information-control safeguard.

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
REGULATION (EU) 2023/2854 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 13 December 2023
on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data and amending Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 and Directive (EU) 2020/1828 (Data Act)
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and in particular Article 114 thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the European Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: After transmission of the draft legislative act to the national parliaments,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Central Bank ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 5
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 6
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the Committee of the Regions ( 3 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 7
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure ( 4 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | In recent years, data-driven technologies have had transformative effects on all sectors of the economy. The proliferation of products connected to the internet in particular has increased the volume and potential value of data for consumers, businesses and society. High-quality and interoperable data from different domains increase competitiveness and innovation and ensure sustainable economic growth. The same data may be used and reused for a variety of purposes and to an unlimited degree, without any loss of quality or quantity.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | Barriers to data sharing prevent an optimal allocation of data for the benefit of society. Those barriers include a lack of incentives for data holders to enter voluntarily into data sharing agreements, uncertainty about rights and obligations in relation to data, the costs of contracting and implementing technical interfaces, the high level of fragmentation of information in data silos, poor metadata management, the absence of standards for semantic and technical interoperability, bottlenecks impeding data access, a lack of common data sharing practices and the abuse of contractual imbalances with regard to data access and use.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | In sectors characterised by the presence of microenterprises, small enterprises and medium-sized enterprises as defined in Article 2 of the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC ( 5 ) (SMEs), there is often a lack of digital capacities and skills to collect, analyse and use data, and access is frequently restricted where one actor holds them in the system or due to a lack of interoperability between data, between data services or across borders.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | In order to respond to the needs of the digital economy and to remove barriers to a well-functioning internal market for data, it is necessary to lay down a harmonised framework specifying who is entitled to use product data or related service data, under which conditions and on what basis. Accordingly, Member States should not adopt or maintain additional national requirements regarding matters falling within the scope of this Regulation, unless explicitly provided for herein, since this would affect its direct and uniform application. Moreover, action at Union level should be without prejudice to obligations and commitments in the international trade agreements concluded by the Union.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | This Regulation ensures that users of a connected product or related service in the Union can access, in a timely manner, the data generated by the use of that connected product or related service and that those users can use the data, including by sharing them with third parties of their choice. It imposes the obligation on data holders to make data available to users and third parties of the user’s choice in certain circumstances. It also ensures that data holders make data available to data recipients in the Union under fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms and conditions and in a transparent manner. Private law rules are key in the overall framework for data sharing. Therefore, this Regulation adapts rules of contract law and prevents the exploitation of contractual imbalances that hinder fair access to and use of data. This Regulation also ensures that data holders make available to public sector bodies, the Commission, the European Central Bank or Union bodies, where there is an exceptional need, the data that are necessary for the performance of a specific task carried out in the public interest. In addition, this Regulation seeks to facilitate switching between data processing services and to enhance the interoperability of data and of data sharing mechanisms and services in the Union. This Regulation should not be interpreted as recognising or conferring any new right on data holders to use data generated by the use of a connected product or related service.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | Data generation is the result of the actions of at least two actors, in particular the designer or manufacturer of a connected product, who may in many cases also be a provider of related services, and the user of the connected product or related service. It gives rise to questions of fairness in the digital economy as the data recorded by connected products or related services are an important input for aftermarket, ancillary and other services. In order to realise the important economic benefits of data, including by way of data sharing on the basis of voluntary agreements and the development of data-driven value creation by Union enterprises, a general approach to assigning rights regarding access to and the use of data is preferable to awarding exclusive rights of access and use. This Regulation provides for horizontal rules which could be followed by Union or national law that addresses the specific situations of the relevant sectors.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | The fundamental right to the protection of personal data is safeguarded, in particular, by Regulations (EU) 2016/679 ( 6 ) and (EU) 2018/1725 ( 7 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council. Directive 2002/58/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 8 ) additionally protects private life and the confidentiality of communications, including by way of conditions on any personal and non-personal data storing in, and access from, terminal equipment. Those Union legislative acts provide the basis for sustainable and responsible data processing, including where datasets include a mix of personal and non-personal data. This Regulation complements and is without prejudice to Union law on the protection of personal data and privacy, in particular Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive 2002/58/EC. No provision of this Regulation should be applied or interpreted in such a way as to diminish or limit the right to the protection of personal data or the right to privacy and confidentiality of communications. Any processing of personal data pursuant to this Regulation should comply with Union data protection law, including the requirement of a valid legal basis for processing under Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and, where relevant, the conditions of Article 9 of that Regulation and of Article 5(3) of Directive 2002/58/EC. This Regulation does not constitute a legal basis for the collection or generation of personal data by the data holder. This Regulation imposes an obligation on data holders to make personal data available to users or third parties of a user’s choice upon that user’s request. Such access should be provided to personal data that are processed by the data holder on the basis of any of the legal bases referred to in Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. Where the user is not the data subject, this Regulation does not create a legal basis for providing access to personal data or for making personal data available to a third party and should not be understood as conferring any new right on the data holder to use personal data generated by the use of a connected product or related service. In those cases, it could be in the interest of the user to facilitate meeting the requirements of Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. As this Regulation should not adversely affect the data protection rights of data subjects, the data holder can comply with requests in those cases, inter alia, by anonymising personal data or, where the readily available data contains personal data of several data subjects, transmitting only personal data relating to the user.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | The principles of data minimisation and data protection by design and by default are essential when processing involves significant risks to the fundamental rights of individuals. Taking into account the state of the art, all parties to data sharing, including data sharing falling within scope of this Regulation, should implement technical and organisational measures to protect those rights. Such measures include not only pseudonymisation and encryption, but also the use of increasingly available technology that permits algorithms to be brought to the data and allow valuable insights to be derived without the transmission between parties or unnecessary copying of the raw or structured data themselves.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | Unless otherwise provided for in this Regulation, it does not affect national contract law, including rules on the formation, validity or effect of contracts, or the consequences of the termination of a contract. This Regulation complements and is without prejudice to Union law which aims to promote the interests of consumers and ensure a high level of consumer protection, and to protect their health, safety and economic interests, in particular Council Directive 93/13/EEC ( 9 ) and Directives 2005/29/EC ( 10 ) and 2011/83/EU ( 11 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | This Regulation is without prejudice to Union and national legal acts providing for the sharing of, access to and the use of data for the purpose of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or for the execution of criminal penalties, or for customs and taxation purposes, irrespective of the legal basis under the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) on which such Union legal acts were adopted, as well as to international cooperation in that area, in particular on the basis of the Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime, (ETS No 185), done at Budapest on 23 November 2001. Such acts include Regulations (EU) 2021/784 ( 12 ) , (EU) 2022/2065 ( 13 ) and (EU) 2023/1543 ( 14 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council and Directive (EU) 2023/1544 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 15 ) . This Regulation does not apply to the collection or sharing of, access to or the use of data under Regulation (EU) 2015/847 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 16 ) and Directive (EU) 2015/849 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 17 ) . This Regulation does not apply to areas that fall outside the scope of Union law and in any event does not affect the competences of the Member States concerning public security, defence or national security, customs and tax administration or the health and safety of citizens, regardless of the type of entity entrusted by the Member States to carry out tasks in relation to those competences.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | Union law establishing physical design and data requirements for products to be placed on the Union market should not be affected unless specifically provided for by this Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | This Regulation complements and is without prejudice to Union law aiming to establish accessibility requirements on certain products and services, in particular Directive (EU) 2019/882 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 18 ) .

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | This Regulation is without prejudice to Union and national legal acts providing for the protection of intellectual property rights, including Directives 2001/29/EC ( 19 ) , 2004/48/EC ( 20 ) and (EU) 2019/790 ( 21 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) | Connected products that obtain, generate or collect, by means of their components or operating systems, data concerning their performance, use or environment and that are able to communicate those data via an electronic communications service, a physical connection, or on-device access, often referred to as the Internet of Things, should fall within the scope of this Regulation, with the exception of prototypes. Examples of such electronic communications services include, in particular, land-based telephone networks, television cable networks, satellite-based networks and near-field communication networks. Connected products are found in all aspects of the economy and society, including in private, civil or commercial infrastructure, vehicles, health and lifestyle equipment, ships, aircraft, home equipment and consumer goods, medical and health devices or agricultural and industrial machinery. Manufacturers’ design choices, and, where relevant, Union or national law that addresses sector-specific needs and objectives or relevant decisions of competent authorities, should determine which data a connected product is capable of making available.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) | The data represent the digitisation of user actions and events and should accordingly be accessible to the user. The rules for access to and the use of data from connected products and related services under this Regulation address both product data and related service data. Product data refers to data generated by the use of a connected product that the manufacturer designed to be retrievable from the connected product by a user, data holder or a third party, including, where relevant, the manufacturer. Related service data refers to data, which also represent the digitisation of user actions or events related to the connected product which are generated during the provision of a related service by the provider. Data generated by the use of a connected product or related service should be understood to cover data recorded intentionally or data which result indirectly from the user’s action, such as data about the connected product’s environment or interactions. This should include data on the use of a connected product generated by a user interface or via a related service, and should not be limited to the information that such use took place, but should include all data that the connected product generates as a result of such use, such as data generated automatically by sensors and data recorded by embedded applications, including applications indicating hardware status and malfunctions. This should also include data generated by the connected product or related service during times of inaction by the user, such as when the user chooses not to use a connected product for a given period of time and instead to keep it in stand-by mode or even switched off, as the status of a connected product or its components, for example its batteries, can vary when the connected product is in stand-by mode or switched off. Data which are not substantially modified, meaning data in raw form, also known as source or primary data which refer to data points that are automatically generated without any further form of processing, as well as data which have been pre-processed for the purpose of making them understandable and useable prior to subsequent processing and analysis fall within the scope of this Regulation. Such data includes data collected from a single sensor or a connected group of sensors for the purpose of making the collected data comprehensible for wider use-cases by determining a physical quantity or quality or the change in a physical quantity, such as temperature, pressure, flow rate, audio, pH value, liquid level, position, acceleration or speed. The term ‘pre-processed data’ should not be interpreted in such a manner as to impose an obligation on the data holder to make substantial investments in cleaning and transforming the data. The data to be made available should include the relevant metadata, including its basic context and timestamp, to make the data usable, combined with other data, such as data sorted and classified with other data points relating to them, or re-formatted into a commonly used format. Such data are potentially valuable to the user and support innovation and the development of digital and other services to protect the environment, health and the circular economy, including through facilitating the maintenance and repair of the connected products in question. By contrast, information inferred or derived from such data, which is the outcome of additional investments into assigning values or insights from the data, in particular by means of proprietary, complex algorithms, including those that are a part of proprietary software, should not be considered to fall within the scope of this Regulation and consequently should not be subject to the obligation of a data holder to make it available to a user or a data recipient, unless otherwise agreed between the user and the data holder. Such data could include, in particular, information derived by means of sensor fusion, which infers or derives data from multiple sensors, collected in the connected product, using proprietary, complex algorithms and which could be subject to intellectual property rights.

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) | This Regulation enables users of connected products to benefit from aftermarket, ancillary and other services based on data collected by sensors embedded in such products, the collection of those data being of potential value in improving the performance of the connected products. It is important to delineate between, on the one hand, markets for the provision of such sensor-equipped connected products and related services and, on the other, markets for unrelated software and content such as textual, audio or audiovisual content often covered by intellectual property rights. As a result, data that such sensor-equipped connected products generate when the user records, transmits, displays or plays content, as well as the content itself, which is often covered by intellectual property rights, inter alia for use by an online service, should not be covered by this Regulation. This Regulation should also not cover data which was obtained, generated or accessed from the connected product, or which was transmitted to it, for the purpose of storage or other processing operations on behalf of other parties, who are not the user, such as may be the case with regard to servers or cloud infrastructure operated by their owners entirely on behalf of third parties, inter alia for use by an online service.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) | It is necessary to lay down rules regarding products that are connected to a related service at the time of the purchase, rent or lease in such a way that its absence would prevent the connected product from performing one or more of its functions, or which is subsequently connected to the product by the manufacturer or a third party to add to or adapt the functionality of the connected product. Such related services involve the exchange of data between the connected product and the service provider and should be understood to be explicitly linked to the operation of the connected product’s functions, such as services that, where applicable, transmit commands to the connected product that are able to have an impact on its action or behaviour. Services which do not have an impact on the operation of the connected product and which do not involve the transmitting of data or commands to the connected product by the service provider should not be considered to be related services. Such services could include, for example, auxiliary consulting, analytics or financial services, or regular repair and maintenance. Related services can be offered as part of the purchase, rent or lease contract. Related services could also be provided for products of the same type and users could reasonably expect them to be provided taking into account the nature of the connected product and any public statement made by or on behalf of the seller, rentor, lessor or other persons in previous links of the chain of transactions, including the manufacturer. Those related services may themselves generate data of value to the user independently of the data collection capabilities of the connected product with which they are interconnected. This Regulation should also apply to a related service that is not supplied by the seller, rentor or lessor itself, but which is provided by a third party. In the event of doubt as to whether the service is provided as part of the purchase, rent or lease contract, this Regulation should apply. Neither the power supply, nor the supply of the connectivity are to be interpreted as related services under this Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) | The user of a connected product should be understood to be a natural or legal person, such as a business, a consumer or a public sector body, that owns a connected product, has received certain temporary rights, for example by means of a rental or lease agreement, to access or use data obtained from the connected product, or receives related services for the connected product. Those access rights should in no way alter or interfere with the rights of data subjects who may be interacting with a connected product or a related service regarding personal data generated by the connected product or during the provision of the related service. The user bears the risks and enjoys the benefits of using the connected product and should also enjoy access to the data it generates. The user should therefore be entitled to derive benefit from data generated by that connected product and any related service. An owner, renter or lessee should also be considered to be a user, including where several entities can be considered to be users. In the context of multiple users, each user may contribute in a different manner to the data generation and have an interest in several forms of use, such as fleet management for a leasing enterprise, or mobility solutions for individuals using a car sharing service.

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) | Data literacy refers to the skills, knowledge and understanding that allows users, consumers and businesses, in particular SMEs falling within the scope of this Regulation, to gain awareness of the potential value of the data they generate, produce and share and that they are motivated to offer and provide access to in accordance with relevant legal rules. Data literacy should go beyond learning about tools and technologies and aim to equip and empower citizens and businesses with the ability to benefit from an inclusive and fair data market. The spread of data literacy measures and the introduction of appropriate follow-up actions could contribute to improving working conditions and ultimately sustain the consolidation, and innovation path of, the data economy in the Union. Competent authorities should promote tools and adopt measures to advance data literacy among users and entities falling within the scope of this Regulation and an awareness of their rights and obligations thereunder.

passages.label: Recital 20
passages.text: (20) | In practice, not all data generated by connected products or related services are easily accessible to their users and there are often limited possibilities regarding the portability of data generated by products connected to the internet. Users are unable to obtain the data necessary to make use of providers of repair and other services and businesses are unable to launch innovative, convenient and more efficient services. In many sectors, manufacturers are able to determine, through their control of the technical design of the connected products or related services, what data are generated and how they can be accessed, despite having no legal right to those data. It is therefore necessary to ensure that connected products are designed and manufactured, and related services are designed and provided, in such a manner that product data and related service data, including the relevant metadata necessary to interpret and use those data, including for the purpose of retrieving, using or sharing them, are always easily and securely accessible to a user, free of charge, in a comprehensive, structured, commonly used and machine-readable format. Product data and related service data that a data holder lawfully obtains or can lawfully obtain from the connected product or related service, such as by means of the connected product design, the data holder’s contract with the user for the provision of related services, and its technical means of data access, without disproportionate effort, are referred to as ‘readily available data’. Readily available data does not include data generated by the use of a connected product where the design of the connected product does not provide for such data being stored or transmitted outside the component in which they are generated or the connected product as a whole. This Regulation should therefore not be understood to impose an obligation to store data on the central computing unit of a connected product. The absence of such an obligation should not prevent the manufacturer or data holder from voluntarily agreeing with the user on the making of such adaptations. The design obligations in this Regulation are also without prejudice to the data minimisation principle laid down in Article 5(1), point (c), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and should not be understood as imposing an obligation to design connected products and related services in such a way that they store or otherwise process any personal data other than the personal data necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed. Union or national law could be introduced to outline further specificities, such as the product data that should be accessible from connected products or related services, given that such data may be essential for the efficient operation, repair or maintenance of those connected products or related services. Where subsequent updates or alterations to a connected product or a related service, by the manufacturer or another party, lead to additional accessible data or a restriction of initially accessible data, such changes should be communicated to the user in the context of the update or alteration.

passages.label: Recital 21
passages.text: (21) | Where several persons or entities are considered to be users, for example in the case of co-ownership or where an owner, renter or lessee shares rights of data access or use, the design of the connected product or related service, or the relevant interface, should enable each user to have access to the data they generate. Use of connected products that generate data typically requires a user account to be set up. Such an account allows the user to be identified by the data holder, which may be the manufacturer. It can also be used as a means of communication and to submit and process data access requests. Where several manufacturers or related services providers have sold, rented or leased connected products or provided related services, integrated together, to the same user, the user should turn to each of the parties with which it has a contract. Manufacturers or designers of a connected product that is typically used by several persons should put in place the necessary mechanisms to allow separate user accounts for individual persons, where relevant, or for the possibility of several persons using the same user account. Account solutions should allow users to delete their accounts and erase the data related to them and could allow users to terminate data access, use or sharing, or submit requests to terminate, in particular taking into account situations in which the ownership or usage of the connected product changes. Access should be granted to the user on the basis of simple request mechanism granting automatic execution and not requiring examination or clearance by the manufacturer or data holder. This means that the data should be made available only when the user actually wants access. Where automated execution of the data access request is not possible, for example via a user account or accompanying mobile application provided with the connected product or related service, the manufacturer should inform the user as to how the data may be accessed.

passages.label: Recital 22
passages.text: (22) | Connected products may be designed to make certain data directly accessible from on-device data storage or from a remote server to which the data are communicated. Access to on-device data storage may be enabled via cable-based or wireless local area networks connected to a publicly available electronic communications service or mobile network. The server may be the manufacturer’s own local server capacity or that of a third party or a cloud service provider. Processors as defined in Article 4, point (8), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 are not considered to act as data holders. However, they can be specifically tasked with making data available by the controller as defined in Article 4, point (7), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. Connected products may be designed to permit the user or a third party to process the data on the connected product, on a computing instance of the manufacturer or within an information and communications technology (ICT) environment chosen by the user or the third party.

passages.label: Recital 23
passages.text: (23) | Virtual assistants play an increasing role in digitising consumer and professional environments and serve as an easy-to-use interface to play content, obtain information, or activate products connected to the internet. Virtual assistants can act as a single gateway in, for example, a smart home environment and record significant amounts of relevant data on how users interact with products connected to the internet, including those manufactured by other parties, and can replace the use of manufacturer-provided interfaces such as touch screens or smartphone apps. The user may wish to make available such data to third party manufacturers and enable novel smart services. Virtual assistants should be covered by the data access rights provided for in this Regulation. Data generated when a user interacts with a connected product via a virtual assistant provided by an entity other than the manufacturer of the connected product should also be covered by the data access rights provided for in this Regulation. However, only the data arising from the interaction between the user and a connected product or related service through the virtual assistant should be covered by this Regulation. Data produced by the virtual assistant which are unrelated to the use of a connected product or related service are not covered by this Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 24
passages.text: (24) | Before concluding a contract for the purchase, rent, or lease of a connected product, the seller, rentor or lessor, which may be the manufacturer, should provide to the user information regarding the product data which the connected product is capable of generating, including the type, format and the estimated volume of such data, in a clear and comprehensible manner. This could include information on data structures, data formats, vocabularies, classification schemes, taxonomies and code lists, where available, as well as clear and sufficient information relevant for the exercise of the user’s rights on how the data may be stored, retrieved or accessed, including the terms of use and quality of service of application programming interfaces or, where applicable, the provision of software development kits. That obligation provides transparency over the product data generated and enhances easy access for the user. The information obligation could be fulfilled, for example by maintaining a stable uniform resource locator (URL) on the web, which can be distributed as a web link or QR code, pointing to the relevant information, which could be provided by the seller, rentor or lessor, which may be the manufacturer, to the user before concluding the contract for the purchase, rent or lease of a connected product. It is, in any case, necessary that the user is able to store the information in a way that is accessible for future reference and that allows the unchanged reproduction of the information stored. The data holder cannot be expected to store the data indefinitely in view of the needs of the user of the connected product, but should implement a reasonable data retention policy, where applicable, in line with storage limitation principle pursuant Article 5(1), point (e), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, that allows for the effective application of the data access rights provided for in this Regulation. The obligation to provide information does not affect the obligation of the controller to provide information to the data subject pursuant to Articles 12, 13 and 14 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. The obligation to provide information before concluding a contract for the provision of a related service should lie with the prospective data holder, independently of whether the data holder concludes a contract for the purchase, rent or lease of a connected product. Where information changes during the lifetime of the connected product or the contract period for the related service, including where the purpose for which those data are to be used changes from the originally specified purpose, it should also be provided to the user.

passages.label: Recital 25
passages.text: (25) | This Regulation should not be understood to confer any new right on data holders to use product data or related service data. Where the manufacturer of a connected product is a data holder, the basis for the manufacturer to use non-personal data should be a contract between the manufacturer and the user. Such a contract could be part of an agreement for the provision of the related service, which could be concluded together with the purchase, rent or lease agreement relating to the connected product. Any contractual term stipulating that the data holder may use product data or related service data should be transparent to the user, including regarding the purposes for which the data holder intends to use the data. Such purposes could include improving the functioning of the connected product or related services, developing new products or services, or aggregating data with the aim of making available the resulting derived data to third parties, provided that such derived data do not allow the identification of specific data transmitted to the data holder from the connected product, or allow a third party to derive those data from the dataset. Any change of the contract should depend on the informed agreement of the user. This Regulation does not prevent parties from agreeing on contractual terms the effect of which is to exclude or limit the use of non-personal data, or certain categories of non-personal data, by a data holder. Neither does it prevent parties from agreeing to make product data or related service data available to third parties, directly or indirectly, including, where applicable, via another data holder. Moreover, this Regulation does not prevent sector-specific regulatory requirements under Union law, or national law compatible with Union law, which would exclude or limit the use of certain such data by the data holder on well-defined public policy grounds. This Regulation does not prevent users, in the case of business-to-business relations, from making data available to third parties or data holders under any lawful contractual term, including by agreeing to limit or restrict further sharing of such data, or from being compensated proportionately, for example in exchange for waiving their right to use or share such data. While the notion of ‘data holder’ generally does not include public sector bodies, it may include public undertakings.

passages.label: Recital 26
passages.text: (26) | To foster the emergence of liquid, fair and efficient markets for non-personal data, users of connected products should be able to share data with others, including for commercial purposes, with minimal legal and technical effort. It is currently often difficult for businesses to justify the personnel or computing costs that are necessary for preparing non-personal datasets or data products and to offer them to potential counterparties via data intermediation services, including data marketplaces. A substantial hurdle to the sharing of non-personal data by businesses therefore results from the lack of predictability of economic returns from investing in the curation and making available of datasets or data products. In order to allow for the emergence of liquid, fair and efficient markets for non-personal data in the Union, the party that has the right to offer such data on a market must be clarified. Users should therefore have the right to share non-personal data with data recipients for commercial and non-commercial purposes. Such data sharing could be performed directly by the user, upon the request of the user via a data holder, or through data intermediation services. Data intermediation services, as regulated by Regulation (EU) 2022/868 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 22 ) could facilitate a data economy by establishing commercial relationships between users, data recipients and third parties and may support users in exercising their right to use data, such as ensuring the anonymisation of personal data or aggregation of access to data from multiple individual users.
