passages.label: Article 20
passages.text:
Article 20
Right to customise the media offering
1. Users shall have a right to easily change the configuration, including default settings, of any device or user interface controlling or managing access to and the use of media services providing programmes in order to customise the media offering in accordance with their interests or preferences in compliance with Union law. This paragraph shall not affect national measures implementing Article 7a or 7b of Directive 2010/13/EU.
2. When placing devices and user interfaces as referred to in paragraph 1 on the market, manufacturers, developers and importers shall ensure that such devices and user interfaces include a functionality enabling users to freely and easily change at any time their configuration, including default settings controlling or managing access to and use of the media services offered.
3. Manufacturers, developers and importers of devices and user interfaces as referred to in paragraph 1 shall ensure that the visual identity of media service providers to whose services their devices and user interfaces give access is consistently and clearly visible to the users.
4. Member States shall take appropriate measures to ensure that manufacturers, developers and importers of devices and user interfaces as referred to in paragraph 1 comply with paragraphs 2 and 3.
5. The Board shall foster cooperation between media service providers, standardisation bodies or any other relevant stakeholders in order to promote the development of harmonised standards related to the design of devices or user interfaces as referred to in paragraph 1 or to digital signals carried by such devices.

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
SECTION 5
Requirements for well-functioning media market measures and procedures

passages.label: Article 21
passages.text:
Article 21
National measures affecting media service providers
1. Legislative, regulatory or administrative measures taken by a Member State that are liable to affect media pluralism or the editorial independence of media service providers operating in the internal market shall be duly justified and proportionate. Such measures shall be reasoned, transparent, objective and non-discriminatory.
2. Any national procedure used for the purpose of adopting an administrative measure as referred to in paragraph 1 shall follow timeframes set out in advance. Such procedures shall be conducted without undue delay.
3. Any media service provider subject to a regulatory or administrative measure as referred to in paragraph 1 that concerns it individually and directly shall have the right to appeal that measure before an appellate body. That body, which may be a court, shall be independent of the parties involved and of any external intervention or political pressure liable to jeopardise its independent assessment of matters coming before it. It shall have the appropriate expertise to enable it to carry out its functions effectively and in a timely manner.
4. Where a regulatory or administrative measure as referred to in paragraph 1 is likely to significantly affect the operation of media service providers in the internal market, the Board shall, on its own initiative, at the request of the Commission or upon a duly justified and reasoned request of a media service provider that is individually and directly affected by such a measure, draw up an opinion on the measure. Without prejudice to its powers under the Treaties, the Commission may issue its own opinion on the matter. The Board and the Commission shall make their opinions publicly available.
5. For the purpose of drawing up an opinion under paragraph 4, the Board and, where applicable, the Commission may request relevant information from a national authority or body that has adopted a regulatory or administrative measure as referred to in paragraph 1 that affects a media service provider individually and directly. The national authority or body concerned shall provide that information without undue delay by electronic means.

passages.label: Article 22
Article 23
passages.text:
Article 23
Opinions on media market concentrations
1. In the absence of an assessment or a consultation pursuant to Article 22, the Board, on its own initiative or at the request of the Commission, shall draw up an opinion on the impact of a media market concentration on media pluralism and editorial independence, where that media market concentration is likely to affect the functioning of the internal market for media services. The Board shall base its opinion on the elements referred to in Article 22(2). The Board may bring such media market concentrations to the attention of the Commission.
2. Without prejudice to its powers under the Treaties, the Commission may issue its own opinion on the matter.
3. The Board and the Commission shall make their opinions as referred to in this Article publicly available.

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
SECTION 6
Transparent and fair allocation of economic resources

passages.label: Article 24
passages.text:
Article 24
Audience measurement
1. Providers of audience measurement systems shall ensure that their audience measurement systems and the methodology used by their audience measurement systems comply with the principles of transparency, impartiality, inclusiveness, proportionality, non-discrimination, comparability and verifiability.
2. Without prejudice to the protection of undertakings’ trade secrets as defined in Article 2, point (1), of Directive (EU) 2016/943, providers of proprietary audience measurement systems shall provide, without undue delay and free of charge, to media service providers, to advertisers and to third parties authorised by media service providers and advertisers accurate, detailed, comprehensive, intelligible and up-to-date information on the methodology used by their audience measurement systems.
Providers of proprietary audience measurement systems shall ensure that the methodology used by their audience measurement systems and the way in which it is applied is independently audited once a year. At the request of a media service provider, a provider of a proprietary audience measurement system shall provide it with information on audience measurement results, including non-aggregated data, which relate to the media content and media services of that media service provider.
This paragraph shall not affect the Union’s data protection and privacy rules.
3. National regulatory authorities or bodies shall encourage providers of audience measurement systems to draw up, together with media service providers, providers of online platforms, their representative organisations and any other interested parties, codes of conduct or shall encourage providers of audience measurement systems to comply with codes of conduct jointly agreed and widely accepted by media service providers, their representative organisations and any other interested parties.
Codes of conduct as referred to in the first subparagraph of this paragraph shall be intended to promote the regular, independent and transparent monitoring of the effective achievement of their objectives and compliance with the principles referred to in paragraph 1, including through independent and transparent audits.
4. The Commission, assisted by the Board, may issue guidelines on the practical application of paragraphs 1, 2 and 3, taking into account, where appropriate, codes of conduct as referred to in paragraph 3.
5. The Board shall foster the exchange of best practices related to the deployment of audience measurement systems through a regular dialogue between representatives of the national regulatory authorities or bodies, representatives of providers of audience measurement systems, representatives of media service providers, representatives of providers of online platforms and other interested parties.

passages.label: Article 25
passages.text:
Article 25
Allocation of public funds for state advertising and supply or service contracts
1. Public funds or any other consideration or advantage made available, directly or indirectly, by public authorities or entities to media service providers or providers of online platforms for state advertising or supply or service contracts concluded with media service providers or providers of online platforms shall be awarded in accordance with transparent, objective, proportionate and non-discriminatory criteria, made publicly available in advance by electronic and user-friendly means, and by means of open, proportionate and non-discriminatory procedures.
Member States shall seek to ensure that the overall yearly public expenditure allocated for state advertising is distributed to a wide plurality of media service providers represented on the market, taking into account the national and local specificities of the media markets concerned.
This Article shall not affect the awarding of public contracts and concession contracts under Union public procurement rules or the application of Union State aid rules.
2. Public authorities or entities shall make publicly available by electronic and user-friendly means information on an annual basis about their public expenditure for state advertising. That information shall include at least the following:
(a) | the legal names of the media service providers or the providers of online platforms from which services were purchased;
(b) | where applicable, the legal names of the business groups of which any media service providers or providers of online platforms as referred to in point (a) are part; and
(c) | the total annual amount spent and the annual amounts spent per media service provider or provider of an online platform.
Member States may exempt subnational governments of territorial entities of less than 100 000 inhabitants, and entities controlled, directly or indirectly, by such subnational governments, from the obligation under point (b) of the first subparagraph.
3. National regulatory authorities or bodies or other competent independent authorities or bodies in the Member States shall monitor and report annually on the allocation of state advertising expenditure to media service providers and to providers of online platforms based on the information listed in paragraph 2. Those annual reports shall be made publicly available in an easily accessible manner.
In order to assess the completeness of the information on state advertising made available pursuant to paragraph 2, national regulatory authorities or bodies or other competent independent authorities or bodies in the Member States may request from the public authorities or entities referred to in the first subparagraph of paragraph 2 further information, including more detailed information on the application of the criteria and procedures referred to in paragraph 1.
Where the monitoring, assessment and reporting are carried out by other competent independent authorities or bodies in the Member States, they shall keep the national regulatory authorities or bodies duly informed.

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
CHAPTER IV
FINAL PROVISIONS

passages.label: Article 26
Article 27
passages.text:
Article 27
Evaluation and reporting
1. By 8 August 2028, and every four years thereafter, the Commission shall evaluate this Regulation and report to the European Parliament, the Council and the European Economic and Social Committee.
2. In the first such evaluation referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article, the Commission shall in particular examine the effectiveness of the functioning of the Board’s secretariat referred to in Article 11, including as regards the adequacy of resources in relation to the performance of its tasks.
3. For the purposes of paragraph 1 and at the request of the Commission, Member States and the Board shall send it relevant information.
4. In carrying out the evaluations referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article, the Commission shall take into account:
(a) | the positions and findings of the European Parliament, the Council and other relevant bodies or sources;
(b) | outcomes of the relevant discussions carried out in relevant fora;
(c) | relevant documents issued by the Board;
(d) | the findings of the monitoring exercise referred to in Article 26.
5. The reports referred to in paragraph 1 may be accompanied, where appropriate, by a proposal to amend this Regulation.

passages.label: Article 28
passages.text:
Article 28
Amendments to Directive 2010/13/EU
Directive 2010/13/EU is amended as follows:
(1) | Article 30b is deleted.
(2) | References to Article 30b of Directive 2010/13/EU shall be construed as references to Article 13(1), point (c), of this Regulation.

impact_families.title: Associated persons’ specific safeguards may require identifying information
impact_families.effect: An associated person holding source-related but non-identifying information could lose Article 4(8)'s express judicial-protection and assistance guarantees when challenging disclosure coercion prohibited by Article 4(3)(a).
impact_families.rationale: The narrowing could remove important express remedial guarantees from people still protected against coercion, and exclude them from the specific intrusive-software deployment safeguard.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general protection duty and Charter support broader protection; independent remedies may remain.

impact_families.title: Spanish may require the shortest sufficient crisis response period
impact_families.effect: During a qualifying crisis, a platform could have to select the shortest sufficient response period instead of allowing additional time within a shortened response window.
impact_families.rationale: The change limits discretion over a procedural deadline. A meaningful response opportunity remains mandatory, and the exceptions for specified legal moderation obligations remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 50 in both languages supports interpreting the provision as permitting ordinary discretionary shortening.

impact_families.title: German codes provision separates monitoring from promoting compliance
impact_families.effect: A code could promote regular monitoring of its own objectives while addressing compliance through guidance and occasional audits, without promoting regular monitoring of compliance with Article 24(1).
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns the intended content of encouraged codes. Direct compliance duties and annual independent audits of proprietary methodologies remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: English coordination, the codes' objectives and the shared audit reference permit harmonizing readings.

impact_families.title: Maltese makes audience measurement guidelines mandatory
impact_families.effect: If the Maltese reading prevailed, the Commission would have to issue practical audience measurement guidelines even if it considered the Regulation and industry codes sufficient.
impact_families.rationale: This creates an ancillary guidance duty. The binding measurement principles, information obligations and annual audit requirements remain unchanged; the provision does not empower guidelines to replace those requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: Multilingual interpretation could preserve discretion; the mandatory wording specifies no issuance deadline.

impact_families.title: German consultation trigger refers to likely market impairment
impact_families.effect: A concentration affecting cross-border media activity without likely impairment could undergo national assessment without advance Board consultation or the associated obligation to address the Board's opinion.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns advisory oversight and related procedural duties. National assessment remains required where applicable; the Board's opinion does not itself authorize or prohibit a concentration.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 67's cross-border examples support a broader, harmonized interpretation of the German trigger.

impact_families.title: Croatian may require merger parties to confer information-gathering powers
impact_families.effect: If the party-facing reading prevailed, a Member State relying solely on statutory information powers could need an additional notification or authorization requirement for merger parties.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns the procedural means of securing information. Article 7(4) preserves regulatory powers, and Article 22 retains the assessment obligation without specifying a different merger-approval outcome.
impact_families.uncertainty: The legislative framework strongly favours treating conferral of public powers as the Member State’s responsibility.

impact_families.title: Surveillance-software definition may include software capable only of overt surveillance
impact_families.effect: A Member State's deployment against a journalist of vulnerability-exploiting software capable only of overt surveillance could become subject to Article 4(5)'s authorisation and serious-crime conditions.
impact_families.rationale: The definition controls a core deployment prohibition and its narrowly conditioned exception. Broader surveillance protections under Article 4(3)(b) do not impose the same serious-crime threshold.
impact_families.uncertainty: The spyware context may support reading an implicit covert-surveillance limitation into Finnish.

impact_families.title: German wording may make the Steering Group mandatory
impact_families.effect: The Board could have to establish and retain a Steering Group even when it considers that additional internal body unnecessary.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns internal organization. The supplied provisions give the group no independent decision-making powers and preserve the Board's voting arrangements.
impact_families.uncertainty: German recital 39 expressly supports discretionary establishment.

impact_families.title: Polish programme definition may require provider preparation of content
impact_families.effect: If provider preparation of content were required, an otherwise qualifying service offering only acquired audiovisual items could fall outside Article 2(1), losing eligibility for Article 4 protections.
impact_families.rationale: The programme definition determines media-service status. Excluding a service on this basis could remove important editorial-independence and source-confidentiality protections under this Regulation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Preparation within a schedule or catalogue can plausibly mean editorial arrangement, preserving coverage of acquired content.

impact_families.title: Competent-authority identification duty could fail after refusal
impact_families.effect: If the Romanian wording governed literally, an authority refusing cooperation for lack of competence could omit identifying the competent authority even when identification was possible.
impact_families.rationale: The change removes an ancillary referral safeguard. The authority must still explain its refusal, and Article 14(5) retains access to Board involvement over insufficient cooperation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The defined roles and surrounding refusal provisions strongly support reading the duty as addressed to the requested authority.

impact_families.title: Competing-views criterion could focus on concentrations rather than the market
impact_families.effect: If the narrower French reading prevailed, an assessor could examine competing views within the participating entities for this particular criterion while still conducting the required market-wide pluralism assessment.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes one interpretative criterion. Article 22(2)(a) and recital 68 preserve consideration of market diversity and alternative media, limiting the supported consequence to the assessment’s analytical focus.
impact_families.uncertainty: The French formulation is awkward; its surrounding market-wide context strongly supports harmonization.

impact_families.title: Danish wording could narrow Board conflict procedures to conflicts between members
impact_families.effect: The Board could adopt procedures addressing conflicts between members without specifying how members must declare or manage conflicting external financial or professional interests.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows an internal procedural safeguard. Article 9 still requires full independence, and the supplied text does not establish permission for conflicted substantive decisions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The technical meaning of conflicts of interest and the independence duty support a broader reading.

impact_families.title: Italian merger wording could shift the information-powers obligation to the parties
impact_families.effect: Parties could be required to notify a concentration despite existing statutory information-gathering powers, unless they themselves provide the powers described in the alternative.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns the procedural route for obtaining assessment information. Article 7(4) preserves regulatory powers, and Article 22 retains the assessment framework without specifying a transaction prohibition or sanction.
impact_families.uncertainty: The national-legislation context strongly supports reading the provision as requiring state-conferral of powers.

impact_families.title: Czech may narrow source protection for regular non-daily contacts
impact_families.effect: A regular but non-daily private contact holding source information could fall outside Article 4's specific protections against compelled disclosure and surveillance and its express judicial-protection entitlement.
impact_families.rationale: Excluding such contacts would materially narrow core source-protection prohibitions and the associated remedy. General protection duties and other rights do not necessarily reproduce all the specific safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: A continuing-relationship or everyday-life interpretation, reinforced by the Charter, could preserve equivalent coverage.

impact_families.title: Czech raises the threshold for coordinating measures against actual security harm
impact_families.effect: Following a qualifying request from authorities in two Member States, actual security prejudice below the Czech threshold could require Board coordination under English but fall outside the Czech mechanism.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects coordination, associated opinions and criteria. Article 17 preserves national powers; it does not itself permit or prohibit the media service concerned.
impact_families.uncertainty: Public-security and fundamental-rights context could support an equivalent implied threshold in English.

impact_families.title: Greek cross-reference may obscure the trigger for follow-up reporting
impact_families.effect: If the Greek reference were applied literally, receipt of the Article 15(3) opinion might not trigger reporting of follow-up actions to the Board, Commission and requesting authority.
impact_families.rationale: The changed outcome concerns ancillary follow-up reporting. Article 15(2)'s separate information duty and Article 15(3)'s mediation and opinion procedures remain operative.
impact_families.uncertainty: The unique preceding opinion procedure makes a corrective contextual reading particularly strong.

impact_families.title: Danish source-protection wording could omit compelled private disclosure
impact_families.effect: An authority could issue a binding order for private identification of a journalistic source without applying Article 4(4)’s specific public-interest, proportionality and authorisation conditions.
impact_families.rationale: Removing those express conditions from compelled private disclosure would materially weaken a core source-confidentiality safeguard, even though general protection and restrictions on coercive enforcement remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The effective-protection duty and surrounding provisions strongly favour covering private disclosure.

impact_families.title: Romanian concentration-review duty omits the significance threshold
impact_families.effect: If the Romanian reading prevailed, a Member State could have to extend its concentration-review framework, including notification requirements or information-gathering powers, to transactions with only minor effects on either protected interest.
impact_families.rationale: Removing significance materially expands the core legislative duty under Article 22(1) and the transactions covered by its required review mechanisms. Proportionality remains, but does not expressly restore the omitted threshold.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recitals 64–66 strongly support harmonization; national notification criteria remain proportionate.

impact_families.title: Greek wording may narrow protection against compelled disclosure
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading prevailed, compelled disclosure of confidential material unrelated to identification could fall outside Article 4(4)'s specific public-interest, proportionality and authorization safeguards.
impact_families.rationale: Removing those specific safeguards would materially diminish a core confidentiality protection, even though the general protection obligation and other applicable law remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general protection duty, broader adjacent wording and recitals strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Spanish expressly requires configuration changes without charge
impact_families.effect: Once Article 20 applies, a manufacturer charging for an otherwise usable configuration function could have to remove that charge under the Spanish wording.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is a pricing restriction on configuration changes. Both versions require usable customization; the supplied text establishes neither substantial financial liability nor loss of access to media services.
impact_families.uncertainty: English 'freely' may already prohibit fees; no fee amount or practical barrier is evidenced.

impact_families.title: Commission participation in Board deliberations could be discretionary in Latvian
impact_families.effect: If participation is discretionary, the Commission representative could decline a Board deliberation without breaching Article 10(6).
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns institutional participation. Voting arrangements, mandatory designation and the Chair’s information duty remain intact; the text establishes no resulting invalidity of Board decisions.
impact_families.uncertainty: English may establish a participation entitlement or institutional role rather than an attendance obligation.

impact_families.title: German AI-content declaration requires two safeguards
impact_families.effect: An otherwise eligible provider exercising editorial control without human review of AI-generated items could be denied declaration-dependent notice, response and dialogue protections when a platform restricts its content.
impact_families.rationale: The cumulative condition could exclude a provider from important procedural entitlements protecting media content against platform restrictions. It does not itself prohibit publication.
impact_families.uncertainty: The safeguards may overlap; paragraphs 4 and 6 refer to submitted declarations, while paragraph 7 permits challenges to rejection.

impact_families.title: Czech makes an appropriate amendment proposal mandatory
impact_families.effect: If an amendment proposal is considered appropriate, submitting the evaluation report alone could satisfy English but breach the Czech conditional attachment duty.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns legislative follow-up to an evaluation. Attaching a proposal neither amends the Regulation nor directly changes the substantive rights of media providers or recipients.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Commission retains substantial discretion in deciding what is appropriate.

impact_families.title: Commission participation in Board deliberations could become optional
impact_families.effect: If the Romanian reading prevailed, the Commission’s representative could decline participation in deliberations without breaching this provision.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns non-voting institutional participation. Mandatory designation and reporting to the Commission remain; the text supports no change to voting, substantive powers or decision validity.
impact_families.uncertainty: English may establish participation status rather than an attendance obligation.

impact_families.title: Portuguese limits audience-measurement code encouragement to proprietary systems
impact_families.effect: If the Portuguese limitation prevailed, a regulator could exclude providers following agreed industry standards from its efforts to encourage development of, or compliance with, audience-measurement codes.
impact_families.rationale: This narrows an ancillary encouragement duty. Article 24(1) still binds all providers to measurement principles, and paragraph 2 retains proprietary systems’ transparency and audit obligations. No major consequence is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 71 supports broader encouragement, but paragraph 3 expressly repeats the proprietary limitation.

impact_families.title: Maltese leaves providers’ discretion over editorial safeguards less explicit
impact_families.effect: If the objective reading prevailed, a provider could have to revise its chosen internal safeguards despite considering them appropriate.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the suitability of safeguards. The independence objectives, established editorial line, constitutional qualification and protection against state interference remain; no particular additional safeguard or sanction follows from this wording.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recitals 34–35 and Article 4(2) support preserving provider discretion; English already permits review against the stated objectives.

impact_families.title: Spanish wording may narrow safeguards for searches and seizures
impact_families.effect: A newsroom search and seizure of source records could fall outside Article 4(4)'s specific authorization and overriding-public-interest conditions if the narrower Spanish reading prevailed.
impact_families.rationale: Excluding those measures could materially weaken a core protection for journalistic sources and confidential communications. The general protection duty and fundamental rights remain, but do not expressly reproduce every specific safeguard.
impact_families.uncertainty: Broad inspection terminology, the general protection duty and recital context could support a harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Portuguese contact-details provision refers to the editorial-independence declaration
impact_families.effect: If the restrictive reading prevailed, a very large online platform could omit functionality for supplying mechanism representatives’ contact details, also limiting their public availability under Article 18(2).
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns ancillary contact information. The substantive declaration under point (d) and the separate obligation to seek confirmation where reasonable doubt exists remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: The verification subparagraph and recital 53 strongly support harmonizing the reference with point (d).

impact_families.title: Maltese may restrict which bodies can request advertising information
impact_families.effect: If regulatory status were required, an otherwise competent independent monitoring body without that status could lack the express power to request supplementary information about state advertising expenditure.
impact_families.rationale: The restriction concerns a supplementary verification power. Publication and annual monitoring duties, national regulators’ powers and substantive allocation requirements remain. The wording does not change an allocation entitlement or sanction.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 73 and the surrounding subparagraphs support treating regulatory as descriptive of the monitoring function.

impact_families.title: Swedish leaves the period for advertising-distribution efforts unspecified
impact_families.effect: If the Swedish reading prevailed, a Member State could rely on distribution across several years to demonstrate its plurality efforts despite a narrower distribution in one year.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the temporal benchmark for an effort-based objective. Objective, proportionate and non-discriminatory allocation requirements remain, and neither wording grants an individual provider an advertising award.
impact_families.uncertainty: Annual disclosure and monitoring strongly support interpreting the distribution objective annually as well.

impact_families.title: State-advertising disclosures may become alternatives
impact_families.effect: A public authority whose recipients belong to business groups could publish their names while withholding its total and recipient-specific annual state-advertising expenditure figures.
impact_families.rationale: This would materially remove a central public financial-transparency duty. Allocation safeguards and regulators' information powers remain, but neither ensures equivalent public disclosure of the omitted amounts.
impact_families.uncertainty: The minimum-information introduction, specific exemption and recital 73 strongly favour cumulative disclosure.

impact_families.title: AI-content declarations require both human editing and editorial control
impact_families.effect: A provider exercising editorial control over AI content without human editing could be denied a valid declaration and advance reasons and reply safeguards before a platform restricts its content for contractual reasons.
impact_families.rationale: The stricter condition changes eligibility for an important procedural protection against suspension or reduced visibility of media content.
impact_families.uncertainty: The safeguards may overlap in practice; Article 18(4) expressly excludes specified statutory moderation measures.

impact_families.title: Latvian could require notification of qualifying media concentrations
impact_families.effect: For a concentration qualifying under Article 23(1), the Board could have to alert the Commission even when it would otherwise choose not to.
impact_families.rationale: The additional duty concerns institutional notification. It does not change assessment criteria, make opinions binding or itself authorize or prohibit a transaction.
impact_families.uncertainty: Existing cooperation, information-sharing and publication requirements may reduce the practical difference.

impact_families.title: Structured dialogue changes whose access it promotes
impact_families.effect: The Board could satisfy the disputed objective by discussing independent media’s access to platform offerings instead of access to diverse independent-media content.
impact_families.rationale: The changed outcome concerns the focus of structured dialogue and associated reporting. Article 19 establishes no corresponding platform carriage duty or individual access entitlement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Bulgarian recital 56 expressly supports harmonising the objective with access to independent-media offerings.

impact_families.title: Stricter national rules may need to improve both protected interests
impact_families.effect: A stricter national safeguard improving editorial independence alone could fail Article 1(3)'s condition for preserving stronger national rules within the specified regulatory fields.
impact_families.rationale: The cumulative condition could materially narrow Member States' expressly preserved ability to provide stronger protection, including safeguards for media providers under Chapter II.
impact_families.uncertainty: A collective reading of the protected interests could avoid the cumulative condition.

impact_families.title: Access entitlement refers to content free from editorial intervention
impact_families.effect: If freedom from editorial intervention controlled eligibility for protection, otherwise independent content revised by editors could fall outside the Article 3 access entitlement and the corresponding framework duty.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed characteristic defines the substance of an express recipient entitlement and the protection Member States must secure.
impact_families.uncertainty: Definitions and the editorial-freedom safeguards strongly favour interpreting the phrase as protection of editorial autonomy.

impact_families.title: Latvian audience measurement definition could cover non-content platform use
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, a provider measuring non-content platform use for advertising allocation could become subject to Article 24, including annual independent audits where its measurement qualifies as proprietary.
impact_families.rationale: Extending coverage could impose a recurring independent-audit duty on an otherwise excluded measurement activity, materially changing the provider’s substantive compliance obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 12 strongly supports limiting platform measurement to content use; no actual affected provider is established.

impact_families.title: Swedish makes AI-content safeguards cumulative for platform declarations
impact_families.effect: If the Swedish reading prevailed, an otherwise qualifying provider using editorial control without human review could lose Article 18(4)’s advance reasons and response safeguard before a restriction based on platform terms.
impact_families.rationale: The cumulative condition could materially narrow eligibility for an important protection against content restrictions. Illegal-content and systemic-risk exceptions, complaint handling and dispute settlement remain, but do not replace that advance safeguard.
impact_families.uncertainty: Editorial control and human review may overlap; contextual interpretation could reconcile the requirements.

impact_families.title: Czech changes which media-provider information platforms must publish
impact_families.effect: A platform could publish identification and contact information while omitting the substantive declarations that English requires it to make publicly accessible.
impact_families.rationale: This changes the information available through the platform's transparency mechanism. Declaration and moderation safeguards remain, while Article 6 already requires providers to disclose legal names and contact details.
impact_families.uncertainty: The internally inconsistent Czech references strongly invite contextual correction.

impact_families.title: Commission guidelines are discretionary in Bulgarian
impact_families.effect: If the discretionary reading prevailed, the Commission could decline to issue declaration-functionality guidelines without violating Article 18(9).
impact_families.rationale: The change removes an ancillary guidance duty. Article 18 independently establishes the functionality, declaration requirements and platform safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 53 supports issuance; the sources establish no particular downstream loss from absent guidance.

impact_families.title: Polish omits express surveillance and search protection for associated persons
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading prevailed, surveillance of a journalist’s regular contact to identify a source could fall outside Article 4(3)(b), avoiding its specific authorisation and periodic-review requirements.
impact_families.rationale: Removing specific safeguards against coercive source identification would materially weaken an important confidentiality protection. General protection duties and other applicable law would remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general protection duty and recitals strongly favour equivalent safeguards for associated persons.

impact_families.title: German wording may narrow express protection for surveillance-review failures
impact_families.effect: A journalist challenging a failure to review ongoing surveillance could be denied Article 4(8)'s express remedial protection and associated assistance because the challenge concerns paragraph 6 alone.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower reference could materially restrict an express remedial entitlement concerning intrusive surveillance. This does not establish the loss of all judicial recourse.
impact_families.uncertainty: Paragraph 3, Article 47 and recitals 21–22 support broader protection and a harmonized reading.

impact_families.title: Czech additionally requires disclosure of influential shareholdings
impact_families.effect: A provider disclosing influential owners' names without indicating their shareholdings could meet the English wording but need additional disclosure under Czech.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence is an additional ownership-information requirement within the existing disclosure and database framework. The supplied provisions establish no major liability or loss of entitlement from this difference.
impact_families.uncertainty: The transparency context might support requiring shareholding information under English as well.

impact_families.title: Best-practice exchanges may require close Commission cooperation
impact_families.effect: The Board could have to involve the Commission closely in organising a best-practice exchange that would otherwise require only the generally applicable institutional cooperation.
impact_families.rationale: The additional requirement concerns how an exchange is organised. It does not confer Commission approval powers, displace Board independence or change substantive regulatory standards.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 41 and the general cooperation framework may support equivalent requirements in both versions.

impact_families.title: Spanish makes concentration alerts to the Commission mandatory
impact_families.effect: When issuing an own-initiative opinion under Article 23(1), the Board could be required to alert the Commission to the concentration rather than retain discretion over that communication.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence is an institutional communication duty. Commission intervention remains discretionary, opinions remain advisory, and the disputed sentence does not change substantive concentration assessment criteria.
impact_families.uncertainty: Existing information exchanges might already satisfy the Spanish duty; no separate notification procedure is specified.

impact_families.title: Swedish omits the required procedural instrument for justification deadlines
impact_families.effect: If the Swedish reading prevailed, the Board could set a national regulator’s justification deadline by a separate decision rather than through its rules of procedure.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns the adoption procedure for an ancillary reporting deadline. The duties to consider the opinion and explain departures remain; the text establishes no resulting change to concentration approval or sanctions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 10(8) and the surrounding deadline provisions could support requiring the same procedural instrument.

impact_families.title: Polish may make surveillance-software capabilities cumulative
impact_families.effect: If all four capabilities were required, qualifying covert extraction software without analysis capability could escape Article 4(5)’s serious-crime thresholds and requirement that less restrictive measures be insufficient.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower definition could remove important additional conditions on intrusive surveillance. General source protection and safeguards applicable to other surveillance measures would not necessarily restore those specific conditions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 25 and an inclusive interpretation of the list strongly support coverage without all four capabilities.

impact_families.title: Polish does not expressly require an accelerated-cooperation reply within 14 days
impact_families.effect: If the Polish reading prevailed, a requested authority could consider an accelerated request and attempt responsive action without communicating a reply within 14 calendar days.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is loss of a fixed communication deadline. The cooperation framework, obligation to explain refusals and possibility of referral to the Board remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Considering the request and taking responsive action could be interpreted as requiring a timely communicated response.

impact_families.title: Croatian installation wording may narrow the spyware safeguards
impact_families.effect: If installation alone triggered the specific safeguards, authorities could activate previously installed spyware against a journalist without meeting Article 4(5)'s serious-offence thresholds.
impact_families.rationale: That reading could materially weaken the specific protection against highly intrusive surveillance. General surveillance safeguards would remain, but would not necessarily reproduce the serious-offence thresholds and stricter necessity requirement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Operative references to use and review, reinforced by recitals 23–26, strongly support applying the safeguards to activation.

impact_families.title: Allocation safeguards may omit government-controlled commercial entities
impact_families.effect: A government-controlled commercial entity could award a media service contract without applying Article 25(1)’s transparent, objective, proportionate and non-discriminatory allocation requirements.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower reading removes a core allocation duty for a defined category of public-resource providers. Advertising reporting and preserved procurement rules do not establish equivalent safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 2(18), Article 25(3) and recital 73 strongly favour including controlled entities.

impact_families.title: Croatian expressly requires configuration changes without charge
impact_families.effect: From 8 May 2027, a manufacturer could be barred from charging for an otherwise accessible configuration-change function under Croatian wording, even if English were interpreted to permit that charge.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is a payment restriction attached to an existing customization function. Both versions preserve customization rights; the supplied text supports no substantial financial liability or wider loss of access.
impact_families.uncertainty: English “freely” may itself exclude charges, eliminating the difference.

impact_families.title: Public-service exclusion refers to separate rather than limited activities
impact_families.effect: If organisational separation determined exclusion, a private provider otherwise qualifying through its substantial public-service remit and public funding could lose Article 5’s management, editorial-independence and funding safeguards.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed exclusion could determine access to the Regulation’s substantive institutional and financial protections for public-service media.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 2(3) and the recital’s distinction between a remit and contracted tasks support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Competence condition omitted from video-platform enforcement requests
impact_families.effect: If the French reading prevailed, an authority lacking subject-matter competence could receive an Article 15 request requiring an explanation of inaction and potentially leading to Board mediation.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence is additional procedural handling under Article 15(2) and (3). Preserved jurisdictional limits and the Directive 2000/31/EC safeguard do not support new enforcement powers or platform duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Due justification and the cooperation framework may imply the omitted competence condition.

impact_families.title: Latvian could require authority identification after additional refusal grounds
impact_families.effect: An authority refusing a disproportionate cooperation request could also have to identify the competent authority, where possible.
impact_families.rationale: The change adds an ancillary information duty. It neither requires execution nor transfer of the refused request, and feasibility remains an express qualification.
impact_families.uncertainty: The competence-related purpose may support restricting the duty to refusals under point (a).

impact_families.title: Danish cross-reference could narrow requests for additional state-advertising information
impact_families.effect: An independent monitor other than a national regulatory authority could lack Article 25’s express power to request supplementary information from a national government.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects supplementary verification. Allocation standards, annual publication and monitoring duties remain, and Article 7 separately provides information powers to national regulatory authorities.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 73 and the verification purpose strongly support interpreting the reference broadly.

impact_families.title: German national-measure safeguards may have a narrower trigger
impact_families.effect: A provider directly and individually bound by a regulatory measure improving editorial independence could be denied Article 21(3)'s appeal entitlement if the measure presents no possible impairment.
impact_families.rationale: Paragraph 3 expressly incorporates paragraph 1's scope. The narrower trigger could remove an important regulation-specific appeal entitlement, even if other remedies remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recitals 60–61 support an adverse-effects reading of English; other appeal rights may remain.

impact_families.title: Different geographical reference for criteria informing media-declaration guidance
impact_families.effect: If the French reading prevailed, Commission guidance on reviewing media declarations could use criteria concerning Union-origin providers instead of the external-provider criteria envisaged in English.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns guidance inputs. Articles 17 and 18 preserve the Board’s external-provider mandate, declaration requirements and procedural protections; the disputed recital does not establish different eligibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: The explicit external-provider mandate and recital 49 strongly favour a harmonized reading.

impact_families.title: Polish may require Commission agreement to the Board’s procedural rules
impact_families.effect: If Commission agreement were required, the Board could not adopt a proposed internal procedural arrangement over the Commission’s objection.
impact_families.rationale: The direct consequence concerns adoption of procedural arrangements. The provision does not give the Commission approval power over substantive opinions or national enforcement decisions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Board’s independence and consultative institutional context favour a reading that does not require Commission assent.

impact_families.title: Italian AI-content declaration requires both safeguards
impact_families.effect: A provider exercising editorial control over AI-generated content without separate human review could be unable to make the declaration and lose advance reasons and a reply opportunity before contractual content restrictions.
impact_families.rationale: The cumulative condition could materially narrow eligibility for Article 18(4)’s important protection before suspension or reduced visibility. Paragraph 7’s dispute-resolution route does not replace that advance protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Editorial control and human review may overlap in practice; contextual interpretation could reconcile the formulations.

impact_families.title: Danish media-service definition could exclude separable media sections
impact_families.effect: A professional, separable news section of a broader non-media service, not independently classified as a service, could lose eligibility for editorial-independence and journalistic-source protections.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed definition controls entry into the regulatory framework and access to its core provider rights, as well as associated duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 11 supports coverage of service sections; a section may also qualify independently as a service.

impact_families.title: Danish wording could omit the express duty to define researcher-selection criteria
impact_families.effect: The Commission could adopt indicators and safeguards while relying on existing researcher-selection criteria without separately defining those criteria in consultation with the Board.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns a methodological deliverable. Independent, continuous monitoring and annual publication of results, methodology and data remain mandatory.
impact_families.uncertainty: The duty to protect selection criteria could be interpreted as implicitly requiring their definition.

impact_families.title: German wording may require an appropriate amendment proposal
impact_families.effect: If an amendment proposal is considered appropriate, the Commission could be required to attach it to an evaluation report instead of retaining discretion over attachment.
impact_families.rationale: The conditional reporting duty does not change substantive rights under the Regulation or require the legislature to adopt an amendment.
impact_families.uncertainty: The appropriateness condition preserves substantial judgment and may harmonize the formulations.

impact_families.title: Coordination trigger omits the express serious-risk threshold and adds defence
impact_families.effect: Authorities from two Member States could obtain Board coordination for a lesser security-and-defence risk, or be denied coordination for a threat to public security alone.
impact_families.rationale: The changed threshold governs coordination and related advisory involvement. National powers remain preserved; Article 17 does not independently authorise prohibiting or restricting a media service.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 13(1)(l) supports a serious-risk threshold; defence may be read as part of public security.

impact_families.title: Company-name wording may narrow disclosure by natural-person providers
impact_families.effect: If company-name wording controlled, a natural-person provider without such a name could omit their personal legal name from Article 6’s public information and the corresponding national database.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence narrows one identity-disclosure element. Contact details and applicable ownership disclosures remain required; the supplied context does not establish loss of a core permission, remedy or protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Company name may be interpreted functionally as each provider’s official identity, consistent with the transparency purpose.

impact_families.title: Greek limits the labelling clarification to age labels
impact_families.effect: If the Greek reading prevailed, a non-age label restricting declared media content for violating platform terms could require prior reasons and a reply opportunity, unless an Article 18(4) exception applied.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is an additional procedural step for qualifying labels. The power to moderate remains, and mandatory illegal-content, systemic-risk and child-protection measures retain their express exceptions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The recital does not itself classify non-age labels as visibility restrictions; English also permits an age-related contextual reading.

impact_families.title: Personal surveillance is not expressly included in the Hungarian prohibition
impact_families.effect: If personal surveillance fell outside Article 4(3)(b), authorities following a journalist to identify a source could avoid the specific authorisation and regular-review requirements attached to that provision.
impact_families.rationale: Removing personal surveillance from the enumerated prohibition could materially weaken a central protection for confidential journalistic sources.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general protection duty, personal inspection wording and recitals support including personal surveillance through contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Monitoring compliance becomes monitoring participation
impact_families.effect: The Board could monitor which participants join protective initiatives without examining whether those participants fulfil their commitments.
impact_families.rationale: The difference narrows a dialogue-monitoring objective and its reporting. It does not itself remove substantive content-protection duties or alter individual remedies.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 56 expressly supports monitoring compliance, making harmonisation a strong possibility.

impact_families.title: Danish wording could require both Union and national authorisation for source-related measures
impact_families.effect: A source-related search authorised only by national law could remain prohibited despite satisfying proportionality, public-interest justification and independent authorisation requirements.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition determines whether a core prohibition on investigative interference with journalistic sources can be derogated from.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 26 supports an alternative legal basis; contextual interpretation could reconcile the operative conjunction.

impact_families.title: Danish monitoring requirement could focus on mergers rather than existing media concentration
impact_families.effect: Annual monitoring could describe merger activity without separately measuring existing concentrated ownership in a media market with little recent transaction activity.
impact_families.rationale: The possible change concerns a specified monitoring topic. Detailed market analysis, an overview of pluralism risks and the separate concentration-assessment framework remain required.
impact_families.uncertainty: Merger level may contextually describe the resulting degree of media concentration rather than transaction activity.

impact_families.title: National-measure safeguards may require effects on both protected interests
impact_families.effect: A provider directly and individually affected by a regulatory measure impairing editorial independence alone could lose Article 21(3)'s express right to appeal to an independent appellate body.
impact_families.rationale: The cumulative threshold could exclude a class of measures from substantive safeguards and an important procedural remedy expressly linked to Article 21(1).
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 60 supports inclusive coverage; other Union-law remedies may remain available.

impact_families.title: Italian cooperation-notice condition names the requesting authority
impact_families.effect: An authority receiving an inadequate cooperation response could omit prompt reasoned notice to its counterpart, while either authority could still refer their disagreement to the Board.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns an intermediate notice obligation. Response duties, accelerated-cooperation deadlines and access to a Board opinion remain intact; no loss of a core entitlement is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The defined roles and preceding response duty strongly favour contextual harmonization.

impact_families.title: Latvian methodology disclosure provision refers to patented systems
impact_families.effect: If patent status determined disclosure coverage, a provider of an unpatented proprietary system could withhold methodology information otherwise owed free of charge to media service providers and advertisers.
impact_families.rationale: This could remove the provision’s core information entitlement for a class of systems. Independent audits and access to measurement results do not replace access to detailed methodology information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 2(17), recital 70 and the adjacent duties strongly support interpreting the provision consistently with proprietary measurement.

legislation.title: REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 13 June 2024
laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
CHAPTER I
GENERAL PROVISIONS

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Subject matter'
1. The purpose of this Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union and supporting innovation.
2. This Regulation lays down: (a) harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union; (b) prohibitions of certain AI practices; (c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; (d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; (e) harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; (f) rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; (g) measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on small mid-cap enterprises (SMCs) and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including start-ups.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
Scope
1. This Regulation applies to: (a) providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country; (b) deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located within the Union; (c) providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union; (d) importers and distributors of AI systems; (e) product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product and under their own name or trademark; (f) authorised representatives of providers, which are not established in the Union; (g) affected persons that are located in the Union.
2. For AI systems classified as high-risk AI systems in accordance with Article 6(1) related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section B of Annex I, only Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 shall apply. Articles 57, 58 and 59 shall apply only in so far as the requirements for high-risk AI systems under this Regulation have been integrated in that Union harmonisation legislation.
3. This Regulation does not apply to areas outside the scope of Union law, and shall not, in any event, affect the competences of the Member States concerning national security, regardless of the type of entity entrusted by the Member States with carrying out tasks in relation to those competences.
This Regulation does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.
This Regulation does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union, where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.
4. This Regulation applies neither to public authorities in a third country nor to international organisations falling within the scope of this Regulation pursuant to paragraph 1, where those authorities or organisations use AI systems in the framework of international cooperation or agreements for law enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union or with one or more Member States, provided that such a third country or international organisation provides adequate safeguards with respect to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals.
5. This Regulation shall not affect the application of the provisions on the liability of providers of intermediary services as set out in Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065.
6. This Regulation does not apply to AI systems or AI models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.
7. Union law on the protection of personal data, privacy and the confidentiality of communications applies to personal data processed in connection with the rights and obligations laid down in this Regulation. Without prejudice to Articles 4a and 59 of this Regulation, this Regulation shall not affect Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or (EU) 2018/1725, or Directive 2002/58/EC or (EU) 2016/680.
8. This Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. Such activities shall be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law. Testing in real world conditions shall not be covered by that exclusion.
9. This Regulation is without prejudice to the rules laid down by other Union legal acts related to consumer protection and product safety.
10. This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity.
11. This Regulation does not preclude the Union or Member States from maintaining or introducing laws, regulations or administrative provisions which are more favourable to workers in terms of protecting their rights in respect of the use of AI systems by employers, or from encouraging or allowing the application of collective agreements which are more favourable to workers.
12. This Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50.
13. For high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(1), the application of specific requirements or obligations laid down in Articles 9 to 15 and 17 to 25 may be limited, where and to the extent that: (a) Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I lays down requirements or obligations providing an equivalent or higher level of protection of health, safety or fundamental rights as the requirement or obligation concerned; and (b) such limitation does not reduce the overall level of protection provided for by this Regulation.
By 2 August 2027, the Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to supplement this Regulation by specifying the high-risk AI systems concerned, the requirements or obligations that may be limited, the conditions under which such limitation applies, and the scope of the limitation.

passages.label: Article 3
Article 4
passages.text:
Article 4
AI literacy
1. Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context the AI systems are to be used in, and considering the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used. This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.
2. The Commission and the Member States shall support and facilitate the efforts of providers and deployers of AI systems, in particular SMEs, in fulfilling their obligation under paragraph 1 of this Article. For that purpose, the Commission shall publish practical examples of how to comply with that obligation on the single information platform referred to in Article 62(3), point (b).
3. The Board shall adopt recommendations, taking into account European competence frameworks, to support the Commission and Member States in the promotion of AI literacy required under paragraph 1, including by setting out common objectives.

passages.label: Article 4a
passages.text:
Article 4a
Processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction
1. To the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction in relation to high-risk AI systems in accordance with Article 10(2), points (f) and (g), of this Regulation, providers of such systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data, subject to appropriate safeguards for the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons. In addition to the provisions set out in Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable, all the following conditions shall be met in order for such processing to occur: (a) the bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data; (b) the special categories of personal data are subject to technical limitations on the re-use of personal data, and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation; (c) the special categories of personal data are subject to measures to ensure that the personal data processed are secured and protected, subject to suitable safeguards, including strict controls and documentation of the access, to avoid misuse and to ensure that only authorised persons have access to those personal data with appropriate confidentiality obligations; (d) the special categories of personal data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties; (e) the special categories of personal data are deleted once the bias has been corrected or the personal data has reached the end of its retention period, whichever comes first; and (f) the records of processing activities pursuant to Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680 include the reasons why the processing of special categories of personal data was strictly necessary to detect and correct biases, and why that objective could not be achieved by processing other data.
2. Providers and deployers of other AI systems and models and deployers of high-risk AI systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data to the extent that: (a) such processing is strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction in view of possible biases that are likely to affect the health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited pursuant to Union law, especially where data outputs influence inputs for future operations; and (b) all of the conditions and safeguards set out in paragraph 1 are applied.
This paragraph does not create any obligation to conduct such bias detection and correction.

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
CHAPTER II
PROHIBITED AI PRACTICES

passages.label: Article 5
passages.text:
Article 5
Prohibited AI practices
1. The following AI practices shall be prohibited: (a) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective, or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or a group of persons by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision that they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person, another person or group of persons significant harm; (b) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective, or the effect, of materially distorting the behaviour of that person or a person belonging to that group in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm; (ba) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts, or of an identifiable natural person engaged in sexually explicit activities, without that person’s freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent for that generation or manipulation; (bb) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that generates or manipulates material or performance within the meaning of Article 2, points (c) and (e), of Directive 2011/93/EU, except where a ‘without right’ defence applies under national law; (c) the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, with the social score leading to either or both of the following: (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons in social contexts that are unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected; (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons that is unjustified or disproportionate to their social behaviour or its gravity; (d) the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons in order to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, based solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics; this prohibition shall not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of the involvement of a person in a criminal activity, which is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity; (e) the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage; (f) the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions, except where the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons; (g) the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation; this prohibition does not cover any labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data or categorizing of biometric data in the area of law enforcement; (h) the use of ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement, unless and in so far as such use is strictly necessary for one of the following objectives: (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons; (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; (iii) the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty for offences referred to in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or a detention order for a maximum period of at least four years.
Point (h) of the first subparagraph is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for the processing of biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement.
1a. For the purposes of paragraph 1, first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb): (a) the placing on the market or putting into service of an AI system that generates or manipulates the material or performance referred to in paragraph 1, first subparagraph, point (ba) or (bb) is only prohibited where: (i) that generation or manipulation is the intended purpose of the AI system; or (ii) the system’s design, training, architecture, capabilities or user-facing functionalities make that generation or manipulation a reasonably foreseeable and reproducible outcome, without requiring significant technical modification, and the system does not have reasonable and adequate technical safety measures and other safeguards to reliably prevent that generation or manipulation, taking into account reasonably foreseeable misuse, and to correct observed or reported misuse; (b) the use of an AI system that generates or manipulates the material or performance referred to in paragraph 1, first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb) is only prohibited where the deployer uses the system for the purpose of generating or manipulating such material or performance.
1b. For the purposes of paragraph 1, first subparagraph, point (ba), an AI system that manipulates material in a way that does not increase the exposure of any depicted intimate parts or alter the nature of any depicted sexually explicit activities shall not constitute manipulation.
2.
