The selected official consolidation omits recitals. Analysis coverage concerns the preserved consolidation's articles, annexes and included notes; it is not a complete review of the act's historical preamble.

One blind Sol Codex scan per aligned source segment; separate Sol Codex evidence and coverage review; bounded additional review and independent Astra source audit. English is a reference among equally authentic language versions.
Consolidated operative text and annexes are primary coverage. Dated preambles and incorporated definitions provide context. Remaining primary objections keep affected comparison segments incomplete.
Independent audits check retained hypotheses with governing source context. Larger language audits are grouped by provision; they do not establish exhaustive independent discovery across the act.
Segments with unresolved source-validation failures remain incomplete; no finding from them is exported.
Model-reviewed legal differences and conditional impact proposals remain provisional; model agreement is not an adjudicated legal error.
English provides navigation; all official language versions are equally authoritative. Findings are potential discrepancies reviewed by agents, not adjudicated legal errors.
Analysis is incomplete. Absence of a published finding does not imply that the remaining passages or languages have been cleared.

impact_families.title: Spanish omits importer identification on the system itself
impact_families.effect: An importer could provide its details only on packaging, satisfying Spanish wording while failing the English requirement where identification on the system is applicable.
impact_families.rationale: The established change concerns identification placement and verification. Contact information and conformity duties remain; proportionate sanctions are possible, but substantial liability from this placement difference is not established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The applicability qualification may remove the additional placement requirement for particular systems.

impact_families.title: The intimate-material editing exception may apply when only one feature is unchanged
impact_families.effect: Once the prohibition applies, a covered deployer intentionally increases intimate exposure without consent while leaving depicted sexual activity unchanged and invokes the Bulgarian exception.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading removes conduct from a core Article 5 prohibition, subject to paragraph 1a. Other legal prohibitions remain unaffected.
impact_families.uncertainty: The final affirmative statement in amending recital 12 strongly supports harmonization.

impact_families.title: Formal-compliance orders may address additional operators
impact_families.effect: A public deployer could be ordered through Article 83 to complete its own missing database registration.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns an additional recipient of a formal correction procedure. The registration duty already exists, and the subsequent proportionate market-restriction powers remain the same.
impact_families.uncertainty: Responsibility for the particular defect limits which additional operators can receive an order.

impact_families.title: Model-access duty may cover only one model category
impact_families.effect: In an applicable conformity assessment requiring both model categories, a provider could claim that giving access only to trained models satisfies the express model-access duty.
impact_families.rationale: Excluding an entire necessary model category materially narrows a mandatory disclosure duty and the assessor's access. Dataset access and the power to refuse certification do not replace that access.
impact_families.uncertainty: Necessity and an inclusive reading of the alternatives could require both model categories.

impact_families.title: Documentation may address unsuitable methods rather than describe bias-detection methods
impact_families.effect: A provider could document measures assessing unsuitable bias-detection methods without separately describing the methods as an express minimum item.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns one documentation component, while broader training, testing and evaluation documentation obligations remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: English also permits the nested reading, supporting harmonization.

impact_families.title: Delegated-act objection condition may permit entry into force despite one institution’s objection
impact_families.effect: If Parliament objects within the applicable scrutiny period while the Council remains silent, the disputed reading could allow the delegated act to enter into force.
impact_families.rationale: This would materially impair an institution’s blocking power over delegated acts, including amendments to high-risk classifications and conformity assessment procedures.
impact_families.uncertainty: The outer either/or construction, simultaneous notification and joint early clearance strongly support a harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Bias-processing permission may exclude purely anticipated rights harms
impact_families.effect: If existing effects were required, an otherwise qualifying deployer addressing anticipated discrimination, without a health or safety risk, could lose Article 4a(2)'s permission to process special categories of personal data preventively.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition controls access to an express sensitive-data processing permission. Its restriction could materially change which preventive processing is authorized under this provision.
impact_families.uncertainty: Generic present-tense meaning, Article 10(2)(f), and the amending regulation’s recital 9 strongly support a preventive reading.

impact_families.title: Earlier starting point for counting market entrants
impact_families.effect: The report would include undertakings entering between entry into force and entry into application under German, but exclude them under the English starting point.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes a monitoring statistic’s population, without directly changing market access, compliance duties or sanctions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Staggered application dates complicate the precise English starting point.

impact_families.title: Model access may be required before alternative methods are exhausted
impact_families.effect: A provider undergoing the applicable conformity assessment must grant necessary model and parameter access after all reasonable alternatives are shown insufficient, although those alternatives have not been exhausted.
impact_families.rationale: Removing a cumulative prerequisite materially expands compulsory access to the models themselves. Confidentiality and intellectual-property safeguards constrain handling and use but do not restore the exhausted-alternatives condition.
impact_families.uncertainty: Necessity may narrow practical divergence; contextual interpretation could reconcile the prerequisites.

impact_families.title: Different conditions for placing CE marking on packaging
impact_families.effect: A provider retains packaging-only marking where system marking is feasible but unwarranted. Under the Spanish reading, persistent non-compliance after a correction requirement could lead to market restrictions or withdrawal under Article 83.
impact_families.rationale: Article 83 expressly makes Article 48 marking violations grounds for correction and, if persistent, proportionate restrictions, prohibition, recall or withdrawal. The conditional consequence therefore extends beyond marking location.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 16(h) favours harmonisation; restrictions require persistent non-compliance and proportionate enforcement.

impact_families.title: Downstream documentation may require a system overview
impact_families.effect: If the system wording prevailed, a non-exempt model provider could need to supply a system-level overview to downstream providers in addition to the model information retained by Article 53 and Annex XII.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence changes one documentary overview. Model capabilities, limitations and detailed subitems remain required. General enforcement powers do not establish a major changed liability or loss of substantive protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 53 and the model-specific subitems strongly support harmonization; the system to be described is not expressly identified.

impact_families.title: Earlier baseline for counting market entrants
impact_families.effect: An undertaking entering the market in 2025 would fall within the Italian reporting period but outside the English period measured from the general application date of 2 August 2026.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects the population counted in evaluation reports. It does not itself alter market access, compliance duties, eligibility for support or penalties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Staggered application dates may affect interpretation of the English baseline, but do not equate application with entry into force.

impact_families.title: Cooperation shifts from developing to applying procedures
impact_families.effect: Authorities could develop procedures separately under Greek, but would need cooperation when applying them; English expressly requires cooperation during development.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the stage of administrative cooperation. Substantive designation requirements and the specific unified-assessment cooperation duty remain in place.
impact_families.uncertainty: Development and implementation may overlap; the text does not establish invalidity of individual notifications.

impact_families.title: Downstream architecture information may be limited to parameter structure
impact_families.effect: Downstream documentation could omit architectural information beyond parameter structure where that information is not independently required by Article 53(1)(b)(i).
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns a specific disclosure item, while the functional duty to enable downstream understanding and compliance continues to apply.
impact_families.uncertainty: The functional duty or a broad reading of parameter structure may require equivalent information.

impact_families.title: Critical-infrastructure incident reporting may require disruption of both functions
impact_families.effect: A covered provider avoids serious-incident reporting for irreversible disruption of infrastructure operation alone, where no other incident category or sectoral reporting exception applies.
impact_families.rationale: Article 73 makes classification determine a core reporting duty and a specific two-day deadline.
impact_families.uncertainty: Management and operation may receive a collective reading; another incident category may apply.

impact_families.title: Periodic inspection penalties are limited to on-site inspections
impact_families.effect: An operator refusing a remote inspection could avoid periodic payments imposed solely under Article 75c(5)(c), although that ground would cover the refusal under the English reading.
impact_families.rationale: The provision directly determines exposure to coercive daily payments, with an express ceiling linked to income or worldwide annual turnover. Removing that ground can materially change financial liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: Other grounds may apply; their availability cannot be assumed for every remote-inspection refusal.

impact_families.title: Annex III review may focus on functions within areas
impact_families.effect: The Commission assesses additional functions within existing Annex III areas but omits consideration of a new area heading from its periodic report and supporting methodology.
impact_families.rationale: The immediate consequence concerns review and methodology scope. Existing classifications remain intact, and Article 112 retains broader evaluation duties and the possibility of amendment proposals.
impact_families.uncertainty: Reading functions by area as encompassing new areas could reconcile the versions.

impact_families.title: Sectoral consideration duty may exclude initial delegated and implementing acts
impact_families.effect: An initial sectoral implementing act is adopted without applying Article 112(12)’s express duty to consider sectoral specificities and existing governance, conformity assessment and enforcement arrangements.
impact_families.rationale: The established consequence is a narrower lawmaking consideration duty. Article 2(2) and the sectoral amendments preserve the sectoral framework; this wording does not itself remove substantive protections or authorities.
impact_families.uncertainty: English also permits an amendment-only reading; contextual interpretation may align both versions.

impact_families.title: Employment-law terminology may narrow coverage of independent work
impact_families.effect: AI determining significant contractual terms for independent service providers could escape high-risk classification where no other classification basis applies and the relevant obligations would otherwise apply.
impact_families.rationale: Exclusion could remove core provider requirements, deployer oversight and, where its conditions are met, the Article 86 explanation entitlement.
impact_families.uncertainty: The heading and recital 57 strongly support inclusion, particularly for platform service relationships.

impact_families.title: Some delegated criminal-risk assessments may lose high-risk coverage
impact_families.effect: When applicable, a lawful reoffending assessment during sentence execution, performed solely by a private delegate outside Article 3(45), could lose high-risk coverage if no other category applies.
impact_families.rationale: Losing classification could remove core provider and deployer duties. Point 6(e) covers profiling during detection, investigation or prosecution; it does not expressly cover sentence execution.
impact_families.uncertainty: Authority use, another high-risk category or a harmonized reading may preserve coverage; Article 5 prohibitions remain.

impact_families.title: Impairment requirement may narrow substantial modification
impact_families.effect: An unplanned change affecting conformity without impairing it or changing intended purpose could escape the French trigger for renewed conformity assessment while meeting the English trigger.
impact_families.rationale: Article 43(4) attaches a core reassessment duty to substantial modification, including where the current deployer continues using the system.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 128 and Annex VII support harmonization; separate assessment and continuing compliance duties remain.

impact_families.title: Explicit consent is omitted from the intimate-material prohibition
impact_families.effect: Once the provision applies, a deployer within its scope intentionally generates covered intimate material with unambiguous but non-explicit consent and invokes the Italian wording to avoid this prohibition.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading materially narrows a core prohibition protecting intimate autonomy. Other applicable law remains preserved, but does not erase the change to this prohibition.
impact_families.uncertainty: The bilingual amending Recital 12 strongly supports explicit consent; Article 113 postpones application until 2 December 2026.

impact_families.title: Organised theft may qualify for the biometric-identification exception
impact_families.effect: Authorities obtain authorization to identify an organised-theft suspect using real-time remote biometrics, although the offence is not robbery, with the sentence threshold and all other Article 5 conditions satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed reading expands eligibility for an exception to a core prohibition on intrusive biometric identification.
impact_families.uncertainty: Uniform interpretation of the offence category may remove the difference; national authorization remains necessary.

impact_families.title: Product images may cease to be an explicit documentation item
impact_families.effect: A provider could omit product photographs or illustrations while supplying the information otherwise necessary to demonstrate conformity under Article 11.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence concerns one ancillary documentation element. Comprehensive conformity information, substantive system requirements and conformity assessment remain required.
impact_families.uncertainty: The annex's structure and Article 11 strongly support restoring the image requirement.

impact_families.title: Potentially narrower high-risk category for biometric categorisation
impact_families.effect: Once the relevant duties apply, a lawful biometric categorisation system using sensitive but unprotected inferred attributes, otherwise high-risk solely under this category and outside Article 6(3), could avoid high-risk compliance duties.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 6, 8, 16 and 43 connect this classification to mandatory safeguards and conformity assessment. Losing that classification can remove core duties despite continuing transparency and data-protection rules.
impact_families.uncertainty: The adjectives may be harmonized; the supplied text does not define their boundary or identify an actual affected system.

impact_families.title: General penalty authorization points to the budget-receipts paragraph
impact_families.effect: An operator within the AI Office’s competence found to infringe Article 5 could contest attaching Article 99(3) penalties to its non-compliance decision through Article 75c(4)'s general authorization.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed authorization incorporates fines reaching EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover, subject to applicable limits. Subsequent express provisions do not clearly reproduce that sanction tier.
impact_families.uncertainty: The impossible paragraph-7 reference and remaining express fine provisions strongly support harmonization; complete immunity is not supported.

impact_families.title: Spanish omits the express requirement for support for human overseers
impact_families.effect: A deployer could appoint qualified overseers but withhold practical support necessary for oversight, escaping this paragraph's express support duty where other obligations do not independently supply it.
impact_families.rationale: The omission can materially weaken the conditions necessary for effective human oversight of high-risk systems, a core safeguard against health, safety and fundamental-rights risks.
impact_families.uncertainty: Instruction-following, monitoring and other applicable duties may independently require equivalent support.

impact_families.title: Common features of widespread infringements may become cumulative
impact_families.effect: Parallel infringements qualifying only under Article 3(61)(b), sharing an infringed interest but different unlawful practices, could follow the ordinary reporting timetable instead of the two-day maximum.
impact_families.rationale: The established conditional consequence concerns reporting timing. Immediate reporting when the ordinary conditions are met, investigation and corrective duties remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: The features may be illustrative; another widespread-infringement or serious-incident trigger may independently apply.

impact_families.title: Risk consultation names a different authority
impact_families.effect: A market surveillance authority could take Article 82 corrective measures without this particular consultation of the relevant fundamental-rights authority.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects a specific procedural step. Article 79 retains full cooperation where fundamental-rights risks arise, Article 77 retains mutual assistance, and Article 82 retains corrective-action duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Article 77 cross-reference strongly supports consulting the intended fundamental-rights authority; institutional roles may also overlap.

impact_families.title: Annex XI names a system as the object of the general description
impact_families.effect: A provider could be required to add system-level descriptive information to the model documentation made available to authorities.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change affects one descriptive component; Article 53 and the model-specific particulars preserve the underlying documentation duty.
impact_families.uncertainty: The heading, model-specific list and Article 53 strongly favour reading the description as concerning the model.

impact_families.title: Reporting supervisory information to the ECB may be mandatory
impact_families.effect: A qualifying national market surveillance authority delays sending information potentially relevant to ECB prudential supervision. Spanish could treat the delay as breach of an express reporting duty.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change concerns inter-authority information sharing. Supervisory jurisdiction and credit institutions’ substantive obligations remain unchanged, and the supplied provisions establish no concrete major sanction for this reporting omission.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation could make both formulations obligatory; other financial-law reporting duties are not supplied.

impact_families.title: Law-enforcement categorisation may lose a separate exception
impact_families.effect: Standalone law-enforcement categorisation otherwise within Article 5(1)(g) could be prohibited under the Italian reading while exempt from that particular prohibition under English.
impact_families.rationale: This changes the boundary of a core prohibition. Preserved data-protection and other Union-law restrictions do not themselves restore the disputed exception.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation could treat categorisation as independently exempt; exemption would not establish lawfulness under other legislation.

impact_families.title: Task-allocation criteria may exclude physical or demographic characteristics
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading prevailed, a new system allocating work solely by age could escape mandatory high-risk compliance and human oversight, where assignment does not affect contractual terms and no other category applies.
impact_families.rationale: The classification boundary controls core duties under Articles 8, 16 and 26. Article 6(3)’s profiling rule operates within Annex III, so it cannot alone cure exclusion from that annex.
impact_families.uncertainty: Relationship-terms coverage or a broader contextual reading may preserve classification; Articles 111 and 113 govern application.

impact_families.title: Interaction disclosures use the system boundary instead of the model boundary
impact_families.effect: A provider omits a description of interaction with software inside the downstream system but outside the model from this minimum disclosure item.
impact_families.rationale: The change narrows one specified information item. Article 53(1)(b) independently preserves information needed to understand capabilities and limitations and satisfy downstream obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: The broader information duty may independently require the particular interaction description.

impact_families.title: Sectoral consideration duty may exclude initial delegated and implementing acts
impact_families.effect: When initially adopting a relevant sectoral delegated or implementing act, the Commission could avoid the specific Article 112(12) duty to consider existing sectoral arrangements.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects a consideration requirement. It does not itself transfer sectoral powers or remove the separate requirements preserved by Article 2(2) and Articles 102–109.
impact_families.uncertainty: The provision’s purpose and sectoral context support applying the duty to initial adoption.

impact_families.title: Dutch product documentation wording may permit descriptions without images
impact_families.effect: A provider submits a sufficient written description of product features, markings and internal layout without photographs or illustrations.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated consequence concerns one documentation medium. Article 11 preserves adequate conformity evidence; Article 83's unavailable-documentation ground does not necessarily cover this otherwise sufficient dossier.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may require images; broader enforcement consequences depend on whether the dossier is substantively insufficient.

impact_families.title: Expert qualifications may require both scientific and technical expertise
impact_families.effect: If the cumulative criterion prevailed, an otherwise qualified scientific AI expert lacking technical expertise could be ineligible for appointment to conduct a model evaluation under Article 92(2).
impact_families.rationale: Article 92(2) expressly applies Article 68(2)'s criteria to individual evaluation experts, supporting a concrete change in eligibility for an enforcement role.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 68(2)'s introductory alternative and collective panel formulation support harmonization and qualify the panel-applicant scenario.

impact_families.title: Enforcement assessment specifies five initial years
impact_families.effect: An assessment relying on a shorter initial observation period would require additional temporal coverage under the Bulgarian five-year wording.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns the evidence considered in an institutional assessment. It does not itself change enforcement powers, sanctions, individual remedies or application dates.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general application date supports harmonization; staggered application complicates the precise five-year reference.

impact_families.title: Replacement responsibility lacks an express immediate start
impact_families.effect: After withdrawal of a body's designation, otherwise eligible certificates could remain provisionally valid despite a delay before the replacement body assumes responsibility.
impact_families.rationale: The timing condition governs continued certificate validity and responsible conformity oversight, materially affecting an important regulatory entitlement.
impact_families.uncertainty: The continuity provisions may require an immediate takeover despite the Polish wording.

impact_families.title: Dutch conformity declarations require both provider and applicable representative details
impact_families.effect: A provider persists in using a declaration identifying only its authorised representative after a correction demand, exposing the system to market restrictions under the Dutch requirement.
impact_families.rationale: Article 83 expressly connects an incorrectly drawn-up declaration and persistent non-compliance to restriction, prohibition, recall or withdrawal. This supports a major conditional consequence beyond adding identification details.
impact_families.uncertainty: Prompt correction avoids escalation; any measure must be appropriate and proportionate, and contextual harmonisation remains possible.

impact_families.title: Documentation may omit detection of unsuitable data sources
impact_families.effect: A provider subject to Article 53(1)(a) could describe source identification and bias detection without describing measures that identified unsuitable data sources.
impact_families.rationale: This narrows one documentation item. Provenance, selection and curation disclosures remain; no substantive screening exemption or major proportionate sanction consequence is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The surrounding data-documentation requirements support restoring the omitted qualification contextually.

impact_families.title: Evaluation of additional voluntary requirements may include high-risk systems
impact_families.effect: The Commission’s three-year evaluation could also cover voluntary environmental requirements for high-risk systems.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns a periodic review’s scope. Article 95 retains voluntary participation and the wording imposes no additional mandatory product requirements or sanctions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The preceding non-high-risk limitation could be read as governing both limbs.

impact_families.title: Prompt conformity assessment may become an efforts obligation
impact_families.effect: During a temporary exceptional authorisation, diligent efforts could satisfy the Polish timing duty despite conformity assessment remaining unfinished beyond an otherwise justified period.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns procedural timing. Authorisation remains temporary, requires substantive compliance under Article 46(3), and may be withdrawn if unjustified.
impact_families.uncertainty: Undue delay and undertaking completion may themselves be assessed by reference to reasonable efforts.

impact_families.title: Model access may be required before alternative checks are exhausted
impact_families.effect: In an applicable conformity assessment, a provider could be compelled to grant access to training and trained models after all reasonable alternatives prove insufficient but before they have been exhausted.
impact_families.rationale: This removes an express prerequisite to mandatory access to models and relevant parameters. Necessity and Article 78 confidentiality protections limit disclosure but do not restore the exhaustion safeguard.
impact_families.uncertainty: Harmonization remains possible; Article 43 and the applicable transitional rules determine whether the assessment procedure applies.

impact_families.title: Compliance reporting loses its express implementation trigger
impact_families.effect: An operator implementing corrective measures could report them later without violating an express requirement in this sentence to report upon implementation.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change concerns the timing of an ancillary report. The reporting duty, corrective measures, specified compliance period and powers to demand information remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: A decision-specific deadline or contextual interpretation could require reporting at the same time.

impact_families.title: Spanish uses crypto-tokens in the dataset measurement example
impact_families.effect: The Commission could treat crypto-token measurement as the stated example when considering dataset quality or size for systemic-risk designation.
impact_families.rationale: The changed example provides ancillary assessment guidance. It neither mandates a measurement method nor changes the underlying criterion or establishes a classification threshold.
impact_families.uncertainty: The AI dataset context strongly supports harmonization; a resulting designation change is not established.

impact_families.title: General-purpose model obligations name system providers
impact_families.effect: If the system-provider wording prevailed, a provider supplying only a general-purpose model could contest paragraph 1 duties, while a separate general-purpose system provider could become subject to them.
impact_families.rationale: The substitution could materially change the addressees of core documentation, information, copyright-policy and training-summary obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 53’s remaining text, Articles 54–56 and 88–93, and Annexes XI–XII strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: General architecture description may be narrowed to parameter structure
impact_families.effect: A provider could give parameter structure and count in the general description without separately describing broader model architecture there.
impact_families.rationale: Detailed model-design specifications remain mandatory, with additional architecture information for systemic-risk models where applicable. The established change concerns a limited disclosure item.
impact_families.uncertainty: Parameter structure may be interpreted as encompassing model architecture.

impact_families.title: Declaration may require both provider and representative details
impact_families.effect: For a standalone high-risk system, a representative-only declaration left uncorrected after an authority’s deadline could trigger market restrictions or withdrawal under the Greek reading.
impact_families.rationale: Article 83 expressly links persistent incorrect declaration preparation to measures affecting market availability. This supports a major conditional consequence beyond adding identification details.
impact_families.uncertainty: Correction can avert escalation; measures must be proportionate, and contextual interpretation may harmonize the identification requirement.

impact_families.title: The sandbox sharing prohibition covers stored rather than created data
impact_families.effect: A provider could be barred from sharing originally collected personal data held in the sandbox even where that sharing complies with Union data-protection law.
impact_families.rationale: The changed category substantially expands an express data-sharing prohibition within the Article 59 regime and restricts its accompanying permission.
impact_families.uncertainty: The preceding sharing permission supports harmonization; Article 59(3) preserves other lawful processing bases.

impact_families.title: Model access may precede exhaustion of other verification methods
impact_families.effect: A provider could be required to grant necessary model access once all other reasonable verification methods are shown insufficient, even though they have not all been exhausted.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence changes assessment sequencing. It does not independently expand the information accessible or remove necessity, justification, confidentiality or the substantive conformity standard.
impact_families.uncertainty: A last-resort interpretation could preserve the cumulative threshold in practice.

impact_families.title: Optional national rules on public-sector fines
impact_families.effect: A Member State could omit a specific determination of the extent of public-sector fines under the Italian reading, while remaining obliged to establish and implement the general penalty framework.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated change concerns a supplementary rulemaking duty. Both versions leave the extent of public-sector fines to national determination; neither establishes a minimum fine or mandatory public-sector liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may reconcile the rulemaking language; the wording alone does not establish the fine regime absent specific national rules.

impact_families.title: Model access may be required before alternative methods are exhausted
impact_families.effect: A provider could be compelled to grant necessary access to models and parameters after other reasonable methods were shown insufficient, even though those methods had not been exhausted.
impact_families.rationale: The alternative test removes an express prerequisite protecting providers against compulsory access to the models themselves. Confidentiality safeguards regulate access but do not restore exhaustion.
impact_families.uncertainty: Necessity and a functional understanding of exhaustion may narrow the practical difference.

impact_families.title: Periodic penalties may cover inspections rather than broader investigations
impact_families.effect: An operator resisting a standalone data-preservation order during an investigation, before a non-compliance decision and outside an inspection, could contest periodic penalties under the narrower Romanian wording.
impact_families.rationale: Article 75a(6)(b) supplies a concrete investigative measure outside the specifically listed grounds. Losing the general ground could remove exposure to substantial recurring penalties.
impact_families.uncertainty: The outcome depends on the order’s legal basis, overlap with other grounds, and contextual interpretation of submission to investigation.

impact_families.title: The procedural-task exemption may turn on precision instead of narrow scope
impact_families.effect: An Annex III system performing a broad, precisely specified procedural task avoids high-risk classification despite meeting no other exemption condition, while satisfying the risk and profiling limits.
impact_families.rationale: Classification determines substantial high-risk requirements and provider duties, including conformity assessment. Assessment documentation and registration remain required under Article 6(4).
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation may treat precise formulation as implying a narrowly bounded task.

impact_families.title: Human oversight may omit a separate option to decline system use
impact_families.effect: A provider enables output rejection and safe intervention but does not separately enable oversight personnel to decline an individual system use before output generation.
impact_families.rationale: The residual change affects a distinct oversight option. Effective oversight, proportionate safeguards and safe stopping remain mandatory; the text does not establish unrestricted autonomous use.
impact_families.uncertainty: Effective oversight and intervention may already require the practical ability to decline use.

impact_families.title: Transport qualification may narrow the sandbox network category
impact_families.effect: An otherwise qualifying sandbox project protecting a non-transport network, outside critical infrastructure and other listed areas, could lose Article 59(1)'s permission to reuse personal data under the French reading.
impact_families.rationale: The difference can determine eligibility for an express personal-data processing permission. The incorporated critical-infrastructure definition narrows the residual category without expressly eliminating it.
impact_families.uncertainty: English may mean transport or critical networks; other listed grounds or independent legal bases may cover a particular project.

impact_families.title: Foreseeability may not limit human behaviour in the misuse definition
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, a high-risk system provider could have to evaluate unforeseeable human misuse and provide corresponding safeguards where mitigation is reasonable and oversight measures are proportionate.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 9 and 14 connect the definition to core risk-management and human-oversight duties. Expanding the covered misuse could materially expand required assessments and safeguards.
impact_families.uncertainty: The defined term and surrounding foreseeability language strongly support harmonization; application dates and scope exclusions remain applicable.

impact_families.title: Bias examination may extend to merely possible harmful effects
impact_families.effect: A provider could need additional bias examination and proportionate mitigation for a possible harmful effect that does not meet the English likelihood threshold.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change is incremental governance work alongside Article 9’s existing preventive duties. No distinct major outcome or substantial sanction follows from the supplied evidence.
impact_families.uncertainty: Preventive purpose and the amending recital’s likelihood language support harmonisation.

impact_families.title: The judicial-system supervision exception is limited to high-risk systems
impact_families.effect: A qualifying private provider of a non-high-risk judicial system failing Article 6(4)'s documentation duty could face the AI Office's Article 99(4) fine regime under Croatian.
impact_families.rationale: Article 75c(4) extends that substantial fine regime to applicable provisions outside Article 99(4)'s list. National penalties remain possible under Article 99(1), but their regime is different.
impact_families.uncertainty: Requires Article 6(3) eligibility and no independent Article 75(1)(b) competence; national penalties may also be substantial.

impact_families.title: Applicability qualification shifts between retained documents
impact_families.effect: Where the importer duties apply, an importer discarding instructions or its declaration could avoid a retention infringement and associated Article 99(4)(c) fine if Greek makes retention inapplicable.
impact_families.rationale: Although retention is ancillary, Article 99 expressly subjects Article 23 infringements to potentially substantial fines. Other actors' retention duties do not replace the importer's liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: Mandatory availability strongly supports applicability; any fine remains subject to proportionality, enterprise-size limits and individual circumstances.

impact_families.title: Two-person verification may apply only to sole reliance on biometric identification
impact_families.effect: Outside the express exception, a deployer could combine an unverified remote biometric identification with other evidence and act without the two-person verification required by English.
impact_families.rationale: This materially narrows a core safeguard governing consequential reliance on remote biometric identification. General oversight duties do not supply the omitted verification requirement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Protective context supports harmonisation, but does not explain away the express sole-reliance qualification.

impact_families.title: Different reference for mechanisms and authorities to be considered
impact_families.effect: In preparing an act affecting a sectoral directive, the Commission could treat AI Regulation mechanisms as the expressly specified arrangements requiring consideration.
impact_families.rationale: The immediate change concerns a mandatory consideration during legislative preparation; it does not itself transfer authority or displace sectoral procedures.
impact_families.uncertainty: The sectoral-specificities requirement and integration framework strongly favour considering sectoral mechanisms in both versions.

impact_families.title: Documentation proportionality may depend on the system rather than the model
impact_families.effect: If the system-based benchmark prevailed, a non-exempt model provider could have to adjust documentary detail to an integrating system’s different size or risk profile while retaining the mandatory model information.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated change concerns documentary proportionality. Article 53 retains minimum model information and Article 55 retains systemic-risk duties; Article 101’s general fine ceiling alone does not establish a major changed sanction.
impact_families.uncertainty: Model-focused provisions strongly favour harmonization; the text does not identify which integrating system supplies the alternative benchmark.

impact_families.title: Standalone emergency patient triage may fall outside the listed high-risk use
impact_families.effect: Once the relevant duties apply, a standalone system materially prioritizing emergency patients, with no independent high-risk classification, could escape high-risk provider and deployer duties.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 6, 9, 14, 16 and 43 connect classification to core risk-management, human-oversight and conformity-assessment duties. Exclusion could remove those safeguards for consequential patient prioritization.
impact_families.uncertainty: Harmonization, medical-device classification or another Annex III use could preserve coverage.

impact_families.title: Employment terminology may narrow coverage of work-related contract decisions
impact_families.effect: A system deciding termination of self-employed service contracts could escape this high-risk category under German, where no other category applies and no Article 6(3) exemption or transitional protection applies.
impact_families.rationale: Once applicable under Article 113, exclusion could remove core provider, conformity-assessment and deployer duties under Articles 16, 43 and 26.
impact_families.uncertainty: The self-employment heading supports a broader autonomous reading of the German employment terms.

impact_families.title: Emergency triage classification may be narrowed to first aid
impact_families.effect: An emergency clinical triage system beyond first aid, materially influencing treatment priority and lacking another classification route, could escape the high-risk requirements under the narrower reading.
impact_families.rationale: Exclusion could remove core risk-management, human-oversight and conformity-assessment duties, subject to the applicable commencement and transitional provisions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Emergency-response context supports harmonization; medical-device classification may independently cover a particular system.

impact_families.title: Bias-detection documentation shifts toward identifying unsuitable methods
impact_families.effect: A provider describes how it detects unsuitable bias-detection methods without separately describing the methods used to detect biases.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns one technical-documentation element. Other training-data and evaluation information remains required; no particular major sanction or deployment consequence is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: English attachment is ambiguous, and contextual interpretation may require the same documentation.

impact_families.title: Technical documentation additionally requires the system's date
impact_families.effect: A provider supplying the purpose, provider identity and version could be required to add a separate system date to its technical documentation.
impact_families.rationale: The identified change is an ancillary documentation item. A major substantive conformity change or substantial sanction from that omission alone is not established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The meaning of the system's date is unspecified, and the annex applies information requirements as appropriate.

impact_families.title: The sandbox condition may require identifying response mechanisms rather than having them ready
impact_families.effect: Personal data collected for another purpose could enter sandbox processing after response mechanisms are identified but before they are available to mitigate emerging high risks or stop processing.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects an express prerequisite for repurposing personal data, weakening advance readiness to protect rights and freedoms while other sandbox safeguards remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Articles 57(5), 57(11) and applicable data-protection law strongly support operational preparedness.

impact_families.title: French may narrow the trigger for a data-protection compliance statement
impact_families.effect: For a standalone high-risk system using optional personal-data processing, persistent omission of the statement after a correction requirement could trigger market restrictions under the English reading but no corresponding defect under French.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 47(2) and 83 connect declaration content to correction and, upon persistent non-compliance, proportionate restriction, prohibition, recall or withdrawal. This supports a major conditional market-access consequence.
impact_families.uncertainty: A functional reading may reconcile the triggers; restrictions require persistent non-compliance and must be appropriate and proportionate.

impact_families.title: Application-day design changes may retain transitional protection
impact_families.effect: A legacy private-sector Annex III system undergoes its only significant design change on 2 December 2027 and retains transitional protection under the Finnish reading.
impact_families.rationale: The boundary could determine continuing exemption from core high-risk compliance duties, rather than merely postponing compliance for one day.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared transitional purpose and the amending recital’s English 'after' wording favour harmonization.

impact_families.title: Registration status refers to withdrawal rather than recall
impact_families.effect: A provider could update registration information with withdrawal status without separately identifying recall of systems already supplied to deployers.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the status information entered and maintained under Articles 49 and 71. It does not remove substantive recall duties, corrective powers or separate notification requirements.
impact_families.uncertainty: The generic status term could encompass recall when interpreted with Article 3 and the registration scheme.

impact_families.title: Gas-supply high-risk category may be limited to natural gas
impact_families.effect: Once applicable, high-risk duties could cease to cover a safety-critical AI component in an essential non-natural-gas supply service, assuming no independent high-risk classification.
impact_families.rationale: The narrowed category could remove core risk-management, human-oversight and conformity-assessment duties under Articles 9, 14, 16 and 43 for a system presenting significant safety risks.
impact_families.uncertainty: The utility context may harmonize scope; independent product classification may preserve duties.

impact_families.title: Willingness to follow guidance may preserve sandbox fine immunity
impact_families.effect: A prospective provider complying with its participation plan but failing to follow separate guidance despite genuine willingness could retain administrative-fine immunity under the French reading and lose it under the English reading.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition controls an express exemption from administrative fines. Article 99 permits substantial fines for applicable infringements; liability and corrective powers remain separate.
impact_families.uncertainty: Good-faith willingness may require demonstrable adherence; guidance incorporated into participation terms remains binding under either reading.

impact_families.title: Withdrawal from testing may be linked to a deletion request
impact_families.effect: A participant who revokes consent without requesting deletion could have withdrawal treated as incomplete if the Portuguese coordination were applied as two required steps.
impact_families.rationale: That reading would materially condition the important entitlement to leave real-world testing at any time.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 61's withdrawal guarantee and the voluntary-consent definition strongly support treating deletion as optional.

impact_families.title: Bias-detection documentation may require different information
impact_families.effect: A provider subject to Article 53(1)(a) could need to document checks on bias-detection methods’ adequacy instead of separately describing the detection methods themselves.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes one documentation component. It does not itself authorize data processing, remove systemic-risk mitigation duties, alter classification or exempt the provider from technical documentation.
impact_families.uncertainty: English attachment is ambiguous; comprehensive documentation may satisfy both readings. Article 53(2) and transitional rules limit applicability.

impact_families.title: Law-enforcement profiling may receive broader high-risk classification
impact_families.effect: Otherwise uncovered lawful profiling solely for executing criminal penalties becomes high-risk and attracts core compliance duties once the relevant provisions apply.
impact_families.rationale: Article 6 connects Annex III classification to the high-risk regime and excludes profiling from its low-risk derogation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Other categories may already cover a particular system; Articles 111 and 113 qualify timing.

impact_families.title: Importer identification may appear only in accompanying materials
impact_families.effect: An importer could provide all required identification in accompanying documents while omitting it from a system on which identification could otherwise be displayed.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated change concerns identification placement. Identification, conformity, documentation and cooperation duties remain. General sanction ceilings do not establish a major financial consequence for this isolated defect.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may restore system placement; any sanction depends on proportionality and the circumstances specified in Article 99(7).

impact_families.title: Annex XI changes the information required about data sources and bias detection
impact_families.effect: A provider could describe measures identifying sources and methods unsuitable for bias detection without separately describing the methods it uses to detect bias.
impact_families.rationale: The established consequence concerns one technical-documentation item. Article 53 and other applicable model obligations remain; a major downstream outcome is not established.
impact_families.uncertainty: The surrounding data-documentation context may restore the separate disclosure requirement.

impact_families.title: Lifecycle change descriptions may be limited to significant changes
impact_families.effect: A provider could omit a minor but relevant change from the lifecycle change description while retaining all information independently necessary to assess compliance.
impact_families.rationale: The residual difference concerns change-history completeness. Article 11 and separate conformity-assessment controls preserve necessary compliance information and substantive review of qualifying changes.
impact_families.uncertainty: Regulatory relevance may determine significance; general penalty ceilings do not establish a substantial sanction for this residual omission.

impact_families.title: Systemic-risk model qualification omitted from binding commitments procedure
impact_families.effect: A provider outside the systemic-risk model category could obtain a decision making mitigation commitments binding and declaring no further grounds for action.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes eligibility for a procedure creating enforceable commitments and permitting closure of regulatory action.
impact_families.uncertainty: Articles 51–52 and the commitments’ systemic-risk purpose may reconcile the versions.

impact_families.title: Market-impact presumption counts Union operations instead of Union establishment
impact_families.effect: Additional users without Union establishment trigger the presumption and tip a systemic-risk designation, causing an otherwise eligible open-source provider to lose the Article 53(2) documentation exception.
impact_families.rationale: The supplied rules connect the criterion to designation, additional systemic-risk duties and loss of an express exemption. These are material changes in eligibility and core provider obligations.
impact_families.uncertainty: A Commission assessment and decision remain necessary; the user count alone does not compel designation.

impact_families.title: Annex XII names a system in the description for downstream providers
impact_families.effect: A provider could have to supply downstream providers with system-level descriptive information alongside the mandatory model particulars.
impact_families.rationale: The potential change concerns one disclosure component; the express duty to enable understanding of the model remains.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 53 and the model-specific particulars strongly support harmonisation.

impact_families.title: Employment terminology may narrow coverage of contractor management
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading prevailed, a new system deciding termination of non-platform independent contractors’ service contracts could escape high-risk compliance and oversight duties where no separate classification applies.
impact_families.rationale: Exclusion would remove core duties attached by Articles 6, 8, 16 and 26. Material determination of termination need not qualify for Article 6(3)’s exception. Articles 111 and 113 govern application.
impact_families.uncertainty: The self-employment heading and recital 57 strongly favour an autonomous, broader interpretation of employment relationships.

impact_families.title: Union law-enforcement support may exceed the polygraph category
impact_families.effect: Once the relevant duties apply, a non-polygraph Union support system outside other high-risk categories and Article 6(3)'s exception could become subject to the high-risk compliance regime.
impact_families.rationale: The expanded category could trigger core provider requirements, conformity assessment and deployer duties under Articles 8, 16, 26 and 43.
impact_families.uncertainty: A shared-purpose reading could apply the polygraph qualification to both Romanian actor branches.

impact_families.title: Educational-programme allocation is expressly included in Croatian
impact_families.effect: A system materially assigning students between programmes at the same institution and educational level could be classified as high-risk only under the broader Croatian wording.
impact_families.rationale: Where Article 6(3) provides no exemption, classification activates substantive provider duties, including risk management, documentation and conformity assessment.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 56 and broader interpretations of access or admission strongly support equivalent coverage.

impact_families.title: Notifying authorities’ cooperation platform becomes a notification function
impact_families.effect: If the Portuguese reading prevailed, the second subgroup could discharge its function by notifying authorities without providing notifying authorities with a cooperation and exchange platform.
impact_families.rationale: This changes an internal cooperation mechanism. Articles 28 and 38 retain notifying authorities’ substantive responsibilities and separate cooperation and knowledge-exchange arrangements.
impact_families.uncertainty: The two-subgroup structure and defined authority roles strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Alternative prerequisites for compulsory model access
impact_families.effect: A notified body could compel necessary model access after demonstrating other methods' insufficiency, despite not exhausting them, whereas the English cumulative condition would defer access.
impact_families.rationale: The difference removes an independent prerequisite protecting the provider against compulsory disclosure of training and trained models and their parameters.
impact_families.uncertainty: Exhaustion and insufficiency may overlap; necessity, confidentiality and intellectual-property safeguards remain binding.

impact_families.title: Sensitive operational data may receive a narrower categorical exclusion
impact_families.effect: Operational information threatening procedural integrity but not independence loses its automatic exclusion from information exchanges and instead requires assessment under Article 78’s general confidentiality safeguards.
impact_families.rationale: The supported residual consequence concerns categorical handling exclusions. Article 78 independently protects criminal proceedings, so harmful public disclosure is not established by the changed definition.
impact_families.uncertainty: Independence may be interpreted broadly; applicable confidentiality law can preserve equivalent protection.

impact_families.title: Environmental codes refer to training in AI
impact_families.effect: Authorities facilitating environmental codes could treat human instruction as the expressly identified training subject instead of the training of AI models.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects an illustrative subject for voluntary codes. It neither mandates human training nor excludes efficient model training from the broader environmental objective.
impact_families.uncertainty: The environmental context may support understanding the phrase as model training.

impact_families.title: Spanish frames model-access timing as a period of access
impact_families.effect: A request stating only a deadline for furnishing access could require an additional access interval under the Spanish reading.
impact_families.rationale: The established consequence concerns required request particulars. Both versions retain the access power and compliance duty; neither establishes a distinct major access burden or sanction through this phrase alone.
impact_families.uncertainty: Both formulations may describe the same access window; implementing arrangements could clarify the required particulars.

impact_families.title: Evaluation of voluntary requirements may include high-risk systems
impact_families.effect: The Commission must include voluntary environmental requirements concerning high-risk systems within its recurring evaluation of codes of conduct.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes the scope of an evaluation duty. Article 95 already permits these voluntary requirements for all systems; classification and binding operator duties remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: The first limb’s restriction might be understood to carry into the second limb.

impact_families.title: Emergency health assessment may extend beyond triage
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, a new emergency health-assessment system without a triage function could acquire mandatory risk-management and human-oversight duties, where no other classification or Article 6(3) exemption applies.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 6, 8, 9, 14, 16 and 26 connect classification to core safety and oversight duties. Article 113 defers the relevant Annex III duties until 2 December 2027, subject to Article 111.
impact_families.uncertainty: Clinical interpretation may confine assessment to triage; medical-device classification could independently impose high-risk duties.

impact_families.title: Public-body fine rules turn on where fines are imposed
impact_families.effect: Where a Member State limits public-body fines, a foreign public body otherwise within Article 99 could claim that limitation despite not being established there.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes eligibility for special treatment of potentially substantial administrative liability expressly regulated by Article 99.
impact_families.uncertainty: Actual treatment depends on national rules; institutional context may confine the Finnish provision to domestic bodies.

impact_families.title: The sectoral-procedure exception assesses a different objective
impact_families.effect: An equivalent-protection procedure could qualify for substitution under one version but not the other because its objective differs from the objective attributed to its parent legislation.
impact_families.rationale: The established consequence concerns selection of enforcement procedures. The retained equivalent-protection condition does not support an additional major loss of substantive protection.
impact_families.uncertainty: Functional interpretation may align the tests; no particular sectoral procedure is established by the supplied evidence.

impact_families.title: Dutch wording may permit compulsory model access before other methods are exhausted
impact_families.effect: During an applicable conformity assessment, if all other reasonable verification methods are shown insufficient but remain unexhausted, the Dutch reading could require model and parameter access on a reasoned request where necessary.
impact_families.rationale: Removing an independent exhaustion safeguard materially expands compulsory access to models and relevant parameters. Confidentiality protections constrain handling of the information but do not restore the provider's ability to withhold access pending exhaustion.
impact_families.uncertainty: Necessity and practical exhaustion may reconcile the readings; confidentiality protections remain, and no actual disclosure or loss is established.

impact_families.title: Standardisation requests may seek results instead of process deliverables
impact_families.effect: The Commission could request reporting results rather than deliverables defining reporting and documentation processes for improving resource performance.
impact_families.rationale: The difference affects ancillary content of a standardisation request. The duties to request standards covering substantive requirements and obligations remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The standardisation context may make results refer to standardisation deliverables.

impact_families.title: A goal replaces the express objectivity requirement for the methodology
impact_families.effect: The AI Office could deliver a goal and participative method without demonstrating compliance with an express requirement that the methodology be objective.
impact_families.rationale: This changes the methodological deliverables guiding reviews, while prescribed criteria and independent conditions for classification amendments remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: The prescribed criteria and institutional context may imply objectivity despite the wording.

impact_families.title: Contractors’ working terms may fall outside the high-risk category
impact_families.effect: A system materially determines independent contractors’ remuneration terms, performs no other listed function and escapes high-risk classification under the Finnish employment-terms limb.
impact_families.rationale: The reading could remove core compliance, human-oversight and conformity-assessment duties attached to high-risk classification under Articles 6, 8, 16 and 43.
impact_families.uncertainty: The self-employment heading and broader contractual wording support an inclusive interpretation.

impact_families.title: Different outer deadline for notifying penalty rules
impact_families.effect: National penalty rules entering into force before the relevant application date could have to be notified by that earlier milestone under German.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns the timing of notification to the Commission, without an express effect on penalty validity or enforceability.
impact_families.uncertainty: The German possessive is ambiguous, and the shared duty to notify without delay limits divergence.

impact_families.title: Market-entry reporting starts at entry into force
impact_families.effect: The Commission must include any undertakings entering between entry into force and the applicable starting date when compiling the undertaking and SME counts.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes the population covered by an aggregate reporting obligation. It does not itself change market access, SME eligibility, compliance duties or penalties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Staggered application leaves the precise English reporting boundary open to interpretation.

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
REGULATION (EU) 2024/3015 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 27 November 2024
on prohibiting products made with forced labour on the Union market and amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and in particular Article 114 and Article 207 thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the European Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: After transmission of the draft legislative act to the national parliaments,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 5
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | As recognised in the Preamble to the 2014 Protocol to Convention No 29 on forced labour (ILO Convention No 29) of the International Labour Organization (ILO), forced labour constitutes a serious violation of human dignity and fundamental human rights, contributes to the perpetuation of poverty and stands in the way of the achievement of decent work for all. The ILO declared the elimination of all forms of forced or compulsory labour as a principle of fundamental rights. The ILO classifies ILO Convention No 29, including the supplementing 2014 Protocol to Convention No 29 and the ILO Convention No 105 on the abolition of forced labour (ILO Convention No 105) as fundamental ILO conventions and issues recommendations to prevent, eliminate, and remedy forced labour, such as the Forced Labour (Supplementary Measures) Recommendation No 203. The ILO has developed several indicators used to identify and indicate cases of forced labour, such as threats and actual physical and sexual harm, abuse of vulnerability, abuse of working and living conditions and excessive overtime, deception, restriction of movement or confinement to the workplace or a limited area, isolation, debt bondages, withholding wages or excessive wage reduction, retention of passports and identity documents or threat of denunciation to the authorities when the worker has an irregular immigration status. Forced labour is very often linked to poverty and discrimination. The manipulation of credit and debt, either by employers or by recruiting agents, is still a key factor that traps vulnerable workers in forced labour situations. According to the ILO supervisory bodies, prison labour, including where it is performed for private companies, does not in itself constitute forced labour, provided that it is done on a voluntary basis, for the benefit of the prisoner and is comparable to the conditions of a free labour relationship. Community work as an alternative penal sanction to imprisonment should always be in the public interest and should, under no circumstances, be abused by states as a means to degrade the convicted person or deprive that person of their dignity. In cases in which work or service is imposed by exploiting the worker’s vulnerability under the threat of a penalty, that threat does not need to take the form of a penal sanction but might take the form of a loss of rights or benefits.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | The use of forced labour is widespread in the world. It is estimated that about 27,6 million people were in situations of forced labour in 2021. Vulnerable and marginalised groups in society are particularly susceptible to being pressured into performing forced labour. Such groups include women, children, ethnic minorities, persons with disabilities, lower casters, indigenous and tribal people, and migrants, especially undocumented migrants, who have a precarious status and operate in the informal economy. Even when it is not state imposed, forced labour is often a consequence of the absence or lack of good governance with regard to certain economic operators and a demonstration of a state’s failure to enforce social and labour rights, particularly for vulnerable and marginalised groups. Forced labour can also take place as a result of authorities’ tacit consent. 86 % of all forced labour cases occur in the private sector, in particular through the forced labour exploitation of 17,3 million people. The obligations of economic operators set out in this Regulation should be predictable and clear in order to ensure full and effective compliance and contribute to bringing forced labour to an end.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | The eradication of forced labour in all its forms, including state imposed forced labour, is a priority for the Union. Respect for human dignity and the universality and indivisibility of human rights are firmly enshrined in Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). In order to achieve Target 8.7 of the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals, the Union should uphold and promote its values and contribute to the protection of human rights, in particular the rights of the child. Article 5 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the ‘Charter’) explicitly prohibits slavery, servitude, forced or compulsory labour and trafficking in human beings, and Article 4 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms provides that no one is to be required to perform forced or compulsory labour. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly interpreted Article 4 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms as requiring Member States to penalise and effectively prosecute any act maintaining a person in the situations set out in that Article. The right to effective remedies for violations of fundamental rights is a human right, and a fundamental element in the process of effective prosecution of crimes. Existing Union law, the United Nations Guiding Principles on the Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), the Council of Europe recommendation on human rights and business and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) guidelines, such as the Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct, affirm that victims have the right to an effective remedy for business-related human rights violations or abuses, including forced labour.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | All Member States have ratified the fundamental ILO conventions in the area of forced labour, namely ILO Convention No 29 and ILO Convention No 105, and ILO Convention No 182 on the Worst Forms of Child Labour (ILO Convention No 182). They are therefore legally obliged to prevent and eliminate the use of forced labour and to report regularly to the ILO.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | Through its policies and legislative initiatives, the Union seeks to eradicate the use of forced labour and promote decent work and labour rights worldwide. The Union promotes due diligence in line with international guidelines and principles established by international organisations, including the ILO, the OECD and the United Nations, to ensure that forced labour does not have a place in the supply chains of undertakings established in the Union.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | Union trade policy supports the fight against forced labour in both unilateral and bilateral trade relationships. The trade and sustainable development chapters of Union trade agreements contain a commitment to ratify and effectively implement the fundamental ILO conventions, which include ILO Convention No 29 and ILO Convention No 105, whereas trade and gender provisions establish a gender lens that is essential for the economic empowerment of women in order to combat gendered forced labour. Moreover, unilateral tariff preferences under the Union’s Generalised Scheme of Preferences may be withdrawn for serious and systematic violations of ILO Convention No 29 and ILO Convention No 105.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | Forced labour has a distinct impact on vulnerable and marginalised groups, such as children, women, migrants, refugees or indigenous peoples, and therefore an intersectional and gender-sensitive approach is essential to combat forced labour effectively. This Regulation is therefore expected to contribute to the objectives of relevant international agreements and conventions, such as ILO Convention No 182, the Council of Europe Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence Against Women and Domestic Violence, the Beijing Declaration of September 1995, the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, the Geneva Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and ILO Convention No 169 on indigenous and tribal peoples.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | Directive 2011/36/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 3 ) harmonises the definition of trafficking in human beings, including forced labour or services, and establishes rules on minimum penalties. Any rules laid down concerning the prohibition of placing and making available on the Union market domestic or imported products made with forced labour, or exporting such products, and the obligation to ensure that such products are withdrawn from the Union market (prohibition of products made with forced labour), should be without prejudice to that Directive, and in particular to the competence of law enforcement and judicial authorities to investigate and prosecute offences related to trafficking in human beings, including labour exploitation.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | Regulation (EU) 2017/821 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 4 ) requires Union importers of minerals or metals falling under the scope of that Regulation to carry out due diligence obligations consistent with Annex II to the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals from Conflict-Affected and High-Risk Areas, and the due diligence recommendations set out therein. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 5 ) contains obligations for economic operators to carry out due diligence in their supply chains, including with respect to labour rights. Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 6 ) requires due diligence regarding certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation, including with respect to human rights.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | Directive 2013/34/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 7 ) requires Member States to ensure that certain economic operators annually publish non-financial statements in which they report on the impact of their activity on environmental, social and employee matters and on respect for human rights, including on forced labour, anti-corruption and bribery matters. Furthermore, Directive (EU) 2022/2464 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 8 ) on corporate sustainability reporting amended that requirement by introducing detailed reporting requirements for companies falling within the scope of that Directive regarding respect for human rights, including in global supply chains. The information that undertakings disclose about human rights should include, where relevant, information about forced labour in their value chains.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | As a member of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), the Union is committed to promoting a rules-based, open, multilateral trading system. Any measures introduced by the Union that affect trade should be WTO compliant.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | In July 2021, the Commission and the European External Action Service published guidance on due diligence for EU businesses to address the risk of forced labour in their operations and supply chains.

passages.label: Recital 13
