impact_families.title: Dutch leaves the duty to conduct necessary field inspections implicit
impact_families.effect: An authority considers a field inspection necessary and the applicable conditions are satisfied. Under the restrictive Dutch reading, considering the risk’s location could suffice without carrying out that inspection.
impact_families.rationale: The direct change concerns one investigative method. Duties to investigate and assess evidence remain; the text establishes no resulting change to the substantive prohibition, evidential threshold, remedy or sanction.
impact_families.uncertainty: Performance may be implicit in Dutch; inspections outside the Union additionally require operator consent and government non-objection.

impact_families.title: Compliance deadlines may depend on product fungibility instead of component replaceability
impact_families.effect: If the Romanian reading prevailed, an authority could use whole-product fungibility when setting a component-disposal deadline, producing a different compliance period within the retained statutory safeguards.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is a bounded deadline-setting consideration. Minimum periods, reasonableness and proportionality remain mandatory, and Article 20(4) preserves component replacement; no major additional consequence is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 20(4) supports harmonization; the English pronoun and the treatment of components as products introduce interpretive uncertainty.

impact_families.title: Swedish assigns database accessibility and publication to external experts
impact_families.effect: If the Swedish assignment prevailed, external experts engaged to help establish the database could also have to perform its accessibility and publication work, even where the Commission intended to do that work internally.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns allocation of implementation tasks. Public accessibility, language coverage, the deadline and the Commission's responsibility remain unchanged.
impact_families.uncertainty: Optional assistance under Article 8(1) supports reading the reference to experts conditionally.

impact_families.title: Preliminary information requests may omit remedial actions
impact_families.effect: A preliminary information request could omit actions providing compensation or restitution to victims while still covering identification, prevention, mitigation and cessation of forced-labour risks.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the required contents of an information request. Broader investigative powers and voluntary submissions remain, and no independent compensation entitlement is removed.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 45 and the references to Commission guidance support including remediation through contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Third-country origin may narrow the customs-control category
impact_families.effect: A Union-origin product returning from a third country for release for free circulation could escape this Regulation's suspension and refusal mechanism despite matching a prohibition decision.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower definition could remove prohibited products from a core border-enforcement mechanism under Articles 26–30. Other customs powers and the market prohibition remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: Origin may mean geographical provenance here; English could also receive an origin-based interpretation.

impact_families.title: Presence in the Union may broaden the end-user exclusion
impact_families.effect: If presence sufficed, a prohibited product supplied to a temporary visitor for personal consumption could become excluded from withdrawal under this Regulation.
impact_families.rationale: The definition determines the boundary of an express exclusion from a core enforcement measure. The general prohibition does not remove that exclusion.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 22 and the market context could support reading presence as residence.

impact_families.title: Alternative recipients for withdrawal and disposal orders
impact_families.effect: An order could be communicated only to another relevant authority, leaving market surveillance authorities without the specific notification required by the English wording.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns an ancillary communication duty. Articles 20 and 23 retain the prohibition and enforcement obligations, while Article 24(2) retains responsibility and coordination. A major changed outcome is not established.
impact_families.uncertainty: Cooperation duties and contextual interpretation may require wider notification despite the alternative wording.

impact_families.title: Forced-labour recital presents defining conditions as alternatives
impact_families.effect: If the alternative test governed, a product involving involuntary work without threatened punishment could become subject to the prohibition and applicable withdrawal and disposal orders.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed definition could change which products trigger Article 3’s core prohibition and Article 20’s mandatory measures, subject to the retained exclusions and disposal derogation.
impact_families.uncertainty: Direct incorporation of the ILO definition strongly favours harmonization; the recital cannot independently replace the operative definition.

impact_families.title: Businesses commissioning free own-brand products may fall outside the manufacturer definition
impact_families.effect: A business commissioning own-brand products supplied only free of charge could be omitted from information specifically identifying the manufacturer.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated effect concerns identification under Articles 18, 22 and 27. Free commercial supplies remain covered by the economic-operator definition and prohibition; other identification categories may also apply.
impact_families.uncertainty: Context may support a broader reading of selling; overlapping supplier or importer classifications may preserve identification.

impact_families.title: Spanish may extend the scope of customs screening
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, Union-destined third-country goods without intended release for free circulation could undergo Article 26 risk-based screening.
impact_families.rationale: The additional consequence is screening. Articles 27–30 retain express procedural conditions for information duties, suspension, refusal and disposal; the definition alone does not broaden those consequences.
impact_families.uncertainty: The surrounding customs provisions strongly support treating intended release for free circulation as a cumulative condition.

impact_families.title: End-user coverage may exclude Union-established individuals residing abroad
impact_families.effect: A product delivered for final professional use on the Union market to a Union-established sole trader residing abroad could remain subject to withdrawal under the narrower Czech definition.
impact_families.rationale: Losing end-user status would remove an express exclusion from compulsory withdrawal, materially changing the protection afforded to products already delivered for final use.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 22 and the shared regulatory context support including Union-established natural persons.

impact_families.title: Maltese investigation priorities refer to quality instead of quantity
impact_families.effect: If the Maltese wording prevailed, authorities could prioritize suspected products using quality alongside volume, changing which products receive investigative attention first.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns prioritization criteria. The substantiated-concern requirement, evidentiary assessment and product prohibition remain; the wording does not independently authorize a ban or penalty based on quality.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 42 strongly supports quantity; neither version specifies how product quality would affect priority.

impact_families.title: Finnish database provision omits institutional organisations as a separate source
impact_families.effect: If the Finnish source list were exhaustive, information from a domestic institutional body that conducts neither research nor academic work could be excluded as a qualifying database source.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns an indicative information resource. Article 14(3) separately requires consideration of all relevant, factual and verifiable information; database inclusion does not itself establish a violation or prohibit products.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 31 and a flexible interpretation of source eligibility could harmonize application.

impact_families.title: Croatian wording may narrow assessment of a forced-labour remediation mechanism
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading prevailed, the Commission could assess a mechanism for ending forced labour without assessing a dedicated mechanism for restoring or compensating victims.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns the scope of a report and impact assessment. Article 38(4) neither establishes a compensation entitlement nor requires implementation of the mechanism assessed.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 36, Article 11(b), and Article 38(3) support a harmonizing interpretation that includes victim remediation.

impact_families.title: Consistency of guidance may become recommendatory
impact_families.effect: The Commission could issue inconsistent guidance without breaching the express consistency instruction, while remaining bound by the Regulation and other applicable legislation.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence concerns coordination of administrative guidance. The supplied text establishes no resulting change to a particular prohibition, entitlement or sanction.
impact_families.uncertainty: The operative setting and recital 36 could support a binding interpretation.

impact_families.title: Cross-border recognition may depend on lead-authority status
impact_families.effect: A receiving authority without lead status could decline recognition of a foreign decision covering identically identified products from the same forced-labour supply chain.
impact_families.rationale: Restricting recognition could prevent the foreign prohibition and associated withdrawal or disposal orders from receiving cross-border effect, materially weakening a core enforcement mechanism.
impact_families.uncertainty: Articles 23–24 and recital 53 strongly support enforcement regardless of receiving lead status.

impact_families.title: Disengagement considerations may exclude workers employed by separate suppliers
impact_families.effect: When deciding how to support an operator’s disengagement, an authority could omit consequences for affected workers employed by a separate supplier.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns an interpretive consideration for support. The supplied provisions do not connect it to loss of a worker remedy, compensation entitlement, or mandatory product-enforcement measure.
impact_families.uncertainty: The protective purpose and supply-chain support provisions favour considering all affected workers.

impact_families.title: Accompanying business support may become discretionary
impact_families.effect: The Commission could omit accompanying support measures, leaving businesses with the separately required guidance and contact points.
impact_families.rationale: The changed duty concerns supplementary administrative support. The provision specifies no funding entitlement, compensation or exemption from compliance, and mandatory guidance and contact points remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The operative setting and recital 33 could support interpreting the support instruction as mandatory.

impact_families.title: Dutch may restrict reliance on other facts after non-cooperation
impact_families.effect: An operator entirely refuses a preliminary information request. If Dutch requires foregoing a request, the authority could lose the Article 17(4) route for establishing concern and initiating the mandatory investigation.
impact_families.rationale: Article 18(1) links investigation to an Article 17(3) or (4) determination. Removing the express alternative after complete non-response could materially obstruct a core enforcement gateway despite available evidence.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recitals 43 and 47 and the surrounding evidence provisions strongly favour treating non-cooperation as an independent ground.

impact_families.title: Highest leverage becomes an investigative objective rather than an express selection criterion
impact_families.effect: An authority could prioritize nearby suppliers during preliminary inquiries without separately assessing which actors possess the greatest leverage to address forced labour.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns investigative prioritization. It does not itself alter the prohibition, substantiated-concern threshold, information duties or available enforcement decisions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Czech recital 42 expressly supports selection of actors with the greatest influence.

impact_families.title: Recital 7 substitutes a cross-sectoral approach for an intersectional approach
impact_families.effect: Implementation guidance could treat coordination across sectors as satisfying recital 7 without specifically addressing overlapping vulnerabilities among children, women, migrants, refugees and indigenous peoples.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns an ancillary interpretive approach to implementation. The text does not establish a changed entitlement, prohibition, investigation threshold or remedy.
impact_families.uncertainty: The listed vulnerable groups and international instruments support an intersectional contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Spanish leaves the customs interconnection deadline without a time unit
impact_families.effect: If the incomplete deadline prevailed, completion of the customs interconnection could escape a determinate four-year limit.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the timing of administrative infrastructure. Article 7(4) continues to require exchanges through the existing information system, and substantive customs controls remain applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 7(3) and multilingual interpretation support restoring years as the omitted unit.

impact_families.title: Romanian confidentiality exception may remove protection when providers remain silent
impact_families.effect: If the Romanian exception prevailed, a provider supplying information without confidentiality instructions could lose Article 32(2)’s default protection for their identity or information.
impact_families.rationale: Removing default confidentiality materially changes an important protection. The supplied context does not establish that whistleblower, professional-secrecy or data-protection rules cover every provider and every item of information.
impact_families.uncertainty: Protective context strongly supports harmonization; independent confidentiality obligations may still prevent disclosure.

impact_families.title: Completed-export wording may delay an export prohibition decision
impact_families.effect: If completed export were required, a forced-labour product supplied solely for export and not covered by an existing decision could pass through the export procedure before an Article 20 decision enabled customs intervention.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 26–30 link customs identification, suspension and refusal to communicated decisions. Delaying that decision could materially impair enforcement of the core export prohibition, although Article 3 and other customs powers remain.
impact_families.uncertainty: The shared customs-procedure definition and preventive context may support intervention at the same stage in both versions.

impact_families.title: Close-cooperation duty identifies different authorities
impact_families.effect: A Member State could arrange information exchange with labour inspectors without establishing the close coordination with them expressly required by the English wording.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns an ancillary cooperation duty. Information exchange, investigation powers, product prohibitions and enforcement obligations remain applicable; no concrete major consequence follows from the supplied text.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 24 expressly supports close cooperation with national labour, judicial and enforcement authorities.

impact_families.title: Maltese support measures refer to the value chain
impact_families.effect: If value chain received a broader reading, the Commission's accompanying measures would need to address relevant business partners outside the defined upstream supply chain.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the scope of accompanying assistance. Article 10 establishes no specified payment or individual financial entitlement, and the difference does not change prohibition, investigation or sanction rules.
impact_families.uncertainty: Value chain is undefined; recital 33 and the Regulation’s purpose support alignment with the defined supply chain.

impact_families.title: Direct penalty powers may require another authority’s cooperation
impact_families.effect: Where national rules permit an authority to act alone, the Latvian reading could prevent valid imposition of a penalty without another authority’s cooperation or a judicial application.
impact_families.rationale: The difference can affect legal competence to impose a sanction for non-compliance with a binding prohibition. Alternative enforcement routes remain, but would not validate an independently imposed penalty.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation may preserve all three routes; national arrangements may already require cooperation.

impact_families.title: Croatian wording changes whose disengagement risk the authority considers
impact_families.effect: If the redirected reading prevailed, an authority could prioritize supporting operators facing termination by business partners rather than addressing those operators' own withdrawal from suppliers.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence is a change in recital guidance informing risk consideration and support. The operative prohibition, investigation requirements, disposal duties, sanctions and review rights remain the same.
impact_families.uncertainty: Business relationships are reciprocal; the remaining recital text supports considering operator-initiated disengagement in both versions.

impact_families.title: Information-source restriction replaces a purpose limitation
impact_families.effect: If decisive independently obtained evidence were excluded under the source restriction, an otherwise provable violation could escape an Article 20 prohibition, withdrawal and disposal decision.
impact_families.rationale: Article 20 links failure to establish a violation to closure of the investigation, and establishment of a violation to mandatory enforcement orders. Excluding decisive evidence could materially change that core enforcement outcome.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 14(3), broad evidence-gathering provisions and the Union-law exception strongly support harmonization; exclusion is not an established outcome.

impact_families.title: Bulgarian recital directs recycling guidance at perishable products
impact_families.effect: If the Bulgarian recycling guidance prevailed where donation was impossible, an authority could prioritize recycling as the means of rendering perishable products inoperable, rather than select another available disposal method.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the choice and priority of disposal methods for already prohibited goods. Article 25 preserves donation where possible; the discrepancy does not independently change the prohibition or establish additional financial liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 25, recital 48 and recital 53’s preceding sentence strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Product replaceability may replace component replaceability in setting deadlines
impact_families.effect: An authority setting a component-replacement deadline could consider whether the whole product is replaceable instead of whether the offending component can be replaced.
impact_families.rationale: One deadline consideration changes, but the authority must still allow reasonable, proportionate time needed for compliance and respect the specified minimum periods.
impact_families.uncertainty: English has antecedent ambiguity; Article 20(4) supports a shared component-focused interpretation.

impact_families.title: Business competitiveness may be omitted from the required evaluation
impact_families.effect: If the Romanian reading prevailed, the Commission could complete its periodic evaluation without specifically assessing the effects of investigation and decision procedures on businesses’ competitiveness.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns evaluation content. General business-impact, compliance-cost and cost-benefit assessments remain mandatory; the disputed wording does not itself change market access, remedies or sanctions.
impact_families.uncertainty: The broad business-impact requirement and recital 67 support including business competitiveness through contextual interpretation.

impact_families.title: Swedish permits alternative recipients for withdrawal and disposal orders
impact_families.effect: If the Swedish alternative prevailed, an authority could communicate an order to other relevant product authorities without separately communicating it to the designated market surveillance authorities under Article 24(1).
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns notification recipients. Withdrawal, disposal, competent-authority responsibility and coordination remain mandatory; the supplied text establishes no further major consequence.
impact_families.uncertainty: Other notification and coordination duties may deliver the same information.

impact_families.title: Disposal enforcement may exclude stock that has not been withdrawn
impact_families.effect: An operator ignores a disposal order covering remaining stock never placed on the market; the narrower reading could exclude that stock from authorities’ express duty to ensure disposal.
impact_families.rationale: This materially narrows a core enforcement duty after operator non-compliance. The continuing prohibition, operator’s disposal obligation and penalties do not themselves secure disposal of the excluded stock.
impact_families.uncertainty: The general enforcement duty, Article 20 and recital 53 strongly support broader coverage.

impact_families.title: Finnish wording may make nine-month investigation closure mandatory
impact_families.effect: If the mandatory-closure reading prevailed, an unresolved investigation could have to end after nine months, preventing continued investigation leading to a product prohibition.
impact_families.rationale: Ending the investigation could materially restrict enforcement of the core prohibition. Article 20(3) permits a new investigation when new relevant information emerges, rather than guaranteeing continuation on the existing information.
impact_families.uncertainty: The disjunction and reasonable-period requirement support an alternative reading that preserves flexibility.

impact_families.title: Information-use restriction shifts from purposes to sources
impact_families.effect: An authority could reuse compelled, non-personal business information in an unrelated regulatory proceeding without a legal requirement for that reuse, provided other applicable restrictions were satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: This reading removes the express purpose limitation protecting information obtained through investigatory duties. Confidentiality obligations do not necessarily prevent internal reuse for another purpose.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation and other applicable law may preserve equivalent purpose restrictions.

impact_families.title: Express access to the information system may be weakened
impact_families.effect: An authority could be denied direct system access while receiving information through arrangements that still satisfy mandatory exchange duties.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the independent administrative access guarantee. Continuing use, exchange and cooperation duties do not support a broader exemption from enforcement.
impact_families.uncertainty: Mandatory system use and exchanges may imply the same access entitlement despite the wording.

impact_families.title: Withdrawal wording may obscure the duty to lift an existing prohibition
impact_families.effect: After proven compliance and elimination of forced labour, an authority could treat withdrawal as concerning only a planned decision, leaving the existing market and export prohibition operative.
impact_families.rationale: That reading would impair the statutory remedy for lifting a prohibition once its specified conditions are satisfied, materially affecting permission to market or export the products.
impact_families.uncertainty: The existing-decision references, portal removal and recital 52 strongly support prospective withdrawal of the operative prohibition.

impact_families.title: Maltese penalty guidance expressly covers minimum thresholds
impact_families.effect: If the Maltese qualification prevailed, guidance could satisfy Article 11(i) while omitting applicable upper thresholds and addressing calculation methods and minimum thresholds.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated consequence concerns mandatory guidance content. Article 37 retains national penalty-setting and proportionality requirements; the difference establishes no particular increase in liability or sanction.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 66 supports broader guidance; the sources establish no resulting change in national penalty amounts.

impact_families.title: German remediation wording could require a stricter restoration benchmark
impact_families.effect: If the stricter reading prevailed, remediation guidance could classify the closest achievable restoration as insufficient where restoring the situation without forced labour is impossible.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns the guidance benchmark. The Regulation creates no independent restoration entitlement, and withdrawal of prohibitions depends on compliance and eliminating forced labour rather than complete restoration.
impact_families.uncertainty: Proportionality, compensation and consistency with other guidelines could support acceptance of practical restoration.

impact_families.title: Greek may narrow required penalty guidance to minimum thresholds
impact_families.effect: If applicable penalty thresholds include upper limits, the Greek reading could allow the Commission to omit guidance on those limits while satisfying Article 11.
impact_families.rationale: The consequence concerns required guidance coverage. Although Member States must take utmost account of that guidance, Article 37 independently governs penalties; the wording establishes no particular change in substantial financial liability.
impact_families.uncertainty: English thresholds could be read as lower thresholds; no specific penalty limits are supplied.

impact_families.title: Distance-sales targeting test expressly refers to consumers
impact_families.effect: If the express test were confined to consumer offers, an authority assessing a professional-only offer could need separately to establish that it targets Union end users.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns establishing targeting. Article 4’s first sentence retains professional users within distance-sales coverage; the wording does not establish a professional-sales exemption.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 22 and the deeming provision’s general formulation strongly support applying the same test to all offers.

impact_families.title: Selling condition may narrow manufacturer status
impact_families.effect: An own-brand business distributing products free of charge could be omitted from manufacturer-specific information, while remaining covered by applicable operator and supplier-information requirements.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns classification and identification in investigations, decisions and customs information. Broader definitions preserve the prohibition and relevant enforcement duties.
impact_families.uncertainty: Selling could be interpreted contextually as commercial distribution, including free supply.

impact_families.title: Finnish recital describes the civic-obligation exception by residence
impact_families.effect: If residence sufficed for the exception, otherwise qualifying compulsory civic work imposed on non-citizen residents could fall outside forced labour, removing the resulting products from the Article 3 prohibition.
impact_families.rationale: The changed personal scope could determine whether the core product prohibition applies. The consequence remains conditional on the broader recital reading controlling interpretation of the incorporated definition.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 2(1) incorporates the same Convention definition, strongly favouring harmonization over an independent recital-based exception.

impact_families.title: Mandatory customs notice cites a different regulation number
impact_families.effect: Customs authorities following the Irish prescribed notice would record Regulation 2024/2015 as the instrument associated with refusal of release or export.
impact_families.rationale: The changed obligation concerns notice content. Article 30 independently requires refusal and governs disposal, so the number difference does not establish an altered entitlement to release or export.
impact_families.uncertainty: The title and surrounding provisions make the intended regulation identifiable.

impact_families.title: Authorities’ express disposal duty may exclude retained products never withdrawn from the market
impact_families.effect: After an ignored disposal order, retained stock never withdrawn from the Union market and outside customs custody could escape the authority’s express duty to secure disposal at the operator’s expense.
impact_families.rationale: The narrower reading removes goods from a core fallback enforcement measure. The continuing prohibition and operator’s disposal obligation do not themselves secure disposal after non-compliance.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 23’s general enforcement duty, Article 20’s disposal order and recital 53 strongly favour comprehensive disposal.

impact_families.title: Customs release is expressed as permission rather than a duty
impact_families.effect: If permission replaced the release duty, customs could continue withholding a product after the applicable deadline or approval, despite fulfilment of all remaining release requirements.
impact_families.rationale: This would materially weaken the entitlement to end customs suspension and obtain release for import or export.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 57 and preserved customs legislation strongly support mandatory release.

impact_families.title: Manufacturer definition may omit businesses commissioning production
impact_families.effect: A business outsourcing both design and manufacture could be omitted from information supplied specifically about the manufacturer under Articles 22 or 27.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated consequence concerns identification duties. Broader information requirements remain, and Articles 2(9) and 3 retain the commissioning seller within the core prohibition as an economic operator.
impact_families.uncertainty: Manufacturing through contractors could be attributed to the commissioning business under a harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Finnish recital describes a court-work exception without expressly requiring conviction
impact_families.effect: If a non-criminal court order qualified, products made through otherwise compulsory work under that order could escape the forced-labour prohibition, provided public oversight and the restrictions on private disposal were satisfied.
impact_families.rationale: Broadening the qualifying judicial basis could change application of the core product prohibition. The remaining safeguards limit the exception but do not themselves require a conviction.
impact_families.uncertainty: The incorporated Convention definition and recital 1's penal context strongly support a conviction-based interpretation.

impact_families.title: Swedish makes the ordinary 30-day compliance minimum advisory
impact_families.effect: If the Swedish reading prevailed, an operator could have fewer than 30 working days to withdraw or dispose of non-perishable products, with enforcement and penalties following non-compliance with that shorter deadline.
impact_families.rationale: Removing the guaranteed minimum materially changes a procedural safeguard governing compulsory withdrawal, disposal and associated enforcement under Articles 20 and 23.
impact_families.uncertainty: Reasonableness and proportionality remain mandatory; contextual interpretation could preserve the minimum.

impact_families.title: Preliminary information requests may extend beyond upstream supply chains
impact_families.effect: An operator could be required to report relevant downstream value-chain actions in its preliminary response, beyond actions concerning the defined upstream supply chain.
impact_families.rationale: The demonstrated change is an information burden. Article 1(3) excludes additional substantive due-diligence obligations, while Articles 2(7), 3 and 20 retain the production-based basis for prohibition.
impact_families.uncertainty: The relevance requirement, recital 45 and Article 17(1)(d) strongly support an upstream-only interpretation.

impact_families.title: German guidance provision could omit repair of victims’ harm
impact_families.effect: If the narrower reading prevailed, the Commission could fulfil Article 11(b) with guidance on stopping forced labour that omits practices for restoring victims’ situations and compensating their harm.
impact_families.rationale: The difference changes required guidance content. Article 1(3) excludes additional operator due diligence duties; Articles 20–21 do not condition lifting prohibitions on compensation or following remediation guidance.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 36 expressly requires remediation guidance and provides a strong harmonizing interpretation.

impact_families.title: Responsible disengagement: escalation measures or steps towards withdrawal
impact_families.effect: If the French reading prevailed, guidance could accept an account of the steps towards ending a supplier relationship as responsible disengagement without requiring that account to describe escalation measures.
impact_families.rationale: The supported change concerns ancillary guidance content. Article 1(3) excludes additional due diligence obligations; the prohibition and the conditions governing investigations, disposal and withdrawal of decisions remain independently applicable.
impact_families.uncertainty: Steps towards disengagement may encompass escalation; the recital does not independently impose an enforceable duty.

impact_families.title: Portuguese omits investigation closure from the nine-month target
impact_families.effect: If the Portuguese reading prevailed, an authority closing an investigation without establishing an infringement would lack the express obligation to endeavour to close it within nine months.
impact_families.rationale: This changes a procedural timing benchmark. The reasonable-period requirement and mandatory closure remain; neither version establishes an absolute nine-month deadline or automatic termination.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual interpretation may extend the nine-month benchmark to closure.

impact_families.title: Negated cessation condition may trigger disposal despite elimination of forced labour
impact_families.effect: An operator proves cessation of the identified forced labour, but the fallback nevertheless requires disposal because elimination without cessation has not been demonstrated.
impact_families.rationale: The disputed condition activates mandatory disposal under Article 20(4)(c), potentially requiring recycling or rendering a withheld non-perishable product inoperable despite evidence supporting withdrawal of the prohibition.
impact_families.uncertainty: The preceding review condition and recital 48 strongly support harmonizing the contradictory fallback.

impact_families.title: Withdrawal orders may be communicated to only one authority group
impact_families.effect: An authority could communicate a withdrawal and disposal order to a relevant sectoral authority without also communicating it to the specified market-surveillance authorities.
impact_families.rationale: The change affects a notification duty. Article 24(2) retains enforcement responsibility and coordination, and Article 20(7) retains communication to all competent authorities; no major changed substantive outcome is established.
impact_families.uncertainty: General information-sharing and coordination duties may require both groups to be informed in a particular case.

impact_families.title: Greek may extend notification to withdrawal orders without disposal
impact_families.effect: For products withheld under Article 20(5), Greek would require notification of the remaining withdrawal order to market-surveillance authorities; a cumulative English reading could omit that notification.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns inter-authority notification. Articles 20 and 23 preserve the substantive measures, and Article 20(7) independently requires communication to all competent authorities, although the recipient groups need not coincide.
impact_families.uncertainty: English may describe withdrawal and disposal collectively, covering either order when applicable.

impact_families.title: Recital identifies different authorities for detained-product conditions
impact_families.effect: Where responsibility for storage conditions requires interpretation, the Irish recital could support assigning their determination to designated competent authorities rather than customs authorities.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns administrative responsibility. Articles 26 and 30 preserve the customs framework and expressly govern refusal and disposal; the recital supplies no separate power to override those rules.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Customs Code reference and operative allocation of functions strongly support a harmonized reading.

impact_families.title: Bulgarian wording may weaken the entitlement to extend delegated-act scrutiny
impact_families.effect: If an initiative did not secure extension, a delegated act identifying products subject to additional customs-information requirements could enter into force after two months, precluding an objection during the requested additional period.
impact_families.rationale: Article 33(6) links entry into force to the objection deadline. Losing the additional period could materially curtail Parliament’s or the Council’s power to prevent a delegated act from taking effect.
impact_families.uncertainty: The permissive wording may instead express either institution’s unilateral option to extend the period.

impact_families.title: Maltese ordinary compliance minimum omits working days
impact_families.effect: If a reasonable 30-calendar-day deadline prevailed, an operator could face compulsory disposal and penalties before the English minimum of 30 working days had expired.
impact_families.rationale: Articles 23 and 25 attach enforcement and disposal to non-compliance. Shortening the protected compliance period can materially accelerate irreversible interference with goods and exposure to sanctions.
impact_families.uncertainty: Contextual harmonization or a longer proportionate deadline could prevent divergence; no actual enforcement outcome is established.

impact_families.title: Spanish may narrow the restoration recognized as remediation
impact_families.effect: If the stricter reading prevailed, guidance could withhold recognition of closest-possible restoration as remediation where full restoration cannot be achieved.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns remediation guidance and its assessment. The Regulation creates no additional due diligence obligation and does not condition withdrawal of a prohibition on exact restoration.
impact_families.uncertainty: Proportionality, compensation and consistency with other guidance strongly support accepting equivalent restoration.

impact_families.title: Notification of amended penalty rules lacks an express promptness requirement
impact_families.effect: A Member State could notify amendments to its penalty rules later than the express requirement to notify without delay would permit.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns administrative notification timing. The obligations to establish and implement effective penalties remain, and the text does not condition their validity on notification.
impact_families.uncertainty: General cooperation obligations may constrain delay, but the supplied provision contains no equivalent express timing requirement.

impact_families.title: Donation of perishable products is expressed as optional
impact_families.effect: An operator or authority could recycle perishable products under the general disposal rule even though charitable donation was possible, treating the Czech donation provision as optional.
impact_families.rationale: The change concerns the method of disposing of products already subject to disposal. It does not remove that duty or permit their commercial return to the market.
impact_families.uncertainty: The conditional fallback, waste hierarchy and recitals 48 and 53 strongly favour donation whenever possible.

impact_families.title: Portuguese importer definition omits associations of persons
impact_families.effect: If the narrower definition prevailed, an importing association without legal personality could fall outside the express requirement to identify the importer in investigation information or a decision.
impact_families.rationale: The supported consequence concerns identification under Articles 18 and 22. Associations remain economic operators subject to the prohibition, investigation duties, enforcement and penalties; no exemption from those core rules follows.
impact_families.uncertainty: General information requirements could independently require identification, and contextual interpretation could include associations.

legislation.title: REGULATION (EU) 2024/3228 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 19 December 2024 repealing Regulation (EU) No 524/2013, and amending Regulations (EU) 2017/2394 and (EU) 2018/1724 with regard to the discontinuation of the European Online Dispute Resolution Platform (Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
REGULATION (EU) 2024/3228 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 19 December 2024
repealing Regulation (EU) No 524/2013, and amending Regulations (EU) 2017/2394 and (EU) 2018/1724 with regard to the discontinuation of the European Online Dispute Resolution Platform
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and in particular Article 114 thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the European Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: After transmission of the draft legislative act to the national parliaments,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 5
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 3 ) established, and mandated the Commission to develop and maintain, the European Online Dispute Resolution Platform (the ‘ODR platform’) at Union level, offering a single point of entry to consumers and traders seeking the out-of-court resolution of disputes arising from online sales or service contracts.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | The ODR platform takes the form of an interactive website where consumers are able to request traders to agree to use an alternative dispute resolution (ADR) entity that is listed on the ODR platform and that complies with Directive 2013/11/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 4 ) .

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 requires online traders and online marketplaces to provide, on their website, an easily accessible link to the ODR platform. That obligation, together with information campaigns organised by the Commission and national stakeholders, has brought between two and three million visitors to the ODR platform every year.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | However, only a minority of visitors use the ODR platform to submit a complaint and only 2 % of those complaints receive a positive reply from traders, meaning that their request can be transmitted to an ADR entity listed on the ODR platform. All in all, this represents about 200 cases per year across the Union.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | The Commission published a call for evidence on adapting out-of-court dispute resolution to digital markets, which ran from 28 September to 21 December 2022. The Commission concluded that the ODR platform had been used by only 5 % of consumers who responded to that call for evidence, and the majority of respondents considered that the ODR platform should be substantially improved or be discontinued as it was not cost-effective. The evidence strongly suggests that, given that no more than 200 cases are transferred per year to an ADR entity, further maintenance of the ODR platform does not correspond to the principles of efficiency and effectiveness as provided for in Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 5 ) .

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | The ODR platform should be discontinued and Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 should therefore be repealed. Appropriate time should be provided to ensure that ongoing cases can be adequately terminated.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | Pursuant to Regulation (EU) No 524/2013, personal data related to a dispute is kept in the database established further to that Regulation for the time necessary to achieve the purposes for which the data were collected and to ensure that data subjects are able to access their personal data in order to exercise their rights. In accordance with Regulation (EU) No 524/2013, that data is to be automatically deleted at the latest six months after the date of conclusion of the dispute which has been transmitted to the ODR platform. The Commission should inform users of the ODR platform with ongoing cases of the discontinuation of the ODR platform in good time, and in any case at least four months before that platform is discontinued. The Commission should offer assistance to those users of the ODR platform who wish to retrieve data related to their cases.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | As the ODR platform is referred to in other Union legal acts as a platform that enables consumers to request traders to agree to an out-of-court dispute resolution, those acts should be amended to remove references to the ODR platform. Regulations (EU) 2017/2394 ( 6 ) and (EU) 2018/1724 ( 7 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council should therefore be amended accordingly. Directives (EU) 2015/2302 ( 8 ) , (EU) 2019/2161 ( 9 ) and (EU) 2020/1828 ( 10 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council also contain references to Regulation (EU) No 524/2013. It is intended that those Directives be amended by a separate legal act,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAVE ADOPTED THIS REGULATION:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 is repealed with effect from 20 July 2025.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
1. The European Online Dispute Resolution Platform (the ‘ODR platform’) shall be discontinued.
2. The submission of complaints to the ODR platform shall be discontinued on 20 March 2025.
3. The Commission shall inform users of the ODR platform with ongoing cases of the discontinuation of the ODR platform by 20 March 2025 and offer such users assistance to retrieve data related to their cases and accessible to them, where they wish to do so.
4. At the latest by 20 July 2025, all information, including personal data, related to cases in the ODR platform shall be deleted.

passages.label: Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
Amendment to Regulation (EU) 2017/2394
In the Annex to Regulation (EU) 2017/2394, point 22 is deleted.

passages.label: Article 4
passages.text:
Article 4
Amendment to Regulation (EU) 2018/1724
In Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2018/1724, point 7 is replaced by the following:
‘(7) | The list of alternative consumer dispute resolution entities established by the Commission pursuant to Article 20(4) of Directive 2013/11/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council ( *1 ) .

passages.label: Article 5
passages.text:
Article 5
Entry into force
This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.
Done at Brussels, 19 December 2024.
For the European Parliament
The President
R. METSOLA
For the Council
The President
BÓKA J.
( 1 ) OJ C, C/2024/2482, 23.4.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2024/2482/oj .
( 2 ) Position of the European Parliament of 13 March 2024 (not yet published in the Official Journal) and position of the Council at first reading of 19 November 2024 (not yet published in the Official Journal). Position of the European Parliament of 17 December 2024 (not yet published in the Official Journal).
( 3 ) Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 May 2013 on online dispute resolution for consumer disputes and amending Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 and Directive 2009/22/EC (Regulation on consumer ODR) ( OJ L 165, 18.6.2013, p. 1 ).
( 4 ) Directive 2013/11/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 May 2013 on alternative dispute resolution for consumer disputes and amending Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 and Directive 2009/22/EC (Directive on consumer ADR) ( OJ L 165, 18.6.2013, p. 63 ).
( 5 ) Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 September 2024 on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union ( OJ L, 2024/2509, 26.9.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj ).
( 6 ) Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2017 on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws and repealing Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 ( OJ L 345, 27.12.2017, p. 1 ).
( 7 ) Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 2 October 2018 establishing a single digital gateway to provide access to information, to procedures and to assistance and problem-solving services and amending Regulation (EU) No 1024/2012 ( OJ L 295, 21.11.2018, p. 1 ).
( 8 ) Directive (EU) 2015/2302 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2015 on package travel and linked travel arrangements, amending Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 and Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 90/314/EEC ( OJ L 326, 11.12.2015, p. 1 ).
( 9 ) Directive (EU) 2019/2161 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2019 amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directives 98/6/EC, 2005/29/EC and 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the better enforcement and modernisation of Union consumer protection rules ( OJ L 328, 18.12.2019, p. 7 ).
( 10 ) Directive (EU) 2020/1828 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2020 on representative actions for the protection of the collective interests of consumers and repealing Directive 2009/22/EC ( OJ L 409, 4.12.2020, p. 1 ).

findings.english_quote: At the latest by 20 July 2025, all information, including personal data, related to cases in the ODR platform shall be deleted.
findings.title: Potentially broader deletion duty in Bulgarian
findings.explanation: English expressly limits deletion to information related to platform cases. Bulgarian can require deletion of all platform information, including case-related personal data. This could extend the duty to information unrelated to cases, although the surrounding case-focused provisions support a narrower interpretation.

variants.quote: Най-късно до 20 юли 2025 г. цялата информация, включително личните данни, свързани със случаите в платформата за ОРС, се заличава.
variants.translation: No later than 20 July 2025, all information, including personal data related to cases in the ODR platform, shall be deleted.
variants.explanation: English expressly limits deletion to information related to platform cases. Bulgarian can require deletion of all platform information, including case-related personal data. This could extend the duty to information unrelated to cases, although the surrounding case-focused provisions support a narrower interpretation.

review.method: One blind Sol API scan; separate Sol API review; independent Astra source audit

findings.english_quote: 4. At the latest by 20 July 2025, all information, including personal data, related to cases in the ODR platform shall be deleted.
findings.title: Estonian deletion duty extends to all platform information
findings.explanation: English limits mandatory deletion to information related to cases. Estonian could additionally require deletion of information unrelated to cases that remains in the platform. Both versions preserve the same deadline and require deletion of case information.

variants.quote: 4. Kogu internetipõhises vaidluste lahendamise platvormis sisalduv teave, kaasa arvatud juhtumitega seotud isikuandmed, kustutatakse hiljemalt 20. juuliks 2025.

review.method: One blind Sol API scan; separate Sol API review; independent Astra source audit

findings.english_quote: The Commission shall inform users of the ODR platform with ongoing cases of the discontinuation of the ODR platform by 20 March 2025
findings.title: Italian March deadline may govern platform closure
findings.explanation: English requires notification by 20 March 2025. Italian can instead require notification that the platform will close by that date. That reading could advance closure and remove the express March notification deadline, contrary to the transition contemplated by recital 7.

impact_families.title: Estonian deletion duty extends to all platform information
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, any non-case information remaining in the platform would also require deletion by 20 July 2025.
impact_families.rationale: The identified additional consequence is broader cleanup of a platform already being discontinued. The sources establish no additional major effect on dispute remedies or data-access entitlements.
impact_families.uncertainty: The sources do not identify particular non-case records; the closure context may support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Italian March deadline may govern platform closure
impact_families.effect: If the closure-date reading prevailed, the platform would have to close by 20 March rather than users merely being notified by that date.
impact_families.rationale: This would materially change the central discontinuation timetable and the transition available for ongoing cases and retrieval of their data.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 7’s four-month notice period and the July repeal strongly support harmonization.

impact_families.title: Portuguese expressly includes assistance with accessing case data
impact_families.effect: A user requesting help obtaining access to case data could invoke an express access-assistance duty under Portuguese.
impact_families.rationale: The supported additional consequence is procedural assistance during closure. The provision does not expressly create new substantive data-access rights or change deletion deadlines.
impact_families.uncertainty: Practical access help may already fall within retrieval assistance; recital 7 supports a common purpose.

impact_families.title: Deletion may extend to platform information unrelated to cases
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, non-case information held on the discontinued platform would also have to be deleted.
impact_families.rationale: The additional consequence concerns information outside the case records covered by the transition. The supplied provisions establish no important continuing entitlement, substantial liability or sanction concerning that additional material.
impact_families.uncertainty: The additional information is unspecified; the case-focused context supports a narrower interpretation.

impact_families.title: Deletion may begin by 20 July 2025 rather than be completed
impact_families.effect: If the commencement reading prevailed, deletion could begin on 20 July 2025 while case information, including personal data, remained afterward without an express final deletion deadline.
impact_families.rationale: Replacing a completion deadline with a commencement requirement materially weakens the core duty to erase platform case information, including personal data.
impact_families.uncertainty: The closure context supports harmonization. Actual retention and its duration are not established.

impact_families.title: Italian retrieval assistance may cover additional accessible cases
impact_families.effect: A user with an ongoing case could request retrieval assistance concerning another case accessible to that user.
impact_families.rationale: The supported extension concerns an ancillary assistance duty. Neither this wording nor the surrounding provisions expressly creates an entitlement to otherwise restricted data.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 7 supports an own-case limitation; the supplied sources do not specify the applicable access controls.

impact_families.title: Latvian deletion duty may include non-case information
impact_families.effect: If the broader reading prevailed, any non-case information remaining in the platform would also have to be deleted by 20 July 2025.
impact_families.rationale: The identified additional duty concerns cleanup beyond case records. The sources establish no additional major change to dispute remedies or personal-data access rights.
impact_families.uncertainty: No particular non-case records are identified; contextual interpretation may narrow the wording.

impact_families.title: Slovenian may leave 20 March available for complaint submissions
impact_families.effect: If the Slovenian reading prevailed, a complaint could be submitted on 20 March when the English reading would already end submissions.
impact_families.rationale: The identified consequence is one additional day to use an intermediary for requesting voluntary ADR. The sources establish no loss of an underlying claim or substantive remedy.
impact_families.uncertainty: Interpretation may align the dates; submission does not guarantee trader agreement or dispute resolution.

impact_families.title: French notification wording may require notice on 20 March
impact_families.effect: If notification must occur on the specified day, the Commission could need to notify users on 20 March even after providing earlier notice.
impact_families.rationale: The difference concerns the timing of an administrative notification. It preserves retrieval assistance and does not itself shorten the contemplated four-month notice period.
impact_families.uncertainty: Recital 7 supports treating 20 March as the latest notification date.
